prompt: I keep getting distracted by trivial things during the day—how do I stop quitting God's conversation for trifles?
completion: Distraction is common, but the remedy is not anxious technique. Prayer is a humble waiting before God like a beggar, and when your mind wanders to trifles you simply recall it to His presence in tranquility, without disquiet. Do not imagine that ordinary work and neighbourly duty are obstacles; the trivial round and common task are the appointed means of self-denial and daily nearness to God. Yet the soul's true business is more than obliged forms: it is persevering in God's presence by simple attention and a fond regard, a silent secret conversation kept up through the day. So meet God in your duties, and beyond them keep that quiet attention turned toward Him, returning gently whenever you have quit His conversation for trifles.

prompt: I've been hindered from returning to friends I long to see—should I pray about something so ordinary as travel and open doors, or is that too small for God?
completion: Nothing is too small for God, and He is nearer than you think. But prayer is not mere sentiment; it is real business with a GOD who hears and answers. Bring the hindrances and open doors to Him specifically and expectantly, trusting His faithfulness for your needs, your safety, and the good of the souls you long to see. Yet this expectant prayer grows from holy habit: we need God's continual help, and praying, being with Him, and thinking of Him often are linked, because we must know Him before we can love Him. So let remembering and adoring Him become your habit in all business and diversions, not neglected. Speak with Him about the journey and the friends, and keep adoring Him, knowing He is always near and faithful to answer.

prompt: I spend so much time devising new methods and organizing programs for my church—am I neglecting the man you would have me be?
completion: Yes, it's worth asking—because God's method is men, not methods. Programs are machinery; the Holy Ghost flows through men, not plans. But the answer is not to withdraw into the heart and leave people behind, nor to throw yourself into prayerless activism that multiplies programs while neglecting prayer. You need not always be at church to be with God—you may make an oratory of your heart and converse with Him in meekness, humility, and love—yet that time with God is useful only as it is expended on men. So reject both the hermit's retreat and the popularizer's busyness. Keep your plans subordinate to the person God would have you be, and let your heart's converse with Him overflow into service, so that what flows through your church is the Spirit through persons, not the momentum of a program.

prompt: I work long hours at an ordinary job and have a family depending on me—can I find God without becoming a monk or nun or leaving my duties?
completion: Yes—you can find God right where you are, without becoming a monk or leaving your duties. The ordinary man or woman in usual everyday work or leisure can find Him, not by a life apart or conspicuous piety, but in faithfully doing what is at hand. Your long hours and family obligations are not obstacles; they are the very place where He is met. You need not abandon those depending on you, nor adopt a dramatic rule of life. Let the work of the Lord be carried on within the landmarks of His word: seek not the patronage of the world, appeal not to unbelievers for money, contract no debts, and depend not on fixed income or human support. The Living God alone is Patron, and prayer is the only appeal. Trust His blessing in answer to prayer, and simply turn toward Him in your work and home, and you will find Him there.

prompt: I want to be perfect as my heavenly Father is perfect—what does Christian perfection actually consist in?
completion: Christian perfection consists in holy love—love of God and neighbor—and such love must aspire to nothing less than perfection. Do not settle for a love content to remain imperfect or that treats shortfall as the norm. Seek constantly the perfection of holy love, aiming at the whole heart given to God and neighbor. Yet do not imagine that perfection depends on your striving alone or that your circumstances are obstacles; rest in the perfection of GOD's way and His minute care in forming your circumstances. Nor is perfection confined to the cloister: every lawful profession and state of life can be sanctified, and you need not leave your station to pursue it. Examine yourself, receive the sacraments, pray, and serve within the life He has given, letting all of it serve this one aim: a love pressing on toward perfection in whatever state you are called to.

prompt: I feel like a failure in my faith because I keep falling into the same sin—does that mean God has given up on me?
completion: No, God has not given up on you—and he does not look on you with blame, but with pity. This passing life does not ask you to live wholly without blame and sin; it asks you to keep turning back. Feelings are not the measure of your standing; his changeless word of promise is. So do not judge yourself by whether you feel forgiven or close to him. Each time you fall, rise again, and let that rising be an act of faith and love; repeated rising builds a habitual state of thinking of God. When joy is lacking, continue steadfastly in prayer and do not abandon communion or service. Confess honestly, renew your love, and rest in this: in falling and rising you are ever preciously kept in one Love.

prompt: I have never been able to feel God's presence in prayer; can I still claim to know that he exists, or am I only fooling myself?
completion: You are not fooling yourself simply because you do not feel God's presence. God understands all things and hears the innermost thoughts and secret prayers of the soul, just as human invention lets people communicate across great distances. So ask in faith, nothing wavering. Worship him in spirit and in truth, with an intelligence and will purified from every phantom of earth, entering the inmost chamber of the heart and shutting the door of the senses with a pure heart, a free conscience, and unfeigned faith. And be assured: our knowledge of God is partial, not exhaustive, yet real—we know substance through phenomena and the infinite as the absence of all limit. So do not measure prayer by feeling; enter the inner chamber and worship in spirit and truth.

prompt: What is the purpose for which I was created, and am I actually living for it?
completion: You were created to know, love, and serve God and to enjoy him forever, and to represent him to others. Begin with holy indifference to health or sickness, riches or poverty, honor or dishonor, and long or short life, desiring and choosing only what most leads to that end—an indifference concerning what is left to free will and not forbidden. Yet it is your first duty to preserve your life on earth by observing the laws of health and balancing labor, study, rest, and recreation, for the intelligence God gave you is first to know how to preserve the present organization. And live toward others as God would: dependable, true to your word, always giving, self-forgetful in love and blessing. Examine your time, energy, and money by that measure.

prompt: I am a poor servant girl and feel that my station makes me unfit to be a teacher of religion—can God really use someone like me?
completion: Yes, God can use someone like you—and your station is no exemption. Do not excuse yourself from service because your capacity or opportunity seems too small. Be faithful in the least, using the one talent and ordinary opportunity actually given, for God places solemn value on humble workers and littleness will not excuse us. In every occasion of virtue, turn to God for enabling grace, and receive strength more than sufficient. And do not think self-offering unrealistic: many helpers gave themselves and their goods to God's work without salary, believing he would supply all their need. Offer yourself and what you have cheerfully, in self-denying service, teaching by example, kindness, honesty, and ordinary words. Trust him to supply your need as you serve.

prompt: I keep rushing through my prayers and chores because I want to be perfect right away—how do I stop being so anxious about my progress?
completion: It is good that you want to grow, but hurry and anxiety will not make you perfect faster. Over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections, and anxious fretting is an obstacle to perfection. So keep yourself in God's presence throughout the day and renounce hurry. Remember that labor done for the love of God, with prayer for grace, becomes easy: do your chores for love of him, asking grace as you begin. And when a blessing is delayed, do not abandon prayer, set God a deadline, or treat long petition as pointless. Continue patiently, believingly, and importunately until the blessing is granted, without prescribing to God the time or manner of the answer—expecting the answer while you wait. Slow your prayers, work steadily, and trust his patience with you.

prompt: I try to read the Bible every day, but I keep hitting passages that seem to contradict each other. Should I just take the plain English at face value?
completion: Keep reading daily—this is right and good. The Holy Scriptures are the one fountain of all wisdom and strength; prefer the Bible above all other books, read it systematically and prayerfully, meditate on it, and translate it into obedience. Where passages seem to contradict, lay aside prejudice and ask simply what the testimony of Scripture is, submitting every matter to the Word and to the Holy Spirit as the only teacher. Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures serves as a key to the Scriptures; its honest study, with the Bible, enables you to prove all things. Let no tradition, custom, or human opinion settle what only the Word can settle. Let daily reading, meditation, and keyed study form the habit of your soul, and let what you learn be lived out in obedience.

prompt: I feel far from God after something I did, and I'm afraid to pray—how should I understand what has come between us?
completion: What has come between you is not God's absence but your own avoidance, and the remedy is to return at once. Continual help of God is needed, so do not wait until you feel worthy or until prayer feels easy. Praying, being with God, and thinking of Him often are linked through holy habit: we must know before we love, and knowledge grows by steady practice. Prayer has real effect—not as capricious interruptions of nature, but as the incoming of energy from beyond the margin of the normal self, working within the ordered life of the spirit. Bring even the smallest matter to God in prayer, honouring Him by asking His guidance rather than taking the matter out of His hands. Let confession and forgiveness be concrete, and let the daily habit of prayer rebuild what avoidance has broken.

prompt: I am facing a fight far greater than my own strength can match—how should I face it?
completion: A fight beyond your strength is real, but strength of character is not fixed by temperament—it is the will's power to control your actions independently of inclinations and the opinions of men. That power grows by repeated virtuous acts and diminishes by yielding to passions. So face this fight by forming habits: each small act of self-command is a self-victory, and progress is proportioned to those victories. Do not excuse yourself by temperament or by what others think. Never seek to gain by injuring another: wrong done to another returns upon the wrong-doer, while right adjusts the balance. And when miseries return, do not give up the fight or meet them with less courage than before—resume your arms and courage, and fight more valiantly than ever against the returning enemy.

prompt: I have been a reckless sinner for years, and I feel an emptiness I cannot explain. Is there any hope that God could receive someone like me?
completion: Yes, there is hope—but do not make light of sin, and do not buy comfort by denying evil, sickness, or pain; that denial is a narcotic, not a Redemption. Forgetting God should not cause disquiet; it should lead you back with greater trust. Yet one mortal sin unrepented is enough to damn the soul, and eternal loss is real. Nourish an intense and abiding fear of sin and of hell, so that fear may restrain you where love is too weak, and let it mature into love. Turn at once, with confidence in God's welcome, and walk the way of Redemption through heroism rather than cowardice: honest turning, concrete confession, and small faithful steps taken even when they cost you.

prompt: I keep feeling that something is chasing me—not a person, but a presence—and I keep running. What is happening to me?
completion: What you describe is not a threat to escape but a pursuit you have misread. The presence chasing you is the very One your soul is seeking; your flight is a misdirected seeking, not a sign of danger. Running never resolves the chase because the pursuer is what you most deeply want. Stop, turn, and listen: the Voice declares, I am He Whom thou seekest. This is not a vague, formless outreach but actual social fellowship with a personal Friend—defined by the God whom we know as Father through His human revelation in Christ. Pass lightly over the pain; do not dwell in it or follow it with mourning. Hold to comfort and sure trust in God's keeping in both woe and weal, and let that defined communion end the flight.

prompt: I prayed for something for three years and God never gave it to me—does that mean my prayers don't work?
completion: Three years of praying without the answer you sought is not a small thing, but it must not be smoothed over or turned into mere pleading. Prayer is not a way to inform the infinite Mind or persuade God to change His mind; the Science of being is unchangeable, and prayer does not alter it. Prayer is humbling work that crucifies pride and signs our bankruptcy, and it is unselfed love and spiritual understanding that bring us into harmony with the unchangeable Principle. Little praying is a worse evil than no praying, a deluding make-believe. Yet do not sink into discouragement. God offers grace at each action unless we forget to ask, so come with confidence, relying not on your own worthiness but on Christ's merits. Ask, not to bend God's will, but to receive the grace already offered, and let your disappointment drive you to love more purely and understand more truly.

prompt: I was disappointed when Christ did not come as I expected; should I now believe he has come in spirit and that this is all we shall ever see of him here?
completion: Disappointment when Christ does not come as we expected is real, but it must not be soothed with the false comfort that all will be well later. If we do not find Christ here, the soul does not simply wait for comfort after death; it enters a dark, lonely, and self-tormenting state, cut off from the light it refused to receive. The remedy must be found now. Yet do not treat Christ's words as merely historical, belonging only to the past. His words are spirit and life, applicable to all time, and they come to us still brightened with that same spirit and life. Do not seek power as your own possession. Receive the Holy Spirit within and upon you, letting Him be the power that causes you to walk in God's statutes, with no power of your own. So seek him now, not as a figure locked in history but as the living Word present to every age.

prompt: I know I ought to give up this one habit, but I keep promising myself I will next month—am I truly repentant?
completion: Recognizing that the habit ought to be given up is good, but promising yourself 'next month' again and again is not repentance—it is delay dressed as intention. Sin consists in doing wrong when we know and can do better. The sin of ignorance is winked at, but once we learn a thing is wrong we must refrain from it immediately and forever. You already know this habit is wrong, so 'next month' is disobedience postponed. Yet do not despair: it is not desperate to have been wounded, but to neglect the cure. Repent now, and take up the cure. Confess your faults and humble yourself before God, for humility and confession help to still wandering thoughts, while many words in prayer often cause the mind to wander. Keep your prayer simple and your confession honest. One who has fallen may rise again, as wrestlers and soldiers have risen after a fall, so rise today rather than waiting for next month.

prompt: I cannot bring myself to believe that this table would still exist if no one were in the room—am I being unreasonable?
completion: You are not unreasonable to trust that the table remains when no one is in the room, but be careful how you dwell on such questions. Thinking too much can overcome the tabernacle and derange the whole organization; endless speculation can unsettle mind and body together. The spirit is the intelligent part of man and can labor to excess, destroying the equilibrium, so those who think much should labor with their bodies, and both should work together for health and strength. Nor suppose that matter or intelligence can be annihilated or become nothing: element is eternal and cannot be annihilated, and no organized being remains stationary—all must increase or decrease. Above all, do not permit the perishable things of this world to swerve you in the least degree from fidelity to the truth, for to be so swerved shows we lack knowledge we ought to possess. Hold the truth firmly and let your life move forward in knowledge and labor.

prompt: Why does the world seem so full of confusion and misery when God's works are so orderly?
completion: Confusion and misery are real, but they do not come from any disorder in God's works; they come from how we use what God has entrusted to us. Time and the ability to labor are capital given by God, and we are stewards of them, not owners. Our acts, words, and thoughts will be brought into judgment. Yet do not lower God's standard to excuse our failure. His commandments and promises are not discounted to fit our weakness; the standard remains inflexibly high, and we must refuse to bring it down to our failures, pressing on until we reach His highest will. This does not require an outward flight to rags and desert, nor a divided allegiance of soul to God and heart to the world. It requires an undivided inward fidelity of heart, will, and mind, placing God first in the exact circumstances of life in which we find ourselves.

prompt: I feel spiritually dry even though I believe in Jesus—why don't I experience the Spirit's power?
completion: Spiritual dryness is common, but the deeper question is whether you are asking for power to enjoy or power to obey. The fullness of the Spirit is not given for private comfort; it is given along the line of duty, as we obey Christ's command to make disciples of all nations. God will not give His power for selfish enjoyment. So do not demand a spiritual experience as a prize; accept whatever God chooses, in quiet submission, without curiosity or craving. Yet do not despise inward experience: the Spirit still speaks, but His inward voice is tested by the supreme revelation of the ages—the written Word and the gospel of Christ—and that history is quickened as you respond in immediate obedience. Take the next step Christ sets before you, and let Scripture, not mood, interpret what you feel.

prompt: I feel spiritually dry and empty—how do I get filled with the Holy Spirit again?
completion: Feeling dry and empty can be a sign that you are only breathing in and never breathing out. The Spirit fills those who empty themselves; there must be a vacuum for Him to fill. So learn to breathe out as well as in: look at the needs near you—the lonely, the unsaved, the hurting—and treat them as vacuums waiting for the Spirit to fill through you. Remember that the Spirit is not a private resource but the life of the Spirit-bearing body, the Church, who consecrates ordinary nature and works gradually and socially among His people while intensifying your personal character. And know that not to advance is to go back: keep pressing forward in obedience. When storms rise within, call on the Lord present within you, and He will calm the soul's tempest.

prompt: I keep praying for God to change my circumstances, but nothing seems to happen—am I praying the wrong way?
completion: It is not wrong to bring your circumstances to God, but the deeper prayer is not that circumstances be adjusted to you—it is that you be adjusted by God to His plan and to the people around you. Ask Him to fit you into every good work, to your surroundings, to those you live among, and to His purposes. In that adjustment you will find rest, power, and freedom. Learn to change places and occupations without changing your love or its object, equally for God in all things. And do not excuse neglect of prayer because you lack the spirit of prayer: keep your appointed times, pray with your family, and remember that prayer asks us to help God accomplish what we seek, not to expect Him to do it all while we sit idle.

prompt: How may I come to the Supersensual Life, so that I may see God and hear God speak?
completion: The desire to see God and hear Him speak is good, but you will not reach it by your own thinking, willing, reasoning, or striving—these are the very things that hinder the seeing and hearing of God. Cease from self-thinking and self-willing. Stand still and silent before God, and become passive to the Eternal Word and Spirit. Do not think your secret prayers are lost: God, who understands all things, hears the innermost thoughts and supplication of the soul, just as human invention lets people speak across great distances. So ask in faith, nothing wavering. But know the price of these high mysteries: extraordinary lowliness, loneliness of spirit, and the drying up of ordinary interests, because God wills to have the whole of you.

prompt: I feel guilty for being happy when others around me are miserable—should I stop enjoying myself?
completion: Guilt over happiness is not from God. The desire for happiness is God-given, and God is to be found here in this world—this world is the Touchstone and Finding-place for Him. So you need not stop enjoying yourself; let your joy be a place where you find God. Yet do not make feelings or sensible enjoyment the measure of your standing with Him, for feelings never accurately gauge our real assimilation to God. Rest on the changeless word of promise rather than on variable moods; when joy is lacking, continue steadfastly in prayer and service. And beware the living death of pleasure-seeking: do not go into debt for fashionable display, and refuse the hunt for pleasure that leads to cheating, lying, and corrupted morals.

prompt: I keep seeking rest in things I love here, and nothing satisfies me—why can't I find ease of heart?
completion: Your restlessness is not a problem to be analyzed but a sign pointing to God Himself, and the desire for happiness in you is God-given, not a fault to be suppressed. Stop gazing back at your own seeking and fix your heart on Him who is lovable above all, delighting to please Him rather than measuring your own performance. He is not found only in the next world: this world is the Touchstone and Finding-place for Him, nearer than your own restlessness. Receive the things you love here as gifts that carry your affection to the Giver, and expect ease of heart in Him now. When trials come, be patient with them, accepting them as God's permission to reveal what you are when left to yourself, and become indifferent to serving Him amid thorns or roses alike, since His love is the same in both.

prompt: Should I use force to stop someone who is doing wrong, or should I simply endure it?
completion: Begin with the law written into things: wrong done to another returns upon the wrong-doer, and right adjusts the balance. You never truly gain by injuring another; the injury recoils on the one who inflicts it. So ask not whether force might profit you, but what is right, trusting that right restores the balance while wrong punishes itself. Yet do not confuse patience with tolerating evil: resist wrong of every sort firmly, for error is opposed to Life and will flee before Truth. Refuse to submit to or compromise with wrongdoing; appeal, warning, and lawful authority are truer means than violence, but where evil must be opposed, oppose it to the end. And begin with yourself: promptly confess and forsake even small sins, abandon questionable practices at once, and give thanks for every mercy of God, cultivating obedience and gratitude.

prompt: I prayed for years for my son's conversion and see no change—should I keep pleading until GOD answers?
completion: Yes, keep praying, but let prayer be the place where you learn God's will rather than a technique for forcing a result. Bring even this smallest and most painful matter to the Lord, asking counsel of His oracles before you undertake anything, and wait until His guidance is clear, since only so can you be blessed in your own soul and prospered in the work of your hands. Pray especially for strength to suffer with courage, humility, and love, and cultivate familiar conversation with God, watching over your thoughts, words, and deeds, for that watchful fellowship brings the peace of paradise even now. And let your prayer be a total self-oblation without secret exceptions: ask, 'Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?' and keep nothing back in your heart—not the outcome, not your son, not your own terms. Surrender all to God, love your son without pressure, and do not measure His faithfulness by visible change.

prompt: I have committed the same grave sin again and again for years; can I still turn to Mary, or have my sins made me unworthy of her help?
completion: Your repeated sin is serious, but it has not made you unworthy of Mary's help, for she is the mother of penitent sinners. She turns her eyes of mercy toward all, beholding our miseries with compassion and relieving them—the just and sinners alike who seek her aid. She receives with mercy any sinner who comes with the intention to amend, embraces the returning child, heals his wounds, and reconciles him to God. She asks only a good intention to amend, not that you be worthy first. True devotion, however, means honoring and invoking her, trusting her intercession, imitating her virtues, and truly intending to amend—never presuming on her mercy while continuing in sin. So come honestly, confess, resolve to change, examine what triggers the pattern, and seek help from a confessor. She will lead you back to her Son.

prompt: How can I find comfort this Christmas when the war makes the angels' song of peace seem mocked?
completion: It is understandable that the war makes the angels' song seem mocked, but lift your eyes: God's goodness still gives the stars, the woods, the harvest, love, and sleep to all. These are His gifts, available even in want, and war does not mock them. So dry your eyes and take comfort. Cherish pity too: see the poor children as flowers of London town raising innocent hands, and beware lest you drive an angel from your door. Yet do not think the weary soul is abandoned or ordinary consolations worthless—Christ is at hand beside the weary, with healing, turning earth's worst and least into a royal feast and strewing your common paths with pensive hope. Grieve honestly, pray for peace, and let small charities make peace concrete. The first Christmas came amid occupation and fear, and the song was sung then too—a promise, not a taunt.

prompt: I feel my thoughts wandering during prayer no matter how hard I try to keep them still—what can I do?
completion: Wandering thoughts in prayer are usually the overflow of a mind allowed to wander everywhere else. Begin by guarding your thoughts through the day, keeping them in God's presence at work and in quiet moments; but above all, treat your prayer as a retreat in which deep recollection is required. During it, avoid unnecessary intercourse with the world—idle conversation, news, business, and curiosity—for such things scatter the heart. Let 'God and I' be the only objects of your thought. And since prayer must be your main assistant in every step of progress, ask God earnestly to enable you to search out and discover your own heart and to reform whatever is amiss in it. A mind thus guarded and a heart thus laid open will grow calm and recollected, and distraction will lose its hold.

prompt: I go to work every day and feel like my job has nothing to do with my religion—should I try to bring my faith into my daily work?
completion: Yes—and the test is concrete. Faith must be demonstrated in works and spiritual understanding, and each must work out his own salvation; another's goodness or suffering cannot lessen your own liability. That working out shows most plainly in your craft: Saints should increase in goodness until their mechanics are so honest and reliable that an employer prefers them for engineers, watchmen, clerks, and managers, and if they are not so preferred it proves they do not live their religion. Yet remember who works: God is the one living Agent, and you are only His instrument. Cast all your care upon Him, and treat anxious self-reliance about being preferred as distrust of Him. Do your work faithfully, and let Him give the increase.

prompt: I have grown up in the Church, but the faith of my childhood no longer satisfies me—how can I know the certainty of the things I was taught?
completion: It is normal for a childhood faith to feel inadequate as you grow, but do not tie your faith to any particular scientific or philosophical theory; faith uses current knowledge as an instrument without identifying with any theory, free to readjust as knowledge advances. More importantly, faith in Jesus Christ is the foundation of hope for remission of sins, resurrection, and exaltation, and the doctrines restored through Joseph Smith confirm and establish belief in His divine mission. Yet faith must be demonstrated in works and spiritual understanding, not merely professed. Each must work out his own salvation, and another's suffering cannot lessen your own liability. So study, pray, keep the commandments, and let your questions drive you deeper into Christ and into a life that proves what you believe.

prompt: I keep meaning to read something spiritually profitable, but I always reach for novels instead; is that really so harmful to my soul?
completion: Reaching for novels instead of spiritual reading is more serious than a private preference. Parents and pastors have a charge to guard the young from corrupting books and to supply them with pious ones; if you have any such care, examine what is put into young hands, exclude what corrupts, and provide good reading in its place. For yourself, neglect of pious reading endangers salvation, and frivolous or worldly books corrupt the mind, nourishing a worldly spirit. Assiduous pious reading is a necessary help to virtue. So limit yourself to legitimate employments, and refuse the curiosity, ambition, and restlessness that create more impediments than works. Set a daily time for Scripture and good books before you open a novel, and let your reading feed the soul rather than the world.

prompt: I wake up each morning feeling like nothing has changed—how can I see God's mercies as new every morning?
completion: It is easy to feel that mornings are just more of the same, but that feeling is not the truth. Each new day is proof of God's unfailing love: new mercies hover around you while you pray, and fresh forgiveness meets you every morning. Yet the day is also a test. God is looking for tested pattern men, and all our experiences come as tests watched by His jealous love; every step is decisive for our eternal future. So do not excuse morning listlessness as a mood—it is an index of a listless heart. The soul following hard after God seeks Him early, with ardor and not mere routine. Rise to meet the day as one watched by a loving Father, and choose to overcome rather than disappoint Him.

prompt: I am so sinful that I am afraid the Lord will not accept me—how can I be sure He will receive me?
completion: Your fear comes from counting your sins, but God does not count as we count. All things are possible to Him: it is as easy for Him to forgive and blot out innumerable and heinous sins as to forgive one. Of ourselves we cannot even think what is right, since all comes to us from God. The only way out of sin's misery is to cease from sin; take courage and forsake it, not from dread of punishment, but because it is good and manly to do so. And do not doubt God's look. He looks upon you with love, as He looks with love upon the most terrible sinner who has any true desire to be converted. Trust His goodness toward the repentant, and come to Him.

prompt: I'm twenty and the world feels like an ocean opening at my feet—should I chase fame and love far from home, or stay near my mother who weeps when I speak of leaving?
completion: The world opening at your feet is a fine sight, but beware the dreamer's error: to leave home and a weeping mother for fame and love is a poor bargain, since life enfolds many ills and the home you leave may never be seen again. Yet our life is not merely the life of roses and leaves; the longings Nature moves in us promise their own fulfillment. So do not sink upon a bed of sloth, and do not let intoxication overcome you. Rise and begin a voyage across the clear sea, that you may reach the Land of Women—go with courage and clear eyes, not in a dream.

prompt: I have been taught the gospel all my life, but I have never had a vision or a sign—should I doubt my testimony because of that?
completion: Visions and signs are not given to everyone, and their absence does not mean your testimony is false. The evangelists were competent and honest witnesses whose testimony cost them worldly interests; imposture must have a motive, and they had none. Besides the records and witnesses, the Spirit of God bears record in the heart of the living Redeemer, and that witness exceeds all other evidence. Do not demand mathematical proof of Scripture facts. Ask only whether the testimony is probably true, and hold it proved when established by the kind and degree of evidence that would satisfy a common man in ordinary affairs—evidence that satisfies an unprejudiced mind beyond reasonable doubt.

prompt: I feel that my faith has become a matter of reciting correct doctrines rather than a living trust in God; how should I understand the relation between the Gospel and dogma?
completion: Keep two standards distinct. Compare dogma with the Gospel where possible: does it faithfully express the good news of what God has done in Christ? And judge dogma by the historical conditions of its time, without mixing the two. Faith in Jesus Christ is the foundation of hope for remission of sins, resurrection, and exaltation; the doctrines restored through Joseph Smith confirm and establish belief in His divine mission. Understand dogma, then, as Harnack defines it: the product of the Greek spirit working on the soil of the Gospel. It preserves both the Christian content—monotheism and the significance of Christ—and the philosophic form. Neither despise the form nor forget the soil from which it grew.

prompt: I find my old arguments for God from design in nature collapsing under evolutionary science—does that mean my faith was false all along?
completion: Do not fear that science has undone your faith. Our religion will not clash with or contradict the facts of science; its leading principles are eternal facts. God never made something out of nothing—He organized the earth from existing matter. Nor is man a fallen being needing to regain a lost state: the relation of God and man is indestructible, with no lapse from harmony and no return to it. If reason itself should be traced to matter, theology would have nothing to fear from such a result. The Creator may have worked otherwise than we thought, but that is covered by the words "in Him was life." So be without alarm.

prompt: How can I build a habit of continually conversing with God instead of only praying at set times?
completion: Building continual conversation with God takes intention, but it begins with the continual help of God, which we must ask for. Praying, being with God, and thinking of Him often are linked through holy habit, and since we must know before we love, let your thinking of Him be fed by knowing Him in Scripture and the faith. Learn from the holy pastors: they made retirement and a life of prayer their apprenticeship, and afterward, amid its functions, remained men of prayer, with God always present to their mind, setting apart intervals in the day and much of the night to attend to Him in the silence of all creatures. And remember that God is always near: He should be remembered and adored in all times, in business and even in diversions, never neglected. So keep your intervals of silence, and carry His presence into everything.

prompt: How can I be sure I'm actually being guided by God and not just following my own preference?
completion: You can be confident of guidance, for God promises to lead those who seek Him. Seek it in prayer, expecting an answer, and test your leading by the agreement of God's Spirit, the counsels and principles of His Word, and His Providence in daily circumstances. Yet do not hurry or fret—over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections. Keep yourself in God's presence and let anxiety go. When hindrances appear, do not treat them as reasons to scheme or worry; wait meekly before God with your hands off the scales, trusting Him to sway your judgment and remove obstacles in His own way and time. Apparent hindrances are occasions for His interposition, not causes for fear. In that meek waiting you will know His guidance.

prompt: My sermon was polished and well received, but I felt nothing in it. What is wrong with me?
completion: Emptiness after a polished sermon may signal that your ministry has become words without demonstration. Christianity is Truth practised and demonstrated, proving its power by the destruction of sin, sickness, and death. Do not settle for theory, however eloquent; let sin be destroyed in you and the power of God be evident in your life. Examine your routine too: sermon-making, study, and diligence are not enough to keep your spirit in trim—sermon-making without prayer can harden and estrange the heart, and much prayer is needed to keep your spirit in harmony with your calling. But do not make feelings the measure of whether prayer is heard or whether you are right with God. Feelings never accurately gauge real assimilation to God. Rest on the changeless word of promise, continue steadfastly in prayer when joy is lacking, and refuse to abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression.

prompt: I want to find God but I don't want to become conspicuously pious or peculiar in front of others. Is that possible?
completion: Yes, it is possible. You need not abandon your ordinary work, family duties, or normal life to find God. The ordinary man or woman in usual everyday work or leisure can find Him without a life apart, without conspicuous piety, and without leaving undone duties to those dependent on them. God is found in faithfulness to the tasks and relationships already given you. When you fail, confess your faults to God without excuse and without discouragement, then peaceably resume the practice of love and adoration. And do not treat the difficulties of this quiet pursuit merely as problems to escape: expect GOD to reveal Himself as a present help in trouble, and let those very difficulties deepen your knowledge of Him.

prompt: How can I remain at peace when I hear about wars, scandals, and troubles in the world?
completion: Remain always at peace, for peace is the passport of the daughters of Jesus Christ. When you hear of wars, scandals, and troubles, do not let disturbance rule you. Be patient with others and equally patient with yourself. Make no account of the judgments or good opinion of men; esteem them as nothing and endure them silently, finding interior peace in that endurance. Yet do not seek peace by avoiding what stirs you. Exercise sweetness and charity in spite of repugnance and disgust—pray for those the news disturbs you about, and meet the unpleasant with kindness. Peace is won through conquest, not through avoiding combat; by charity in the face of disgust you conquer unrest and keep the calm that marks those who belong to Christ.

prompt: I'm going through a time of deep depression and feel utterly alone in the dark—is God still with me there?
completion: I'm sorry you're in that dark place. Hear this first: you are not abandoned. God is with you in the dark, closer than your feelings tell you, and He alone is the portion and satisfaction your soul is seeking. Abandon yourself wholly to Him there—not to your emotions, not to fixing yourself, not to anything created. Do not be anxious about distractions or about making every moment a conscious offering; walk with Him in quiet simplicity, turning your heart to Him as you are able, and do your ordinary work and rest for Him without strain. Let your one absorbing aim be to glorify Him in complete surrender to His will. Cry out as David and Job did; receive help from others as His gift, not as a substitute for Him. He holds you.

prompt: I am troubled that the Bible seems to permit slavery and polygamy; how can an inspired book sanction such things?
completion: This is a fair and serious question. The Bible records and regulates slavery and polygamy as realities in ancient cultures, but regulation is not endorsement; Scripture's trajectory moves toward the New Testament's call to love neighbor and treat others as equals in Christ. On marriage, ethical considerations must guide and restrict the intention to marry: improvident marriage is immoral, not neutral, and substitutes for rational self-restraint are to be condemned. Love is not mere sentiment; it is the outgoing of the entire nature in self-sacrificing service, the supreme proof of the reality of Christian profession. Here is the deeper answer: the New Testament's moral system is comprehensive, spiritual, simple, and practical, running counter to men's natural passions, and it surpasses human powers of invention. A system so pure and perfect must have had a supernatural and therefore divine origin—which is exactly what inspiration means.

prompt: I have been chasing a promotion and more money for years. Is that what I am for?
completion: That's a good question, and the fact that you're asking it suggests you already sense the answer isn't simply 'more.' Ambition isn't evil—working hard and providing for family are good—but do not pray for riches or make wealth a proper object of prayer. Pray only for the means to keep yourself and your family from want, and do not hurry frantically after wealth; be calm, contented, and patiently diligent. Receive blessings the appointed way: attend your meetings, pray, read the scriptures, and meditate, keeping your dish right side up for the shower of blessings. Beware the living death of pleasure-seeking: do not go into debt for fashionable display, and remember that the hunt for pleasure leads to cheating, lying, and corrupted morals. When money and status become the goal they never satisfy; you were made for God and neighbor. Ask whether your work serves those ends or has replaced them.

prompt: My parents are old and ignorant of the things of God, and I have been converted while they have not—what is my duty toward them?
completion: This is a tender and difficult situation. Your duty is to honor your parents—that command doesn't expire—while being faithful to what you now believe. Honor means patience, respect, and practical care, especially as they age; it does not mean hiding your faith, but sharing it with gentleness and without contempt. Parents and pastors are charged to guard the young from corrupting books and to supply pious reading, and that responsibility is real wherever souls are formed. But do not rely on your own judgment: God directs souls through the ministers He has appointed, so learn His will through them and set aside presumption. Above all, remember that conversion is not produced by human persuasion, technique, or effort but by the almighty power of the HOLY GHOST. Your great need as a worker is to know GOD; pray for your parents, let your life speak, care for their needs, and leave the outcome to Him.

prompt: I have a big decision next month and I can't stop worrying about what might go wrong—should I keep planning for every possibility?
completion: It's understandable to want to plan before a big decision, and some planning is wise—gather the facts, list the real risks, and talk to people you trust. But planning for every possibility is impossible, and waiting to settle every question before you move will only paralyze you. At some point you must cut the Gordian knot with the sword of decision. Launch out into the deep with a bold plunge, using the light you already have, and leave the speculations to Christ. Do not fixate on dates and timing or assume everything will unfold slowly as in former times; trust that God will cut His work short in righteousness, and prepare yourself for events that are hastening. And do not anticipate future accidents with fear: await them with perfect hope, trusting that God, whose child you are, will deliver you according as they come. Set a fixed time to plan, then act, and release what you cannot control.

prompt: I'm not a scholar and I don't know Greek or Hebrew. Does that mean I can never really understand the Bible?
completion: No. Much of Scripture's obscurity lies not in the languages but in the will, for we resist what it shows us. Jesus said that anyone willing to do God's will shall know the teaching; obedience, not expertise, is the organ of spiritual knowledge. Greek and Hebrew are useful preliminaries, but they cannot give what only a surrendered heart receives. Consider also its unity: some forty writers across seventeen centuries, of very different rank, speak with one spirit and aim concerning Christ. That cannot be explained by collusion or chance; it points to a superhuman guiding mind. Yet we should be frank: no one masters all of it, and much remains beyond us. Read in a good translation, pray, do what you understand, and the humble will find enough to know and enjoy God.

prompt: Does it matter whether Jesus really lived in history, or is the inward Christ enough?
completion: Yes, it matters. The inward Christ is the continuation of the revelation God made in the historical Jesus, not a substitute for him. Acquaintance with the Jesus of history is the supreme education of the soul: his character, words, and obedience unto death train the heart as nothing else can. Yet the inward must govern the outward, and Jesus alone is to be chosen as Heaven in weal and woe. We should also examine the early testimonies honestly: the first witnesses, their plain reports, their readiness to suffer, and their sudden proclamation of a crucified Messiah. These features are best explained from the faith that Jesus is Messiah, risen and Lord, not by imposing a later dogmatic scheme on them. Read the Gospels, weigh the earliest testimony, and let the inward Christ make that history live.

prompt: My enemies outnumber me and I am afraid; is there any aid for me?
completion: Yes, there is aid. Count your enemies rightly: the greatest are within. Outward foes touch only the body, while passion and unchecked weakness can ruin the soul. So first conquer yourself, submit to the Father's will, and then oppose error and evil by persuasion, patience, and love unfeigned, without violence or interfering with the agency of others. Beware the enemy's false dread, which whispers that you are too wretched to behold God; that is his device to drive you from your Everlasting Friend. Do not leave the blissful beholding of him. And if you fall, do not count it his final victory: rise by charity and meekness, and his gain becomes his own sorrow. Trust God, seek help where danger is real, and keep your heart before the Lord.

prompt: I am a leader, and I have been tempted to use funds designated for one part of the work to meet another pressing need. What should I do?
completion: Do not use designated funds for another purpose without proper authorization; that breaks trust and damages the work's integrity. If a need is pressing, bring it openly to your board and those responsible. But do not turn to personal solicitation or collections, and do not rely on pressure or on guaranteed incomes. Leave your hearers burdened before God to ask what he would have them do, and depend on voluntary contributions sent without solicitation. Nor should the work be carried on by borrowed money or debt when funds are lacking; trust God alone for supplies and refuse to go beyond what he provides. I can testify that God supplies all need. Integrity in small matters protects the whole work and honors him.

prompt: I believe in God, but I am afraid that if I give in to Him I will lose everything else I love. Is that fear justified?
completion: That fear is understandable, but love God fervently and without servile fear, trusting that he does not wish to harm you but to do you great good. He is not a rival to what is good in your loves; he is their source and center. Jesus said whoever loses life for his sake finds it. Yet do not make light of eternal loss: one mortal sin unrepented is enough to damn the soul, and an abiding fear of sin and of eternal loss should be nourished, so that fear may restrain us where love is too weak. Remember that God never forsakes us until we first forsake him. So fear to leave him, and remain always in his presence; he will keep what you entrust to him.

prompt: How do I know whether an answer to prayer was really from God or just happened anyway?
completion: This is a common and honest question. Scripture sets conditions for prevailing prayer: humility, forsaking known sin, faith without doubting, obedience, and asking in Christ's name according to God's will (2 Chronicles 7:14; James 4:3; 1 John 5:14). Where sin or unbelief are cherished, prayer is hindered, so examine your heart and repent where needed. Yet prayer is not an occasional transaction or a mere verbal exercise; it is like breathing or feeding—the constant, often unconscious drawing in of the heavenly life from without, which nourishes the seed of the Divine Life within. Real prayer opens the soul to an actual incoming of help from beyond the margin of the normal self, and its effects belong to the ordered life of the spirit rather than capricious interruptions of nature. So pray continually, look for fruit—gratitude, humility, love—keep a record, seek trusted counsel, and trust that God genuinely responds to those who ask aright.

prompt: My church teaches that the kingdom of heaven is the visible church. Is that what Christ established on earth?
completion: This is an important question. The kingdom of heaven is not the visible church, and Christ has not yet set up his everlasting kingdom on the earth. He taught his disciples to pray, 'Thy kingdom come,' which means his people still wait and pray for it. The visible church is a body of professed believers and an instrument in God's hands, but it is not itself the kingdom; the kingdom is God's own reign, inaugurated in Christ's first coming and to be fully established at his return. Nor does it come by human organization, legislation, or moral persuasion. It must be revealed from heaven: an angel restores the everlasting gospel as a warning to all nations, a Zion is built up, and judgments prepare the way for Christ's reign. Yet this revelation is not reserved for the learned or the great. Christ was first announced to lowly shepherds, and Heaven in mercy will guide even the simplest and homeliest heart to where He dwells. So seek Him humbly, trust His guidance, and join God's people in waiting and praying for the kingdom to come.

prompt: I have been deeply convicted of sin for years but never found peace; what am I missing?
completion: Long-lasting conviction without peace is painful, and it deserves honest attention. Do not rush to soothe it away. Conviction from God calls you to face justice and truth honestly—naming your sin plainly without excusing or concealing it. Confess it specifically to God and, where needed, to those you have wronged; make restitution and change what can be changed. Be clear about the gospel: the curse is disobedience, not obedience; transgression brought the curse. Christ was made a curse for us on the tree, bearing that curse in our place, and He has thereby loosed us from sin so that we need not sin any more. Redemption is not liberty to keep sinning but freedom from sin's bondage. Beware of treating unrepented sin lightly: sin accumulates, and a guilty conscience repeatedly ignored hardens the heart and destroys the ability to do right. So repent and reform without delay, talk with a pastor or trusted counselor who will help you be truthful, keep engaging Scripture, prayer, and community, and let honesty, not denial, be the path toward peace.

prompt: If everything I know is always matter plus my own mind, how can I be sure there is any matter at all?
completion: This is a classic question, and it deserves a careful answer. Notice first that everything you know comes as matter-plus-mind: sensations, and also the spatial relations between things. But relations no less than sensations imply a mind which knows them; space, order, and connection are not self-existing stuff. Matter, then, has no existence of its own apart from a mind which knows it. What we call the material world is a mode of experience, not a substance standing alone. This does not mean nothing is real; it means reality is fundamentally mental or spiritual in character. Further, the senses of Mind are never lost, and matter has no sensation of its own; what appears as loss of limb or sense is a belief to be overcome, not a final fact. Here is the scientific statement of being: there is no life, truth, intelligence, nor substance in matter. All is infinite Mind and its infinite manifestation, and man is spiritual, not material. So the question 'is there any matter at all?' can be answered: not as an independent thing-in-itself, but as the orderly appearance presented to Mind.

prompt: If human governments have failed for so long, why should I trust any new political movement to fix things?
completion: Your skepticism is understandable given the long record of failed governments. History shows that political movements often overpromise and underdeliver, and institutions can be captured by self-interest. But the deeper issue is that self-government is the root of all true government. External laws can only do so much; a people who cannot govern themselves will not be well governed by any scheme, however clever. Rulers, too, should be wiser and better than the governed—fit to lead by character, not merely by office. And when the work repels us, when natural repugnance rises and the time seems lost, we must not be discouraged; we must persevere to death through natural repugnance and apparent lost time. Yet we must also be honest: the proposed human means are not commensurate with the end. The fountain being impure, the streams must be impure, and every religious, political, or social scheme that claims to regenerate the world by human power must fail as such schemes always have. So cultivate self-government, judge leaders by character, persevere in duty—but do not put your trust in any movement to redeem what only a higher power can renew.

prompt: Is the Holy Spirit just an influence or force, or is he actually a person I can relate to?
completion: The Holy Spirit is not merely a force or influence but a divine Person, co-equal with the Father and the Son. Jesus called him the Paraclete, the Comforter sent in his name, who teaches, reminds, convicts, and guides. Because he is a person, you can genuinely relate to him: he speaks, commands, and leads, and Scripture warns that he can be grieved and quenched. Yet he is not a private inward influence set against the Church or the body; he is the life of the Spirit-bearing body, consecrating nature and grace together, working gradually and socially among believers while deepening personal character. So yield to the gentle Dove-Spirit, letting him subdue every coarse and harsh habit and make your life gentle like Christ's. Listen quietly, welcome his guidance, and honor him as God among his people.

prompt: What does it mean to have my life given 'for a prey' in hard places?
completion: Having your life given 'for a prey' does not mean being removed from the noise of battle or the presence of foes. It means God preserves your life in the face of continual pressure, like a prize held safe in the midst of danger. He spreads a table before you in the presence of your enemies and is a fortress amid the foe, a help when you are pressed out of measure. Yet this is no warrant for trusting the crowd or the broad way; rather, flee the dangers of the world and secure your one necessary affair, remembering that the gate of life is narrow and the multitude perishes. And do not imagine you must first change your circumstances—home, marital state, or wealth. Undergo the whole process just where you find yourself, in your own home or another's, married or single, rich or poor, with obedience, patience, and simplicity.

prompt: I am a mother with young children and want to know how to care for their illnesses.
completion: When your children seem unwell, do not fix your attention on symptoms or name the disease. Avoid talking illness; instead hold before the child only health and harmony. Speak of strength and wholeness rather than of fevers and complaints, and let your calm confidence surround the child with peace. Refrain from expecting things to grow worse; expect rather that health is the true order and that harmony will be restored. Yet remember that a mother who takes tea, coffee, liquor, and narcotics while bearing a family lays the foundation of weakness, nervous affections, and disease in her offspring from the cradle to the grave; if she does injury to her child, she sins. So guard your own system, and teach your children early the truths of health and holiness, excluding sinful and diseased thoughts from their minds, tending them gently with rest, nourishment, and quiet.

prompt: How is it that such a one can get his good friends into his possession?
completion: A person gets good friends into his possession not by utility or self-assurance but by rightly ordered love. Trust in God can never be excessive, and the love of friends must never encroach on the principal love due to God. When God holds first place, friendship is purified and becomes a real possession rather than a mere convenience. So do not stand in your own opinion as though it could not err; invite friendly conference, offer your gifts and knowledge in love, and try things one with another, holding that which is best. And since all friendship is gathered into friendship with Christ, form the habit of brief mental pictures of the Saviour: walk beside him, join his daily life, and ask what he would do, look, and think. This takes deliberate effort, but in that order friends are truly gained and safely kept.

prompt: My anger at a friend is eating me alive because I never told them. What should I do?
completion: Anger that is never expressed can be very painful, so it is understandable that you feel eaten alive. But do not try to manage it with smiles, tears, or deceitful wiles, hiding your wrath behind a pleasant face. Telling wrath openly ends it, while concealing it lets it grow into a poison tree that bears harm. So go to your friend and speak the truth in love, naming the injury plainly and without cruelty. Remember that it is good to hold on to an old friend; no matter how many new friends you have, hold fast to the old, and let only wicked conduct break the thread of fellowship. And when rebellious murmurings or sudden impatience rise within you, compel your heart to suffer tranquilly and to remain kind to your neighbor despite them.

prompt: I accuse myself overmuch, thinking all my tribulation and woe is my own fault—is that right?
completion: Do not accuse yourself overmuch, for our Lord wills not that you be indiscreetly heavy. Howsoever you do, you shall have woe; so see your penance wisely, and count all your living penance profitable. Yet lay the axe at the root of the tree of self: self-denial is not the lopping off of a few branches while self-will and self-glory remain, but a voluntary renunciation taken up for Christ's sake. And when you fall, see your wretchedness meekly for a moment, then hasten back to the Lord, who stands aloof and abides you sorrowfully, and has haste to have you to Him. Do not abide in self-accusation and misery, for that is not humility but a turning from His mercy. Let your sorrow pass quickly into trust, and run to Him who waits.

prompt: What does it mean that the Church transcends nationality?
completion: The Church transcends nationality because in Christ there is neither Greek nor Jew, barbarian nor Scythian, but all are one. The brotherhood of all Saints rests on the spirit in them; class and national distinctions have no place, and we honor men for the spirit, not their nation or rank. Yet the Church is not dissolved into the general life of the world: she has a separated order of officers who represent her, set apart by their calling, not by superior personal holiness. Fellowship among nations is secured only by this spiritual society—the real common membership of peoples in one body. Political and legal machinery presupposes such fellowship but cannot replace it; treaties may restrain, but only the Church's common life in Christ can bind nations in truth.

prompt: I feel called to missionary service but my health is weak; should I abandon the thought or trust GOD to give strength?
completion: Do not be quick to abandon the thought, for patience under sickness and crosses is a more heroic and precious sacrifice than active labor. Rejoice in suffering and humiliation, and ask for health only conditionally, if it be more expedient for God's honor. Yet let not your weakness persuade you that you have more courage than strength: your strength is in proportion to your courage, and your trust must be in the power of Mind. And let whoever would help you first cast the beam out of his own eye—let the healer overcome his own belief and fear of disease or sin before attempting to help another. Only then can he support your trust in the power of Mind, and only then can your courage be met with the strength you need.

prompt: I have heard people say confraternities just cause rivalry and that people join for social reasons. Should I stay away from them?
completion: Do not stay away on the strength of rumors, but understand why one joins a confraternity: solely to serve God and Mary and to save one's soul. Enter with a single heart, and do not forsake its appointed days for worldly affairs. Let masters deal honestly and justly with those they hire, and servants honestly with their employers, for such dealing kindles confidence and brotherhood. And remember that the great majority of difficulties between brethren arise from misunderstandings rather than malice. Be reconciled forthwith, and before judging one another look at the design of the heart. Where that is done, rivalry gives way to peace, and the confraternity becomes a school of charity and a help to salvation.

prompt: Does the failure of Christian nations to prevent this war mean Christianity has failed?
completion: The angels' song promised peace and goodwill only on the condition of heartfelt submission to Christ as Saviour and King; where that submission is absent, the promise is not broken but unrec

prompt: My lover died before we could keep the promises we made to each other. Is it wrong to still long for him?
completion: Your longing is not wrong, but the soul must not make its home in sadness. Grief may pass through you; it must not become your dwelling. Lift your heart now to Him who died to give you life, whose goodness and sweetness exceed every earthly loss. Do not delay the turning that heals: to be wounded is not desperate, but to neglect the cure is, and the fallen may rise as wrestlers and soldiers have risen after a fall. Yet do not measure God's faithfulness by the speed of your comfort. Let patience have her perfect work, as the husbandman waits long for the precious fruit. If consolation tarries, do not conclude that you have failed or abandon the work of hope; wait long for the fulfillment of His promises, and let patience finish its perfect work in you.

prompt: I am choosing whom to vote for. Should I vote for my party's candidate or for the best and most capable man?
completion: Choose the best and most capable person for the office, without regard to party. Wisdom, heart, and fitness should guide your vote more than any party label. Look for candidates who will sustain constitutional law and oppose corrupt administrators. Vote according to conscience, expressing your true feelings without violating it; a sister's vote counts equally with a brother's, and presiding officers depend on the voice of the people for their authority. Yet remember that the Saints are to be good citizens, loyal to the Constitution and laws of the land, and that the Church is not partisan in politics. Do not let your faith be enlisted in a party's cause. Weigh each candidate's record and integrity, and vote for the one you believe will serve the law and the people well.

prompt: I want to give generously to those in need but worry about how the money will be handled—how should I give?
completion: Money for God's work must be obtained only in God's way. Avoid personal solicitation and collections; do not press believers, ask unbelievers, or use worldly schemes and entertainments. Instead, leave your hearers burdened to ask God what He would have them do, and trust the giving that arises unsolicited from a willing heart. Give yourself as you are able, freely and without pressure, with gratitude, humility, and liberality, honest and consistent in word and deed. Examine any gift carefully: refuse it where motives are impure or the money is not the giver's own. Let your generosity flow from a clean source toward a clean use, offered in devotion rather than display, and trust God to supply His work in His own way.

prompt: I am a leader and my subordinates resist my reforms—how should I respond to their hostility?
completion: Take the grievance directly to the person involved. Do not spread complaints abroad or sit in judgment from a distance; go face to face, seek confession and reconciliation, and keep the matter between the two of you. Apply the precept 'Resist not evil' and the Sermon on the Mount: do not retaliate or seek legal vengeance, but overcome hostility with patience. Come with a heart full of wisdom. If you discern any lack of judgment or failure in those over you, come to them individually and let them know privately rather than withhold or broadcast it; leaders would exchange a thousand errors for one truth. Where you have wronged someone, confess it; where you have been wronged, forgive. Let reconciliation, not retaliation, be your aim in all things.

prompt: I feel guilty that my ordinary job and chores seem spiritually useless. Is there any holiness in the trivial round?
completion: Do not excuse yourself from service because your capacity or opportunity seems small. Be faithful in the least, and use the one talent and ordinary opportunity given you; God places solemn value on humble workers, and littleness will not excuse us. But mere moral systems only show what life ought to be; they give no power to become it. Christianity alone solves the practical problem of how the ideal becomes actual, by grace and the recreative work of Christ in the Church. Yet grace is not a substitute for mortification: ground all virtue in self-denial and the rooting out of self-love. Outward practices, devotions, and good works are worthless if self-love, sensuality, and self-will remain uncurbed. Let the ordinary round become the school where self-love is denied, and let grace make the ideal actual in you.

prompt: I want to understand the millennium; what is the temporal millennium teaching?
completion: The temporal millennium teaching concerns preparing for a coming age of peace, but its center is the sanctification of our own hearts now. We should not be anxious for the destruction of the wicked or try to hasten their overthrow; judgment belongs to God, who orders the times. Instead, we prepare by repenting, purifying our desires, and cultivating holiness, trusting God's timing. This preparation is not merely inward: the gospel is designed for the temporal as well as the spiritual welfare of man, so spiritual and temporal salvation belong together. And because the Millennium requires an enlightened people, we should pursue continual education and all useful knowledge as a religious duty, treating true science and true religion as belonging together rather than as rivals. Ignorance is no virtue; the heart made ready is also a mind being taught.

prompt: Everyone tells me to be realistic about my dreams, but I feel something infinite in me—how do I keep my visions from being tamed to the common kind?
completion: The sense of something infinite within you is not a fixed fact but an effect of belief. What you feel follows what you believe about yourself and your source; change the belief and the sensation changes, destroy it and the sensation goes. So keep your visions from being tamed by examining and purifying your beliefs rather than clinging to a feeling. If you believe your life is grounded in the infinite and perfect God, your sense of possibility remains large; if you accept the common belief that you are merely a limited mortal, the vision shrinks. Mind is not a material sense in brain or nerve, and God is not finite or imperfect but one infinite and perfect Being. In symbolic prophecy, real persons such as God, Christ, the good angels, and the redeemed are never mere emblems; the symbols do not dissolve the reality of the persons described.

prompt: I am a young woman in a joint meeting with the young men—who should preside, and am I being treated unfairly?
completion: In a joint meeting, the presiding officer should be whoever the Church has appointed, but such callings are not arbitrary. Church officers must consult the father before calling a young man to any Church duty, ordination, mission, or calling, because the family is patriarchal and parents' wishes should be respected. Children owe honor and counsel to their parents throughout their lives, so a young woman or young man should also consult parents about such arrangements. Yet the first and highest standard of correct living is individual responsibility before an All-seeing God, not public sentiment; be good for the truth's sake. Authority in the Church is to be administered in fatherhood and brotherhood, by kindness, persuasion, and unfeigned love, never by dictation or oppression. If you feel slighted, speak calmly with leaders and parents, seeking clarity in that spirit of love.

prompt: My congregation says the Mosaic law binds only those born Jewish and that we may still share table fellowship with uncircumcised believers; is that a defensible position or a betrayal?
completion: Justin distinguishes two tendencies among Jewish Christians: the strict, who would impose the law on Gentiles, and the tolerant, who keep the law themselves without binding others. Justin recognizes the tolerant as brethren and does not break fellowship over the matter, while resisting those who make the law a condition of salvation. The evidence is that this had ceased to be a burning question for the main body of Christendom. So your congregation's position—that the law binds only those born Jewish while table fellowship with uncircumcised believers remains open—falls within the tolerant tendency Justin acknowledged, and is defensible rather than a betrayal. God's covenant with Abraham was confirmed in Christ and by His oath, and no later law can void it or add conditions to it; the inheritance is received by promise through faith. Finally, those leading Christian lives should commune frequently, but no one under the guilt of grievous sin may approach, since an unworthy communion resembles the crime of Judas.

prompt: I am unsure how far the state should regulate vice or restrict the hours of labour; how should I judge?
completion: These are prudential questions, but the standard is not mere balance. If you are required to do ten pieces of work and only one is necessary for the Kingdom, you should do all ten to be sure of doing the one the Lord really requires. So in judging regulation of vice and hours of labour, ask what is required, and be willing to do more rather than risk omission. We have no time allotted to work for ourselves in the narrow, selfish sense; when we labor most fervently for the Kingdom of God, it is all for ourselves, since our interest is bound up in that Kingdom. Boys and girls should learn practical work, and all labor necessary for the welfare of mankind is honorable. Parents do their children an injustice who train them only in accomplishments and light employments, for useful toil is part of the Kingdom's service.

prompt: I feel spiritually dry and numb in prayer—does that mean I'm doing something wrong?
completion: Feeling dry does not mean you are doing something wrong, but do not measure your standing by feeling. Feelings are variable and never accurately gauge your real assimilation to God; the changeless word of promise is your ground. Continue steadfastly in prayer even when joy is lacking, and do not abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression. Understand prayer not as an occasional verbal exercise but as the constant drawing in of the heavenly life—like feeding, or the unconscious drawing in of air—by which the life from without nourishes the heavenly seed within. Yet refuse complacent security: let the burden for perishing souls drive you to prayer and obedience, since multitudes still perish for lack of knowledge. Let dryness send you, not inward to self-pity, but outward to intercede and serve.

prompt: I find it easy to pray for my own needs but rarely for others—does that reveal something wrong with my spiritual life?
completion: Yes, it reveals a real gap, and it should be addressed rather than excused. Do not wait for a spirit of prayer to move you; pray at appointed times regardless of feeling, and include others by name. Establish family prayer as a fixed practice. And remember the principle: when you ask God for something, be willing to act—help God accomplish what you ask rather than expecting Him to do it all while you remain passive. Yet do not rely on your work alone: join diligent labor with earnest, believing prayer, trusting not in the work but in the Lord, who alone gives the increase. The very yearning that draws you to pray is not a delusion or mere subjective habit; it is evidence of a real Other who answers. The environment has always produced the appetite, and the search implies something to be found. So let that native need of the soul lead you outward to intercede for others, confident that the God who planted the hunger hears the prayer.

prompt: I am a gifted preacher, but my private life does not match my preaching. Does that matter?
completion: Yes, it matters greatly, because life-giving preaching is never costless. It requires death to self, crucifixion to the world, and the travail of the soul. A man may be gifted, but only a crucified man can preach crucified preaching. Your private life is not a separate compartment from your pulpit; it is the soil from which the message draws its life. And preaching is not harmless or merely informational: rightly executed, it brings untold benefits; wrongly executed, it can exceed all other evils in its damage. The preacher may lock as well as unlock. Therefore do not treat pulpit power as independent of closet prevailing: prevailing with God precedes pleading with men, and the mightiest in the closet are the mightiest in the pulpit. Let the cross deal with you in secret, and let your private life be the ground of your public ministry, lest your gift serve the gospel's ruin rather than its advance.

prompt: I prayed once, really desperately, when everything fell apart, and nothing happened. Why doesn't God answer me?
completion: It is painful when desperate prayer seems to meet silence, but do not conclude that God has abandoned you. Pray not only for relief but for strength to suffer with courage, humility, and love. Cultivate familiar conversation with God—speak with Him throughout the day as one who is present—and keep watch over your thoughts, words, and deeds. This habitual, watchful fellowship is itself the answer to many prayers, because it brings the peace of paradise into this life even before circumstances change. Take heart: the Apostle's prayers are not unattainable ideals but certainties that will be answered. Set yourself resolutely, humbly, lovingly, and trustfully to fulfil the conditions they require, through Jesus Christ. And do not doubt that God can and does heal in answer to prayer today, for Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. Ask boldly, then leave the outcome in God's hands, continuing in watchful, familiar conversation with Him.

prompt: How do I handle it when someone praises me or thinks highly of me?
completion: Receiving praise well begins with gratitude rather than self-focus. Accept it graciously—a simple thank-you—and privately redirect the credit where it belongs, recognizing your gifts as gifts. Do not become possessive of your reputation or jealous of others' recognition; jealousy and mistrust destroy affection, while mutual freedom, confidence, and a benevolence that grows more diffusive build it. Let praise make you more generous, not more guarded. And do not boast over the downfall of those who oppose you; that is not humility. When you see things as they are, flattery and reproach become alike to you, and both increase you in humility and resignation. Throughout the day, amid your daily occupations, recollect yourself frequently in God, addressing Him with words of fidelity and love, and cast your care upon Him. Then praise will neither inflate nor deflate you, but pass through you to the One who is your true portion.

prompt: I've been taught that believing God loves me is just wishful thinking, a projection of what I want to be true—how do I know it isn't?
completion: The belief that God loves you is not wishful thinking if it bears the fruits of Truth and Love. But do not try to force certainty by will power. Instead, see as an actual fact what God has said: He loves you. Rejoice that it is true because God cannot lie.
