Yet do not stop at receiving; make it your constant endeavour to enter up into God's estate and offer Him love. In that ascent, adoration becomes your mode of entry. Rest in the promise, but actively love Him who first loved you. Let your life demonstrate the supreme good—heal, love, show truth—not to prove anything, but as the natural fruit of dwelling in His love. So, cease begging Him to come down; instead, rise up and offer Him your love.

prompt: I feel that Confucius and Buddha offer noble teaching; why should I regard their systems as defective?
completion: Confucius and Buddha offer noble teachings, but their systems are defective because they are man's vain effort to lift himself to God, whereas Christianity is God's coming down to save man. Heathenism identifies God with nature, knows no clear revelation of His holy will, and so its virtue is self-righteousness. Yet it is our privilege and duty to be as wise in our generation as the children of this world, and even wiser because we have superior advantages through faith and obedience to the Gospel. We ought to know more about all matters than any other people. Therefore, while appreciating their ethical insights, we recognize that only in Christ do we find the atonement, forgiveness, and the Spirit's power to fulfill the law. Adhering strictly to the divine Principle, we affirm our superior wisdom in the Gospel.

prompt: I am offered a comfortable, easy life. Should I prefer it to a harder life that serves God more?
completion: The choice between a comfortable life and a harder life that serves God more requires abandonment to God in both interior and exterior suffering. Do not seek comfort or hardship for their own sake, but abandon yourself to God's will, living, working, and rejoicing only in Him. Remember that patience under sickness and crosses is a more heroic and precious sacrifice than active labor. So, rejoice in suffering and humiliation, and ask for health only conditionally, if it be more expedient for God's honor. Keep both beholdings at once: the higher, keeping you in solace and enjoying in God, and the lower, in dread and shame of self. Hold much more in the higher, so that in all things you may serve Him more fully.

prompt: I love fine clothes and dressing above my station; is this a spiritual danger, and how do I put it off?
completion: Loving fine clothes and dressing above your station is a spiritual danger because it springs from pride, the very sin by which Elizabeth was awakened. The Bible warns against pride in outward adorning and commends the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is of great price in God's sight. To put off this habit, humble yourself and ask God for grace to turn from vanity. Focus on inner beauty and character, and choose modest apparel that suits your station. Remember that God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble. By His grace, you can turn from the love of finery and cultivate humility. Likewise, we must condemn clergy living under the same roof with deaconesses or spiritual sisters as an occasion of evil and a scandal, even where the persons claim security. Yet in all this, remain in a holy nudity of spirit, assuming no care, desire, affection, or pretension, resting on no breast but God's.

prompt: I committed some small fault this morning and now I feel miserable all day—am I a bad person for this?
completion: Committing a small fault does not make you a bad person. In divine metaphysics, man is unhurt and whole, and we must reverse the belief of injury. Accidents are unknown to immortal Mind, and under divine Providence there can be no accidents. The fault is not a real event; it is a false claim with no power. Do not affirm pain or misery as real and continuous. Instead, declare that man is unhurt and trust God as All. Your true identity is spiritual and perfect. Yet, see in this fault an occasion to wish to be corrected, for the desire to be corrected is the principal fruit of humility and an evident sign of perfection. So, reverse the belief of injury, acknowledge the fault only as a false claim, and know that in God's sight you are whole. Let go of the misery and rest in the truth that God's creation is intact.

prompt: My pastor says I should read the critics and modern scholars. How much of what they say should I actually accept?
completion: Reading critics and modern scholars is useful, for the School of the Prophets is established to increase in knowledge. The favorite study of the Elders is theology, and every Elder should become a profound theologian; every branch of science taught in the world should also be taught among the Saints. Yet Scripture is the primary source and final standard of appeal. Nature, scholarship, and Christian experience are subordinate and must be tested by it. Accept what is true, tested, and consistent with Scripture; set aside speculation. Teachers should preach only what they know and say plainly when the Lord has not revealed a matter rather than guessing. A confident tone is not proof. Study deeply, weigh evidence, and hold fast to what is good, letting Scripture anchor you.

prompt: What does it mean that the Redeemer suffered in my behalf rather than in my stead—do I still have to suffer?
completion: When we say Christ suffered in your behalf, we mean His suffering was for your benefit, on your account, and for your sake. It was not a substitute transaction that leaves you untouched; it was an act of love that opens a way. So yes, you will still suffer, and those who follow Him enter into the fellowship of His sufferings and the ongoing work of redemption. Do not delay: repent now. It is not desperate to have been wounded but to neglect the cure; one who has fallen may rise, as wrestlers and soldiers have risen after a fall. Forgive injuries after the example of the good thief and of Christ on the cross, and so become a true imitator of Christ and heir of His disciples' privileges. Take up your cross, and your suffering will be caught up in His and bear fruit.

prompt: I had a dream in the night that seemed to promise victory—should I trust it?
completion: Dreams can be vivid and moving, and the dreaming Muse, lovely in her sorrow, should be left to dream rather than roused by jarring Truth, lest she die; the old dreams of gods and heroic Greece are lovely and may be allowed to persist. Yet begin with an intimate conviction of your own inability: no human learning or skill can convert or sanctify a soul, and all human power cannot save. Join to that firm confidence in God's power to sanctify yourself and others through supernatural means. Do not trust only when things go well; learn strong faith by standing firm amid severe testings, trusting most when all else fails, and thank God for the school of sorrow. Test any dream that claims to promise victory by Scripture, and trust God rather than the dream.

prompt: I am a parent choosing a school for my child. What should I look for in those who will teach and train my child?
completion: Choosing a school is a duty owed to your child, not merely a private preference. It is a duty to educate and train children in every useful branch of learning, and good schools should be established throughout the settlements. The School of the Prophets is established to increase in knowledge: the favorite study of the Elders is theology, and every Elder should become a profound theologian, and every branch of science taught in the world should also be taught among the Saints. So look for qualified, patient teachers, promptly and willingly paid, who teach both Scripture and sound learning. Commend spiritual education, obedience to the moral law, and restraint of indulgence, so that children grow in the understanding of man's higher nature.

prompt: I have tried to hide from God in my work, my studies, and my pleasures, but none of them give me peace. Why do they all fail me?
completion: They fail you because none of them was ever meant to carry the weight of your soul. Work, study, and pleasure are good in their place, but when they become a hiding place from God they cannot give peace, because the heart was made for Him. The very failure of these things is a mercy, showing you that no created thing can fill the place of God. Do not multiply explicit offerings or grow anxious over distraction in your necessary work; do all your actions for God simply and quietly. When you lapse in remembering Him, do not be disquieted; return with greater trust. And do not measure spiritual worth by outward station, education, or visibility, nor reject the piety that ripens in seclusion because it does not fit a favorite system. Honor the weak and despised whom God has chosen, and refuse to reject those who name the name of Christ and depart from iniquity.

prompt: Is it wrong to ask God for small, everyday things like a hat or a coat?
completion: No, it is not wrong. God is a loving Father who cares for the details of our lives, and Scripture invites us to cast all our cares on him, including the smallest ones. Asking for a hat or coat is simply bringing ordinary needs to a Father who delights to provide, for nothing is too great for his power or too small for his love. Yet we must remember that God may deny a request in kindness, and we should resign our will to his, trusting that his denial can be better than the thing we asked for. Prayer does not excuse us from ordinary means: we should work, use medicine, and receive food with thanksgiving, rejecting both presumption and unbelief. So ask freely about small, everyday matters, use means wisely, and trust his wisdom and love.

prompt: If the New Jerusalem is a real city, where is it now, and where will it be located when it comes down?
completion: The New Jerusalem is a real city, not merely a symbol of the church. It is the capital of Christ's everlasting kingdom, now existing in the third heaven, and it is about to descend out of heaven to be located in the midst of the promised land. This Holy City encloses the garden of Eden, the Paradise of God, with the tree of life and the river of water of life issuing from the throne; these are realities belonging to the sanctuary, for the city is God's sanctuary. It is a real city measuring fifteen hundred miles square, with many mansions prepared by Christ, in which there is abundant room for all who are written in the Lamb's book of life. So we should look for a physical city established in the land, the dwelling place of God with his people.

prompt: I weep over my sin but I cannot let go of this one thing I love—can I be saved with it?
completion: Your weeping shows your conscience is alive, but do not be deceived: one mortal sin unrepented is enough to damn the soul. Scripture warns that those who love a lie have their part in the lake of fire. An intense and abiding fear of sin and of eternal loss should be nourished, so that fear may restrain you where love is too weak. Yet I do not speak from superiority: I too must confess my own faults and feebleness, for we are all sinners. Let us together point to the fountain opened for sin, following Christ who took our sins and made them his own. Meekly acknowledge your sin and feebleness, then trust God's courteous excusing, who is gentle with the contrite. Bring this loved thing to God honestly, confess it, and ask him to change your heart, letting holy fear guard you until love grows strong.

prompt: I am drawn to the idea that only matter is real and that thoughts are just by-products of the brain—can that view be true?
completion: That view, materialism, cannot be true. The ultimate Reality is Mind, not matter, for mind explains matter while matter cannot explain mind. Consciousness, reason, and meaning cannot be derived from blind particles. To posit a Something that is neither mind nor matter is both unintelligible and gratuitous. Mind is first and cannot produce its opposite, matter, for like produces like; nor can matter produce Mind, for the less cannot produce the greater. Mind is the one reality that can account for both thought and the order of the material world. The senses of Mind are never lost, and matter has no sensation, so loss of limb or physical sense is a belief to be overcome, not a real and permanent loss. So while it is understandable that you are drawn to materialism, it is not adequate to explain reality. It is more reasonable to hold that Mind is first and that matter is dependent on Mind.

prompt: I want to help the poor and reform society—what means are actually adequate to the task?
completion: Wanting to help the poor and reform society is admirable, and the means must be both practical and moral. We must be honest that much poverty comes from lack of discretion and sound calculation, and from wasteful spending on unnecessary finery, so reform must include teaching prudence, budgeting, and thrift alongside meeting immediate needs. Yet we must never treat poverty as degrading or value people by wealth and position. The destitute have a right to food and fellowship, and we should esteem persons by character rather than by wealth or station. Remember that evil holds no abiding pleasure, and material indulgence cannot satisfy; lasting reform comes through affection for good as Science reveals it. Address root causes through education, job training, and fair laws, build community institutions, and work through both personal service and public advocacy, measuring success by whether people are actually helped to flourish.

prompt: I was baptized and confirmed, but I've never felt anything like what happened at Pentecost—is that experience for me today?
completion: Pentecost was God's once-for-all gift of the Spirit to the church, and each believer appropriates that gift personally by faith. Your baptism is no empty form: joined with faith, it is a means of real blessing, signifying cleansing from sin and entrance into close relation to Christ. You need no second Pentecost—yet you may ask the Spirit to fill you afresh. Remember, though, that since Pentecost the church itself is the Spirit's dwelling place and temple, the body of Christ indwelt and embodied by the Holy Spirit. Your experience is not a private pursuit but a life within that body. So pray for the Spirit's fullness, trust the promise, and let your baptismal identity shape your daily life among God's people.

prompt: I'm facing a difficult situation at work—could this be an opportunity to witness rather than just a problem to escape?
completion: Yes—and more than an opportunity, this difficult situation is to be undertaken as God's business, without uneasiness. Testimony is a personal possession, not to be forced on everyone or used to fill time, and it is no substitute for the instruction people need; intelligence is required of those who speak in the Lord's name, and a neglected gift is withdrawn. So be brave and true to your convictions from the beginning; don't let Satan see that you are afraid, but trust God to stand by you. Do even the distasteful tasks as God's business, free from uneasiness, letting your conduct and fitting words bear witness.

prompt: I've been told my worth depends on my intelligence or my body. Is that true?
completion: No, that isn't true. Your worth doesn't rest on intelligence or appearance, and success is not measured by material advancement or worldly honor. The true standard is faithfulness and the salvation of your soul, and worldly judgment is not that standard. Your worthiness does not come from personal merit: God counts the believer worthy by grace, not for any worthiness of our own—though grace brings responsibility in how we use what we've been given. Man is not structural; intelligence and life are spiritual and cannot be measured by brain, bone, or sinew. So don't let others' standards define you; rest in grace and respond with faithful stewardship.

prompt: What then is the Body of Man?
completion: The body of man is not a material structure that generates life or mind. Man is God's spiritual idea, individual and eternal, whose origin and life are in Spirit; mind and life do not inhere in matter. Yet man took a body for exaltation through Christ's redemption and for propagating a pure seed, so purity of body is of the greatest importance. The body is not merely touched by power from outside: it receives Christ Himself in vital union with its mortal body, knowing Him as strength, health, and full physical redemption. So the body serves the person, is kept pure for God's purposes, and shares in the redemption Christ brings.

prompt: I was taught that my body and skin color make me lesser. How do I see myself as whole?
completion: What you were taught is false, yet wholeness means holding two beholdings at once. The lower sees yourself honestly, in dread and shame over the contempt you've carried; the higher keeps you in solace, enjoying God, who made you in His image and loves you equally regardless of body or skin color. Hold both, weighting the higher far more. Forsaking base things and rising to Divine things comes not by exterior labour or bodily health but by labouring with the heart and inward aspiration—repose of the senses, effort of the heart, silence of the mind. Remember too that man took a body for exaltation through Christ's redemption and for propagating a pure seed; purity of body is therefore of the greatest importance. Your body is not your shame but a vessel for God's purposes.

prompt: I am afraid of God's majesty and dread His presence; how can I also know Him as homely and courteous?
completion: It is natural to feel awe before God's majesty, but He also invites you into a marvelously homely and courteous intimacy. Instead of trying to escape your fear, expect God to reveal Himself as a present help in your trouble. In Psalm 34:4, David says, 'I sought the LORD, and he answered me and delivered me from all my fears.' Your fear can become an occasion to know God more deeply as your Comforter and Deliverer. At the same time, keep a courteous reverence, remembering that He is sovereign. Approach Him with the boldness of a child but with the respect of a subject. As you bring your dread to Him, He will show Himself faithful and gentle, deepening your knowledge of His character. The more you experience His help, the more you'll rejoice in His homely courtesy, and love will cast out fear while reverent dread remains.

prompt: Is there any hope for a world at war?
completion: Yes, there is hope for a world at war, but it begins with humble repentance. On a day of humiliation, we must confess that we have shared in the tone of thought and life that led to this catastrophe. Wars stem from human sin—greed, pride, and hatred—and we are all implicated. Men precipitate war upon themselves by wickedness; God did not design it. Rather than claiming superiority over the enemy, we pray, 'God be merciful to me a sinner.' Peace will never come until mankind receives God's truth, and the gospel of Jesus Christ is the only true solution, as it changes hearts and reconciles people to God and one another. We must remain always at peace, patient with others and equally patient with ourselves, for peace is the passport of the daughters of Jesus Christ. While conflicts may continue, ultimate hope is in God's promise of a new heaven and new earth where righteousness dwells. Until then, Christians are called to be peacemakers, demonstrating God's love in a broken world.

prompt: I am not my own; should I decline a lucrative career offer because the LORD may call me elsewhere?
completion: Discerning a career offer requires prayer and honesty. Since you are not your own, your life belongs to God, and He may indeed call you elsewhere. All work and business should be done in the name of the Lord, so ask: Can I do this work in the name of the Lord? Will it honor Him and align with biblical values? A lucrative offer is not inherently wrong, but it must be work that can be offered to God. Limit yourself to legitimate employments, refusing the curiosity, ambition, and restlessness that create more impediments than works. Be willing to decline even available human support if doing so enables a fuller dependence on God's faithfulness. Seek His guidance above all, and if He gives you peace and the work is honorable, you may accept it, trusting Him to redirect you if needed. Be willing to decline if He clearly leads otherwise, remembering that your ultimate purpose is to glorify Him in all things.

prompt: I am afraid of suffering and complain when trials come; how can I bear crosses with patience?
completion: It is natural to fear suffering, but patience in trials comes from trusting God's purpose. Instead of resenting trials, be patient with them, accepting them as God's permission to reveal what you are when left to yourself. This is an occasion to see your weakness and turn to Him. Become indifferent to serving God amid thorns or roses—your service should not depend on comfort. The Bible tells us to consider it pure joy when we face trials because they produce perseverance and maturity (James 1:2-4). Every trial and vicissitude is necessary for experience and preparation for glory, and the Saints must be tried as Abraham was. Accept trials and persecution as necessary and meet them cheerfully, examining your own obedience while trusting God to overrule the efforts of enemies. Focus on God's promises and His presence. Remember that He is with you in the fire, and He will never leave you. Pray for strength and a changed perspective. Look to Jesus, who endured the cross for the joy set before Him. With the Holy Spirit's help, you can develop patience and find peace even in suffering.

prompt: Why is there so much suffering in the world if God is good and all-powerful?
completion: The problem of suffering is deep, but God is not absent from it. While God is good and all-powerful, He employs suffering as a remedy for sin, not as evidence against His goodness. All from God's hand, sweet or bitter, should be received equally, for His love makes both acceptable. Afflictions seen as from a loving Father become consolation. Much suffering results from human choices, but God can bring good out of evil. He includes His righteousness in the problem: He is just and merciful, and He uses suffering to refine and restore. Christ's own agony on the cross was submitted to in perfect love, proving that agony is compatible with the most perfect love between God and the sufferer. God entered into suffering through Jesus, who suffered and died for us. He promises a future where suffering will end, and He offers comfort and strength now. In divine metaphysics, we reverse the belief of injury and declare man unhurt, trusting God as All. We trust that God's wisdom is beyond our understanding, and His love will prevail.

prompt: I have been offered a life of ease at court, but I keep longing for a small hut in the woods. Which should I choose?
completion: The longing you feel is worth honoring rather than dismissing. The hermit's wish is for a hidden little hut in the wilderness, with a lark singing beside it, a clear pool in which to wash away sins, a wood around it for shelter, and a southern aspect to catch the light, with a small company of humble, obedient men praying to the King. Yet do not imagine holiness must be cold: wish rather that the Church would give ale and a pleasant fire, so that souls regale and are as happy as birds in the spring. And do not despise the visible world. Study God's works with love; observe the equal care shown to the humblest and the proudest; consider with love that God fashioned our eyes to see and enjoy them. Choose the hut, and there study, enjoy, and give thanks.

prompt: I'm struggling to forgive someone who hurt me deeply—how do I let go of the bitterness?
completion: Keep Christ closely as a bouquet of myrrh; the bitterness you feel is yours, not His. God is not bitter—He allows us to be bitter to ourselves, and He does not will your wounding. So refuse to be angry over your own agitation; gently place the troubled heart in the hands of our Lord, ask Him to cure it, and renew good resolutions. Know that forgiving enemies and bearing injuries patiently is the best revenge: by it grace and the pardon of your own sins are gained without trouble or expense. Forgiveness is not pretending nothing happened or instantly trusting again; it is releasing your claim to revenge. Pray for the person, name the wound, set wise boundaries, and let Christ's myrrh sweeten what is bitter in you.

prompt: I want to be morally pure, but I also feel guilty enjoying ordinary pleasures like good food and friendship. Is enjoyment wrong?
completion: Enjoyment is not wrong in itself, but beware of making pleasure your goal. Understand that sin confers no real pleasure: the wrong-doer is cheated, for the craving for pleasure is a living death. People go into debt for fashionable display, and the hunt for pleasure leads to cheating, lying, and corrupted morals. Let this knowledge strengthen your moral courage to master evil. Do not linger in the cheerless tomb of passion or glamorize its storm; when the storm is laid, mark the silent growth of grace and light in your soul. Receive good food and friendship with thanksgiving, keep them in proportion, and let them deepen love for God and neighbor. Purity is a rightly ordered heart, not the refusal of good things.

prompt: I am a magistrate and a friend has offered me a gift to overlook a small irregularity in a contract. May I accept it?
completion: No—accepting a gift to overlook an irregularity is a bribe, even if the irregularity seems small. The Saints should fulfil their contracts and sacredly keep their word; honest hearts produce honest actions, and I have no fellowship for a man who makes a promise and does not fulfil it. As a magistrate you hold public trust, so decline politely and handle the contract according to the law. Do not solicit gifts or take up collections; leave hearers burdened to ask God what He would have them do, and trust unsolicited giving. Let your office reproach you where you are richly covered while the poor are ill accommodated, and part with comforts for their sake. If the irregularity is minor, correct it openly through proper channels.

prompt: I want to be closer to God, but I can't leave my family and work for a monastery. Am I missing my calling?
completion: Not necessarily—but let yourself be corrected rather than merely reassured. Allow yourself to be treated, planed, and polished, all angles effaced, so as to be joined and fastened to the will of God. Abandon yourself to God in interior and exterior suffering alike, seeking life, work, and joy but in God. The trivial round and common task are the appointed means of self-denial and daily nearness to Him. You need not forsake neighbour or work to find Him; faithfulness in small things, charity toward those around you, and prayer within your home are the road itself. A monastery offers structure and solitude, but your family and workplace are where holiness is forged. Ask how God is inviting you to meet Him right where you are.

prompt: I want to sow beside all waters but feel I have no platform; what can I do from my own desk?
completion: Sowing beside all waters begins where you are, and the vision before you is abundance, not lack: the coracle of lard on New-milk Lake, the fort of custards and butter, the well of wine, the lake of pottage under cream of lard, a household of generous welcome around the fire. From your desk you share that welcome—notes of encouragement, answers, hope to the discouraged. But do not sink upon a bed of sloth, and do not let intoxication overcome you; rise and begin the voyage across the clear sea, that you may reach the Land of Women. Let no practice be valued except as it serves union with God by love, for continual love is the shortest way. So write from love, return to love, and set out—the feast is spread and the voyage is before you.

prompt: I want to warn my younger brother about the disappointments ahead, but I remember being told not to disturb the young's delight—should I speak or stay silent?
completion: You are right that the young's delight should not be disturbed—youth's joy is real and worth protecting. Yet honesty has its place: eager hopes are inevitably followed by disappointment, misunderstanding, tears, wronged love, spoiled hope, mistrust, and the fears that come with ageing. So do not crush his delight with a lecture, but do not fall silent either. Speak the Word whether men hear or forbear, trusting God with the outcome. When you speak, speak plainly so he can hear and understand; say what you have to say and then stop, and do not darken counsel by many words. Stay close and available, let your life model resilience, and be a safe person he can come to when things go wrong.

prompt: Why did the Saints settle in a desert instead of a fertile land? Was that a curse?
completion: It was not a curse but the Lord's guidance. The Saints were led to the mountains, and what seemed a barren desert has proved a blessing, fulfilling the prediction that Zion should flourish and the desert blossom as the rose. The earth is not worthless or doomed: it abides its creation and is destined for renewal, so the Saints build up Zion here rather than despise or flee it. Persecution drove them, but behind the driving was divine direction. And because this inheritance is precious, they are to get out of debt in times of prosperity and keep out of debt, first paying their obligations to the Lord and then to their fellowman. They should avoid mortgaging their homes and farms, which jeopardizes their families and their inheritance in Zion. Read the desert not as misfortune but as a place prepared, to be kept free and faithful.

prompt: I am poor and in want; is it right to fast in order to give the saved food to those in need, and is such giving a sacrifice?
completion: Fasting to share with those in need can be good, but the fast is a matter of conscience and wisdom, not an iron-clad rule. The reasonable law is observed from even to even, with the food or its equivalent given to the poor. Yet it is left to your conscience and wisdom, and it is not required of the weak, the sick, or nursing mothers; little children should not be compelled to fast. Remember that fasting or feasting does not make one better morally or physically—God, Mind, sustains being. Poverty is not degrading, and the destitute have a right to food and fellowship; esteem persons by character, not by wealth or station. Give as you are able, cheerfully, without harming your health or taking pride, and let love, not the practice, be the measure.

prompt: I am tempted to think criminals are simply victims and society alone is guilty; is that true?
completion: It is not simply true. Social conditions shape behavior, but crime is not located in matter or the body—mortal mind is the criminal in every case. Motive determines guilt, and law should recognize this mental causation. Yet fairness is not measured by what a man deserves or has earned; render to every man according to his need, asking what is due from the one acting rather than what is owed to the other. So society bears real responsibility for unjust conditions without absorbing all guilt and leaving the offender a passive victim. Face justice and truth honestly: refuse to excuse or conceal guilt, for excusing sin only perpetuates it. Acknowledge social causes without erasing moral agency, and meet need with compassion while naming the wrong done and the mind that willed it.

prompt: How do I stay faithful when prayer feels irksome and pointless?
completion: It is normal for prayer to feel irksome, but do not abandon it after delay or set God a deadline. Continue patiently, believingly, importunately until the blessing is granted, without prescribing to God the time or manner of the answer, and expect the answer while waiting. Prayer is more than a transaction: it is an elemental attitude of the soul, older than any city, not explained by utilitarian straits. And do not explain away answers as coincidence or natural law—the exact and repeated correspondences between request and supply are too many and too exact to admit the doctrine of chance. They compel belief in a God who hears and answers. So keep asking, and watch for His replies.

prompt: Is it really possible to love everybody, including people I find thoroughly unlovable?
completion: It is possible to love everybody, though not to like everybody. Liking is an affection of taste; love is a movement of the will and heart. We cannot like everyone, but we can love everyone with the love of compassion—wishing them good, bearing with them, and refusing to withhold mercy. Bear patiently with the imperfections of others, for such forbearance is a great part of perfection and the practice of love of neighbor. Yet this love is not blind. Let your love abound more and more in full knowledge and all discernment, so that you may distinguish things that differ and approve the things that are excellent. Love and discernment belong together: love all, bear with all, and still distinguish good from bad, better from best, and best from excellent.

prompt: How much of my week should actually go to prayer rather than to sermon preparation?
completion: Practice is the greatest sermon; the life lived before God preaches louder than polished discourse. Do not exalt fine language over the Spirit's guidance. Seek the Spirit for a word in due season, and prefer short sermons fitly spoken. A preacher's estimate of prayer is measured by the time he gives to it, and great praying is the sign of God's great leaders. Trace superficial and dead ministries to lack of praying rather than to circumstances, methods, or audiences. Let the text, the sermon, and the study be bathed in prayer, so that preparation is not produced apart from communion but born within it. Give prayer its rightful hours, and let everything you prepare be soaked in it.

prompt: I've wanted God for years and still can't find Him. What am I doing wrong?
completion: The search is double. Your quest for God is real and grounded in experience, matched by the Divine Companion's quest for you; God is seeking you and spares no cost to bring you into fellowship. Do not manufacture comfort by denying evil, sickness, and pain—such denial is a narcotic, not a Redemption. Face these truths and walk the way of Redemption through heroism rather than cowardice. Yet know that finding God increases both joy and the power of suffering. In the one who has found Him, joy becomes greater than pain, and Good so much greater than Evil that Evil becomes negligible. Keep seeking, then, with courage and hope, trusting that the One you seek is seeking you and will be found.

prompt: How do I know whether I'm a religious in truth or only in name?
completion: Truth is the eternal conformity of God's being and knowledge, logically prior to His veracity toward creatures, grounded in His being rather than arbitrary will. True religion is not defined by external observance, doctrine, or feeling, but is Christ recognised, known, adored, and living within the soul—the New Life and the New Birth. Ask whether Christ is recognised, known, adored, and living in you, for that is the mark of the religious in truth rather than in name. And do not think that knowledge of the Gospel's truth is for leaders only: every Saint may and should know for himself that the work is true, and such knowledge is as good as a voice from heaven.

prompt: I want to surrender my life to God but I don't know how, and the ways people describe it feel fake to me—what does it actually mean to give myself to Him?
completion: Surrendering your life to God is not first about getting things from Him—guidance, strength, better feelings, or a smoother life. It is about giving Him yourself through love. Open yourself to Him not by asking for gifts but by offering great love, and in that offering you receive not a gift but God Himself, who gives Himself to the soul that loves Him. Do not wait until you feel more, weep more, or feel some greater power before you begin. This very moment you can renounce sin in will and purpose—not in feeling, but in the settled choice of your heart—and God Himself supplies the strength for what you cannot do. Feeling comes after the surrender, not before it. And when you forget Him, do not be disquieted; return with greater trust. So set aside petitions for your own needs, offer your heart as love now, and when you drift, come back calmly. That is what surrender actually is.

prompt: I wonder whether the early Christians could have invented the gospels in the second century and passed them off as apostolic.
completion: It is very unlikely. The deeper reason is content: the gospel could not be a mythical product of Jewish hopes, because what it proclaims contradicts those hopes at every point. The Jews expected a national deliverer who would restore Israel and crush her enemies; the gospel announces salvation for all nations. They expected a triumphant temporal Messiah; the gospel announces a crucified Messiah. No one inventing a story to fit Jewish expectations would have produced a suffering Messiah or a salvation thrown open to Gentiles. And this was no abstract idea: it took root among real people—plain folk, slaves, tradesmen—who needed a real gospel and found one that met them. Nor was its power confined to the past. The everlasting gospel is to be restored with apostles, prophets, baptism, the gift of the Holy Ghost, healings, tongues, and revelations, as in former days—the same gospel, the same gifts, the same living power among ordinary people who need it.

prompt: I am seriously ill. Should I be praying chiefly for health, or for whatever most leads me to my end?
completion: Pray for health—it is right to ask for healing—but make prayer chiefly your main assistant in every step of this illness, for prayer is how God works in us. Above all, pray that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart, to see what is amiss, and to reform whatever He shows you. And do not stop at generalities: bring each particular emergency to God in prayer—the pain, the fear, the sleepless night, the doctor's report—expecting Him to honour the Name of JESUS and supply the help you need. Remember that you need His continual help, and that praying, being with God, and thinking of Him often are bound together by holy habit. Form the habit now, for we must know Him before we can love Him. Let your prayer be: 'Lord, show me my heart and reform what is amiss, meet this need in Jesus' Name, and teach me to know You more.'

prompt: I was awakened under a sermon but the people around me laughed and called me a hypocrite—should I keep going?
completion: Yes, keep going—but beware of two dangers. First, do not appear outwardly more holy than you know yourself to be; let your religion be inward and honest, not a performance. Second, do not seek or desire human praise, for woe comes when men bless you, and those who call you blessed deceive you and destroy the way of your steps. Toward those who laughed and called you a hypocrite, do not retaliate or seek vengeance: apply 'Resist not evil' and the Sermon on the Mount—bless those who curse you and leave judgment to God. And remember that moral ignorance or sin hinders the demonstration of God's healing power and must be overcome; examine yourself honestly, repent where their accusation has truth, and press on toward purity of heart. Keep your religion between you and God, and let a changed life answer their laughter.

prompt: I feel nothing when I pray lately, and I wonder if God has abandoned me—what should I do?
completion: Feeling nothing in prayer is common, and it does not mean God has abandoned you. But do not expect prayer to be easy or naturally congenial—it is humbling work that crucifies pride and signs your bankruptcy before God. So wait before Him like a beggar, keeping your mind in His presence and recalling it in tranquility when it wanders. At the same time, pray with confidence, relying on Christ's merits, for God offers grace at each action unless we forget to ask. Ask boldly, in the Name of Jesus, and do not be discouraged by dryness or sin. And beware of excusing little prayer as acceptable: little praying is a worse evil than no praying, a deluding make-believe. So give yourself to prayer as the humbling work it is, and keep at it.

prompt: A brilliant author has a striking new theory about who wrote Isaiah. Should I build my faith around it?
completion: You should not build your faith around any human theory, but you also need not fear that God could have used literary methods suited to an undeveloped age. Dramatic composition, primitive tradition, or idealizing history are not fraud; they are simply ways that ancient writers communicated. God can inspire truth through such methods. Historical study of the New Testament, pursued with prayer, can serve reverent obedience by deepening your understanding of how God spoke. It should not become an end in itself or a threat to faith, but a means to a more stalwart and intelligent faith. Consider also the evidence of divine power: a religion so unprepossessing and uncompromising, proclaimed by unlearned men, could not have conquered the Roman Empire in three hundred years without divine power. The cross, a punishment for slaves, and a gospel that humbles human pride, yet paganism was converted within three centuries. This cannot be explained without supposing that divine power attended its promulgation. Let that strengthen your faith, and let study lead you to worship and to living out the Word.

prompt: Can I be counted righteous without actually becoming righteous?
completion: No, you cannot be counted righteous without actually becoming righteous. Salvation is not a legal fiction where righteousness is merely credited to you while you remain unchanged. It is an actual redemption of the entire self, made righteous by living in Christ's power the life He lived. Any merely credited righteousness is a false hope. When you surrender to Christ, His Spirit transforms you from within. This transformation often comes through trials. Count it all joy by faith, reckoning the trial a blessing, even when feelings fail. Fix your heart and choose to rejoice, until praise becomes a habit. Do not wait for joyful feelings before rejoicing; rejoice because God is at work. Remember that salvation is an individual operation: each must receive or reject it for himself. No one is saved by another's righteousness. So do not seek a righteousness that is only imputed; seek the actual transformation that comes from abiding in Him and rejoicing by faith.

prompt: What does it mean to look to heaven for help instead of trusting my own host?
completion: Looking to heaven for help means recognizing that your ultimate trust should be in God, not in human resources or your own strength. If you are a pastor or teacher, you must not neglect your own soul while busy in external works. Regular retirement, self-examination, reading, meditation, and private devotion are your first duty to your own soul. Without these, you cannot kindle charity in others. But looking to heaven also means attending to the sick and dying. Visiting and instructing the sick is a strict duty for every Christian, not just the minister. Seize the time Providence affords in lingering illness, and warn the dying to flee from the wrath to come, remembering that while there is life there is hope. Yet do not be too solicitous for sensible devotion, sweetness, and tears. Chiefly care to remain inwardly united to God by good will in the intellectual part of the soul, denying yourself to follow Christ, Who was truly poor, obedient, chaste, humble, and suffering. So look to heaven by keeping up prayer and devotion, by caring for the sick, and by seeking union with God above all feelings.

prompt: I am troubled about the practice of pew-rents in my church. Is it right to continue with them?
completion: Pew-rents are not right to continue with. They create distinctions between rich and poor in the house of prayer, which contradicts the gospel. The Lord's work should be supported by free-will offerings alone, not by fixed salaries or pew-rents that promote caste. In the New Testament, giving was voluntary and cheerful, not coerced or tied to privilege. If your church uses pew-rents, you should advocate for their abolition and encourage a return to biblical stewardship. This may require trust in God's provision, but it honors Him and upholds the equality of all believers. Additionally, parents and pastors have a duty to guard the young from corrupting books and to supply pious ones. This includes ensuring that the church's literature and teaching promote sound doctrine and godly living. Furthermore, do not neglect congregational worship on the ground of getting nothing out of it. Attend chiefly for the edification of the whole body and of the stranger, under the governance of love. So do not continue with pew-rents; instead, support the ministry through free-will offerings and encourage your church to provide wholesome reading for all ages and to gather for worship in love.

prompt: I love my family deeply, but lately I feel that even that love leaves me empty. Does that mean human love is worthless?
completion: No, human love is not worthless. The emptiness you feel may be a trial, not a sign that your love is false. In times of dryness, sadness, terrors, and temptations, you must serve God purely for love of His will, refusing the suggestion that your love is useless or false. Invincible fidelity in such trials is the mark of true love. But also name your piteous futility honestly: you feel empty, and that is real. Yet God alone makes much of naught. Your very nothingness is the place where love works. So do not conclude that your love for family is worthless because you feel empty. Instead, persevere in love, serving God and family not for feelings but for His sake. The emptiness may be a refining fire, drawing you closer to God and purifying your love. Remember that true love of Christ is the pulse and glow of the regenerate heart, and love is the only sign of the regenerate heart. No soul is worthless because Christ has shined on all. So hold fast to love, and let it be rooted in God's unchanging love for you.

prompt: My child is very sick and the doctors say there is no hope—should I keep praying for healing?
completion: It is right to keep praying for your child's healing, and you should not give up asking God for mercy. God can and does heal in answer to prayer today, for Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. Do not excuse neglect of prayer because you lack a feeling of devotion; keep appointed times of prayer regardless of feeling, and gather the family to pray together. Bring your request boldly and persistently, and act as far as you are able to help accomplish what you ask. Understand God as ever-present and omnipotent, for as the testimonies describe, children's complaints have disappeared through this understanding of divine power and presence. Trust his goodness, and leave the outcome in his hands.

prompt: Is the Holy City the saints themselves, or is it a real city prepared for the saints to enter?
completion: The Holy City is not the saints themselves but a city prepared for them to enter. The saints are being built together as a temple, yet the city is prepared for them, and the righteous dead have not yet been caught up to enter it. The New Jerusalem is a real city, the capital of Christ's everlasting kingdom, now in the third heaven and about to descend out of heaven to be located in the midst of the promised land. While they wait, the Saints must be a self-sustaining people, producing everything they need to eat, drink, or wear, living within their means, and always having a year's or two years' provision on hand, laying up grain against a day of scarcity.

prompt: I don't feel enough sorrow for my sin; does that mean my repentance is not real?
completion: Repentance is not chiefly a matter of intense emotion but of turning from sin and turning to God. Sin is doing wrong when we know and can do better; the sin of ignorance is winked at, but when we learn that a thing is wrong we must refrain from it immediately and forever. Repent at once and do not delay. It is not desperate to have been wounded but to neglect the cure, and one who has fallen may rise again, as wrestlers and soldiers have risen after a fall. Beware, for unregretted sin accumulates and destroys the ability to do right, and a guilty conscience grows harder. Examine whether you are still doing what you know to be wrong; if so, stop at once and reform your life.

prompt: If colours and sounds only exist for minds, what becomes of the solid, shaped objects I touch and handle?
completion: Colours and sounds may depend on the mind that perceives them, but the objects you touch and handle are not thereby dissolved. We have direct knowledge of substance underlying phenomena, both external and spiritual. Every thought is owned by a self that acts from within rather than passively receiving impressions. Mind is first and cannot produce its opposite, matter, nor can matter produce Mind, for like produces like. Matter has no existence of its own apart from a mind which knows it, and relations no less than sensations imply mind. Thus the solid, shaped object you touch is real, yet its reality is not independent of mind; spatial relations themselves imply a mind that knows them.

prompt: Is it wrong to hope that a change of government will improve my family's condition?
completion: It is natural to hope for better conditions for your family, but do not expect a change of government to regenerate society or produce happiness. Forms of government do not materially alter the people's condition; happiness and peace are gifts of God, and revolutions only change men and parchments. Be peaceable and submissive to existing authorities, pray for rulers, and patiently wait for the Lord to establish his own government in his own time. Do not turn to revolt or violent resistance. Instead, care for your own relatives and the poor, for it is a disgrace not to do so, and plan for them work they are able to perform. Place your hope in God and in faithful labor.

prompt: How do I know the Holy Spirit is actually dwelling in me?
completion: You can know the Holy Spirit dwells in you because He is the divine Person, the Paraclete whom Christ promised to send, co-equal with the Father and the Son. He speaks, guides, commands, and can be grieved. Our common condition is un-Godlike thoughts of heart and mind, and their alteration is not self-improvement or willpower but the work of the Holy Spirit, set in motion by taking Christ into the heart. He bears witness with your spirit and forms His fruit in you. Do not doubt His presence because Scripture or the Church shows imperfection; the Spirit works personally and gradually, as in the Old Testament and the Church, allowing imperfection without denying real inspiration. Assurance rests on Christ's promise and fellowship with the Person who lives in you.

prompt: Is it wrong to enjoy Christmas when so many people are suffering?
completion: The Christmas spirit is not mere enjoyment; it is a call to humility, joy, sacrificial love, worship, and missions. To share in its joys while living for yourself alone is a contradiction. The birth of Christ demands glad surrender to God and joyful sacrifice for others. But we must not wait for joyful feelings before we rejoice. We are to count it all joy by faith, reckoning even the trial a blessing. We fix our hearts and choose to rejoice, even when feelings fail, until praise becomes a habit. Yet we must also examine our own hearts, for we are prone to blame the hardness of hearers while ignoring our own coldness and lack of distress for souls. The worker must first be broken before God, crying out with intense distress for souls and tears, for this is the path to the results desired. Only then will our joy be by faith and expressed in sacrificial love, and only then do we have a right to share its joys.

prompt: I cannot sleep and am worn out with pain; can reading this book help me?
completion: Reading the book can help you find peace, since its ideas turn thought away from the body toward a calmer, spiritual view. If the reading stirs you up or makes the pain seem worse, do not take that as a sign to stop or as proof the book fails. That stir is the favorable action of Truth destroying error. The pain and sleeplessness are not fixed material facts; they are effects of belief, and when the belief changes or is destroyed, the sensation changes or is removed. But before you would help another, first cast the beam out of your own eye: overcome your own belief and fear of disease and sin, so that you heal from a clear, unafraid thought rather than from one still bound by the error you would remove.

prompt: What is it that I must leave in order to abide in repentance?
completion: To abide in repentance, you must leave all things that love and entertain the will—every visible and sensible delight that feeds the appetite—and instead love that which hates thee, embracing the reproach of the World and the Cross of Christ as a daily exercise of penitence. True repentance is not mere sorrow or a last-moment confession; it requires turning from evil, reforming your life, and making restitution, with cleansing coming through Christ's atonement. Moreover, abiding in Christ is not automatic: if your will abides in his words, his Word and Spirit abide in you; but if your will goes into the creature, you break off from him. Therefore, keep yourself by abiding in resigned humility and a constant course of penitence and daily dying from the creatures, so that your repentance may be continual and your union with Christ unbroken.

prompt: My parents force me into strict religious rules that make me feel dead inside. Is that really what God wants?
completion: It sounds like you're feeling suffocated by your parents' strict religious rules, and that's a valid feeling. God does not want you to feel dead inside; He desires a relationship with you, not mere rule-keeping. However, your parents likely believe they are doing what's best for you. It might help to have an honest conversation with them about how their rules affect you emotionally and spiritually. But parents must be warned: do not withdraw your children from a state of perfection or sow vanity and covetousness in their tender minds. Instead, form your children in virtue. Parents and pastors have a duty to guard the young from corrupting books and to supply pious ones. Above all, parents should never drive their children but lead them along, governing them by faith rather than the rod, never correcting them in the heat of passion, and teaching them to love rather than fear their parents. If your parents' rules are truly oppressive, seek guidance from a wise pastor who can help them see the harm. Your faith must become your own, rooted in love, not fear.

prompt: I want to be wise in this life, but I do not know what the most wisdom for a creature really is.
completion: The most wisdom for a creature is to hold fast to Jesus as highest sovereign Friend, fastening to Him homely in whatever state, foul or clean, and never fleeing from Him for weal nor for woe. Yet this loyalty is not passive; we must apply our hearts to wisdom and seek diligently for understanding, for God will as soon put bread and meat in our cupboards without our endeavor as give us wisdom without our trying to get it. The Word of Wisdom, supposed by some to have become stale, is like all the counsels of God, in force today as much as ever, and there is life everlasting in it for those who observe it with a good and willing heart. So we hold to Christ, labor in His strength, and live by His Word, which is our life.

prompt: How can I know whether a new idea is good simply because it is new?
completion: To know whether a new idea is good simply because it is new, you must first put into practice the truth you already understand. Prove good by demonstration before seeking more. Test the new idea against the known truth, and live out what you already know to be right. Then, with a foundation of practiced truth, you can evaluate the new idea by its fruits. But be careful not to bind faith inseparably to any particular scientific or philosophical theory, for faith uses current knowledge as an instrument without identifying itself with any theory, remaining free to readjust as knowledge advances. Recognize that the world is an organism with internal ends, whose adaptations and beauty furnish a worthier teleology than the mechanical theory. The dysteleological significance of natural selection is at an end; we can see purpose in nature. Thus, you can embrace new insights without fear, as long as they align with the eternal truth you have already practiced.

prompt: How much of my income should I set apart for the LORD's work, and does that include money given to me for expenses?
completion: The Bible encourages generous giving, but the Lord asks how wealth was come by and what will be done with it. Greater means bring greater responsibility to spread righteousness and relieve misery. All property belongs to the Lord, and our business is to dispose of it as He dictates—whether all, a tenth, or the surplus. Money given to you for expenses is not your income; it is entrusted to you for a specific purpose, so you should not count it as personal income for tithing. Instead, live from day to day upon the Lord's bounty, treating hoarded provision for the future as a snare. Make one investment in His work and the poor, trusting that God will provide. Thus, you steward all He gives, not as owner, but as a faithful servant.

prompt: I am poor and struggling to provide for my family; does God care about my poverty?
completion: Yes, God cares deeply about your poverty. Throughout Scripture, God shows special concern for the poor and vulnerable. He promises to provide for your needs and encourages you to trust in Him. The church is called to help those in need, and church revenues belong to the poor; even sacred vessels may be devoted to their relief. So do not hesitate to seek support from your community. Remember that poverty is not a sign of God's displeasure; many faithful people have been poor. God values you for your character, not for your wealth or station. Trust in divine providence, which will provide, and do not hoard church goods. Yet know that God may deny a specific request in kindness, for His denials are often better than the thing asked. Resign your will to His, and trust that He will sustain you.

prompt: How should I think about the death of my son on the battlefield?
completion: The death of a son in battle is a profound tragedy, and we must voice the mothers' charge: the killers slay infants, wound fathers, and kill mothers. Hell is full with the deed and Heaven shut, and the blood of guiltless innocents has been spilt. This is the horror of war. Yet excessive mourning is a want of faith and confidence in God, who takes away friends because He will be loved without a rival. So do not allow your soul to dwell in sadness, bitterness, or scrupulous fear. Instead, ground your consolation in the goodness and sweetness of Him who died to give you life. Honor your son's memory by cherishing the good he did and by supporting others who suffer similar loss. Trust that God is near to the brokenhearted and will sustain you.

prompt: I am old now and my beauty is gone. How should I think about the years I have left?
completion: It is natural to grieve the loss of youth, but you are not a rose that simply withers. Roses and leaves pass away, yet our life is not theirs. The longings you feel now—for beauty, meaning, permanence—are promises of their own fulfillment. The world itself grows old and its mirth fades, yet it still needs Youth to come joyously like the wind at morning, bringing freshness, strength, and radiance and keeping alive the hope of Spring. You can be that morning wind, not by clinging to bodily vigor, but by spiritualizing thought: forsaking the mortal sense of yourself as a fading body and turning to Truth, which is ever fresh. Let your remaining years be spent in that renewal of mind. Then care for the body follows thought, and your presence brings morning to others.

prompt: We came here with almost nothing and built everything from scratch, but no one seems to remember. How should I see our history?
completion: It is painful when sacrifice goes unrecognized, but you should see your history by a truer measure. The greatest wealth you possess is not the buildings you raised or the credit you were given; it is the knowledge of how to direct your labors rightly and to spend every hour advantageously for the benefit of your family and neighbors. By that measure your history is already rich. See further: your people's gift is not a rival to others but an excellence meant to be perfected and combined with theirs, for God's method in history is to guide each people's gift into a richer common life in which all find a place. And beneath all of it stands the one idea no reason can uproot: Christ was foreknown before the foundation of the world and manifested for our sake (1 Peter 1:20). God has been directing history from the beginning. Offer your labor into that larger purpose, and your history lives on in a common good that includes many peoples.

prompt: I want to know whether the Jesus of the Gospels is one person or several conflicting portraits.
completion: The Gospels do not give us a small figure we can fully comprehend; they give us a picture so manifold that it is self-evidencing. Jesus appears there as Lawgiver, Teacher, Healer, Ruler, and Saviour, in the richness of a mysterious person too deep for any single account. Mark shows his action and suffering, Luke his compassion, John his divine depth. Yet we must hold the theologia Christi rightly: Jesus is Lord, Saviour, and Son of God, and one must think of him as of God—but he was never placed on an equality with the Father. In the early faith two Christologies stood beside each other: the man who has become a God, and the Divine being who appeared in human form. They were held together without any doctrine of two natures. So read each Gospel on its own terms, let the whole picture stand, and think of him as of God while honoring the Father he serves.

prompt: I've been away from the sacraments for years—how do I come back?
completion: Coming back after years away is more common than you might think, and you can begin simply. Speak with a pastor or priest who can welcome you without judgment. Begin attending worship again, even before you feel ready to receive. Baptism and the Lord's Supper are chosen means of blessing, related to faith as the sign is to the thing signified—not magical guarantees, yet not negligible, and not to be neglected without adequate cause. But remember: not advancing is going back. Return is not one act but a continuing advance. And when the soul's storms rise, call on the Lord present within you; awakening him calms the storm. Above all, understand the Eucharist spiritually: it is communion with God, where Truth is the bread, the cross the cup, and the inspiration of Love the wine. Come with faith, keep advancing, and let the community support you.

prompt: At night I feel alone and afraid of dying. How do I face the dark without despair?
completion: Fear at night is common, but you need not face the dark alone. It is not night if Christ be near. Ask him to abide with you from morn till eve, and when night is nigh, to stay. Without him we cannot live or dare to die; with him, the darkness loses its terror. Do not dwell on fearful names for what you feel, and let no frightening diagnosis be impressed on your thought; deny the error mentally without voicing it. And do not treat your solitude as a failure. Each heart's bitterness is its own, and God alone knows us fully. Accept the hidden solitude as Heaven's will, trusting him with your secret throbbings. Rest in the Lord, who knows all yet loves us better than he knows.

prompt: I am putting together an order for tracts—what quantity earns the discount, and what about postage?
completion: If you are ordering tracts to spread the truth, order generously so the literature reaches as many as possible. Buyers receive a 40 percent discount on purchases of 100 or more in unbroken packages, and postage is always added when this discount is allowed, so plan for shipping on top of the reduced price. As you order, seek out some sad and needy heart for whom nothing is prepared, pray for one who has none to pray for him, and love even the unworthy as Christ loved. Let no personal solicitation or collection be made for GOD's work; rather leave each hearer burdened to ask GOD what He would have him do, trusting that unsolicited giving will supply what is needed. Confirm the invoice, including postage, before paying.

prompt: I feel the world is old and tired and I'm supposed to bring something fresh to it—is that a real calling or just my vanity?
completion: The world is old and tired, and its mirth has gone; yet that is why Youth is called to come joyously like the wind at morning, bringing freshness, strength, and radiance, and keeping alive the hope of Spring. But before any such renewal, lay the foundation: self-renunciation, watchfulness, humility, and compunction, without which exterior mortification and devotions bear little fruit. Be indifferent to health or sickness, riches or poverty, honor or dishonor, and long or short life, desiring and choosing only what most leads to the end for which man was created—this indifference concerns what is left to free will, not what is forbidden. Test the calling by whether it turns outward in patient service rather than self-display, and let the aged world be refreshed through a self-renounced life.

prompt: I'm a young person who has been wasting evenings playing cards and I feel my time slipping away. What should I do instead?
completion: It is good that you notice the drift. Persistent card playing tends to beget the gambling spirit and the desire to get something for nothing; it wastes precious time and destroys religious feeling, so chance games should be banished from families. Take up instead the habits of King Cormac: listening in the woods, blindness to secrets, mildness in the mead-hall, sternness in battle, gentleness to allies; do not deride the old, do not speak of anyone in his absence, and give rather than ask. Fill your evenings with reading, service, and family. And when distraction comes in prayer, do not meet it with violence or discouragement: gently bring the wandering heart back to its Master and lay it tenderly at His feet without distress.

prompt: I am a teacher who has received a charism of knowledge; may I use it freely for the good of all, even if some cannot understand it?
completion: A charism of knowledge is given for service, so use it freely—but remember that continual education and the pursuit of all useful knowledge are a religious duty. Education does not consist only in learning letters and scholastic lore; it also means learning to classify oneself and others rightly, and a firm, unchangeable course of righteousness secures true intelligence. So do not accept ignorance as normal; teach at your hearers' level with plain examples and call them onward, keeping essentials accessible while never setting true science against true religion. Yet do not rely on intellectual instruction alone to convey the things of God: the true knowledge of God and of Christ comes by the Spirit's anointing and illumination. Teach, therefore, with humility and prayer, trusting the Spirit to open understanding where explanation alone cannot.

prompt: My spouse and I married chiefly for happiness and now feel empty; what should marriage aim at?
completion: Marriage aimed chiefly at happiness will disappoint, since happiness is a byproduct, not a foundation. Wait prayerfully on God for guidance, and make true godliness the first and absolutely needful qualification in a companion, then calmly weigh other suitableness. Now practice patience, mutual compromise, and tender care; separation should not occur without a Christian demand, and divorce warns of fundamental error, so do not treat emptiness as a verdict on the marriage. Yet do not rest in bare faith or theological book-learning as though these sufficed for full happiness. Seek the Responsive God, who answers the heart that takes Jesus Christ firmly and faithfully into heart and life; there emptiness gives way to a living fellowship that marriage can share and reflect.

prompt: I keep failing at the same faults—should I be discouraged?
completion: Repeated failure is not a reason to be discouraged, but neither is it a reason to lower your effort. Bring the utmost fidelity to your exercises and remain untroubled and unastonished when infirmity causes failure. Yet do not make light of wilful small faults: deliberate minor sins are dangerous beginnings from which the most dreadful falls arise. Distinguish infirmity from presumption, repent seriously where you chose the fault, and amend. But do all this without hurry, over-eagerness, or anxious fretting. Keep yourself in God's presence, for anxiety is an obstacle to perfection and over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections. Strive calmly, return quietly, and stay present to God.

prompt: What does it actually mean to be holy—is it about being purified or about something else?
completion: Holiness is not a vague process but a life wholly yielded to God, and the filling of the Holy Ghost is not an optional privilege but a command to be claimed. Bring an empty, honest, trusting heart before God and ask to be filled—not half-filled, but filled for purity, victory, and power. Receive sanctification as God's gift through the Holy Ghost, not as human self-improvement or laborious mortification; it is received by faith, and He walks you in His statutes by His own impulse. Yet this gift is formed in us through real praying: prayer-force is the maker of saints, and where praying increases, true saints increase. So claim the filling as commanded, expect it by faith, and give yourself to prayer. Holiness is the Spirit-occupied life, received as a gift and lived out in trusting, praying obedience.

prompt: I preach every Sunday but rarely pray. Can my preaching still give life?
completion: Preaching can communicate truth, but life-giving preaching is costly. It is not a matter of technique or a small scheduling adjustment. Life-giving preaching flows from death to self, crucifixion to the world, and the travail of the soul. Only a crucified man can preach crucified preaching. Yet preaching is not harmless or automatically beneficial: rightly executed, it brings untold benefits; wrongly executed, it can exceed all other evils in its damage, for the preacher may lock as well as unlock. Much prayer is necessary to keep the preacher's spirit in harmony with his calling. Sermon-making and ministerial diligence alone cannot keep the spirit in trim; sermon-making without prayer hardens and estranges the heart from God. So let prayer, not routine, shape your preaching, so that you unlock rather than lock and give life rather than damage.

prompt: I go to church regularly and keep the commandments—isn't that enough to make me a Christian?
completion: Going to church and keeping the commandments are good, but they are not enough to make you a Christian. Christianity is a life, not an act done by hands. Mere commandment-keeping, baptism, or believing that Christ lived and was crucified does not make one a Christian. Nor must you always be at church to be with God: you may make an oratory of your heart, conversing with Him in meekness, humility, and love. But do not stop at trivial, changing devotions. Enliven your faith and take it as the rule of conduct, for the way of faith suffices to bring us to perfection. The real question is whether Christ lives in you and whether your life is shaped by His Spirit. Let faith, not mere form, govern your conduct.

prompt: How do I resist temptation without becoming anxious and scrupulous about it?
completion: Resisting temptation without anxiety begins with a right view: temptation itself is not sin, and displeasing temptations are harmless. Their suffering is merciful, because the displeasure they cause proves your will does not consent. So despise the temptation and embrace the tribulation it brings, rather than fearing it. The deeper practice is prayer: wait before God like a beggar, keeping your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, recall it in tranquility without disquiet. Do not hurry or fret. Keep yourself in God's presence and avoid anxiety, which is an obstacle to perfection; over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections. Acknowledge tempting thoughts calmly, turn to God, and choose to act rightly. When you fall, confess quietly and move on. The goal is humble, peaceful waiting before God, trusting that the suffering of temptation is a mercy showing your will does not consent.

prompt: I've done something terrible in my past and the memory hunts me down—can I ever be safe from it?
completion: The memory that returns is not a verdict to rehearse but a call to take every fault seriously: wilful small faults are dangerous beginnings from which dreadful falls arise, so nothing should be slighted. Yet do not impress the wrong upon your thought or name it repeatedly as though it had power. Deny it mentally; refuse to accept relapse as a real reaction, and meet its cause mentally and courageously—trace the fear to its source in thought and answer it with what is true. There is no real relapse in Truth, only a false belief to be corrected. Make amends quietly where you can, without self-punishment. A trusted counselor may help you hold thought steady. Safety comes not from dwelling on the fault but from meeting its cause in mind, conquering fear, and holding thought to what is true and good.

prompt: I want to know whether my love for others should be guided by what they want or by what they truly need.
completion: Love is not chiefly a feeling of warmth but the will to please and benefit the beloved, even at cost to yourself. Yet such love is not blind: it abounds in full knowledge and all discernment, distinguishing good from bad, better from best, and best from excellent. So ask not only 'what does this person want?' but 'what is truly good here?'—and beware the self-seeking love that binds another to your delight or rejoices when they surrender their ease to you. True love seeks not itself to please; it gives its ease for another and builds a heaven even in hell's despair. What people want matters because love honors dignity, but love does not merely gratify wants; it seeks their real good at cost to itself. This love grows by frequent acts of service and by considering what has been done for us. Serve quietly, offer what is needed as invitation, and let discernment guide the sacrifice.

prompt: I am afraid of dying young. How should I think about a long life versus a short one?
completion: It's natural to fear dying young, but consider that the exhortation in this Church and Kingdom is not to prepare to die but to prepare to live. We should teach children in the morning of their days to lay the foundation of health, strength, and constitution, so that longevity may begin to return. Rather than fearing a short life, focus on building a healthy, purposeful life that honors God. Mortal existence is a school of experience and probation, where we are meant to learn, improve, and increase continually. Yet ultimately, mortality is not real; being is immortal and inseparable from Deity. Do not wish life away; instead, embrace each day as an opportunity to progress. Cultivate gratitude, serve others, and grow in faith, making the most of the time you have, and leave the number of your days in God's hands.

prompt: I delayed speaking to a friend about his soul and he died suddenly; can I be forgiven for that neglect?
completion: I'm sorry for your loss. It's important not to let your soul dwell in sadness or scrupulous fear. God is merciful and forgiving, and His goodness and sweetness are greater than your neglect. While you may have missed an opportunity, you can be forgiven if you confess it and ask for forgiveness. Do not let this burden weigh you down; instead, ground your consolation in Him who died to give you life. However, understand that while we should forgive those who err through lack of judgment, the Spirit of truth will not tolerate or forgive determined, premeditated wrong. There is no forgiveness for such without humble and most contrite repentance. If your neglect was deliberate, you must repent deeply. Yet do not treat the sick from self-condemnation, guilt, or doubting trust; rather, work from the moral might of Mind and firm trust in Truth. Learn from this and be more attentive in the future, but do not live in guilt. Trust in God's grace and forgiveness, and allow yourself to receive His peace.

prompt: I get so irritated by my coworker's habits that I snap at them—how do I stay kind when I'm at my limit?
completion: It's understandable to feel irritated by a coworker's habits, but snapping at them is not the way. To stay kind when you're at your limit, first bridle your tongue and subdue your anger. Take a deep breath and pause before responding. Examine yourself: why does this habit provoke you? Attend to your own duties and mind your own business rather than judging or meddling with your coworker. Learn contentment from the willow, which lives thankfully on the least Heaven gives and recovers its willing smile after being assailed. Droop patiently under rude hands and wear again a willing smile. Moreover, as much as possible, withdraw from acquaintance and from men; abstain from affairs that hinder your purpose; seek with jealous care the place, time, and means most suited to quiet and contemplation; lovingly embrace silence and solitude, and fly the agitation of a world never at rest. You cannot control others, only your reaction. Practice self-control and remember that kindness is a choice. If you must speak, do so calmly and gently, but avoid unnecessary confrontation. Focus on your own work and let go of the need to correct others. With practice, you can respond more gracefully even in frustrating situations.

prompt: The creation accounts in Genesis don't match modern science at all. How am I supposed to read them?
completion: Read Genesis one as the spiritual account: the Science of Mind and its formations, where God creates by His word and all is pronounced good. Chapter one sets forth divine order and spiritual formation, not material mechanism, so it does not compete with modern science; the second account is the material, figurative picture. As 1 Peter 1:20 says, Christ was foreknown before the foundation of the world and manifested for our sake—the one idea of pre-existence no reason can uproot. When our Lord appeals to the Old Testament, He is not resting on questions of authorship or date but on its abiding spiritual testimony to Himself. His authority stands whole and unfallen; read Scripture as He did, for the truth that speaks of Him.
