prompt: How do I handle the sense that my failures have piled up into a pattern I can't break?
completion: It is common to feel that failures have piled into a pattern you cannot break, but that sense must not be accepted as your fate. Resist evil of every sort firmly, for error is opposed to Life and will flee before Truth. Bring the utmost fidelity to your exercises: examine yourself daily, keep watch over thought, word, and deed, pray constantly, and take one concrete right step today. Seek leaders who will rise up, tell you plainly your iniquity, chasten you, and teach the way of salvation; if they cannot be chastened and set right, they have proved recreant to the faith, and if they dare not speak, they have fallen from their station. Yet when infirmity causes an occasional failure, remain untroubled and unastonished—return at once to your exercises and persist.

prompt: Should I bear a sign of the cross before me into a struggle?
completion: Yes—bear the sign of the cross before you into the struggle, for it is an impregnable rampart against the devil, made with great faith and devotion rather than by mere custom. Let it confess that you stand under Christ's victory. Yet do not choose your own cross: accept being fashioned by whatever means God pleases, whether consolation or humiliation. Christ suffers still in His lowly members, and the Cross alone sweetens life's bitterest griefs. Desire that the cross before you be wholly the cross of Jesus Christ—His sign, His victory, His patience—and receive from His hand the particular shaping He appoints, trusting His good pleasure in all.

prompt: I am a young believer, and I want to learn to pray as George Muller did. What are the conditions of prevailing prayer?
completion: George Muller prayed as a child speaks to a father—simply, naturally, and constantly. Do not turn prayer into a complicated procedure or a set of man-made rules; bring God your everyday needs, for He is a Father who delights to be sought. And do not set Muller on a pedestal: he was a man of like passions and infirmities, and his strength lay wholly in leaning on God. What he knew, ordinary believers may know if they live according to His will. Above all, let prayer be continual—not an occasional exercise but like breathing or feeding, the constant drawing in of the heavenly life that nourishes the seed of the Divine Life within. So ask plainly, trust His promises, and keep drawing near throughout the day.

prompt: I have made a mess of my youth and I feel like my life is already ruined. Is there any way back?
completion: It is painful to feel that your youth is wasted and your life ruined, but deny any real relapse in Truth and meet its cause mentally and courageously; fear must be conquered, not managed. Do not trust your own powers to save you: the soul is stripped piece by piece, its harness hewn away, its dreams failing, standing naked before God's uplifted stroke—and that stripping ends self-reliance, not hope. For the world is old and its mirth has gone, and it is Youth that must come joyously like the wind at morning, bringing freshness, strength, and radiance and keeping alive the hope of Spring. So rise: own your part, make amends, refuse to plan for falling back, and let your renewed youth carry freshness and strength into a weary world.

prompt: I feel guilty that I prayed for my child's healing and she died. Did I do something wrong?
completion: I am so sorry for your loss. Your prayer for healing was not a sin, and her death is not a punishment for a faulty request. Let your desires be purged of self-concern—worry about your reputation or comfort—and grounded on what your child could be for God and His kingdom. Take comfort in her baptism: the baptismal stream works a wonder through faith and prayer, marking her with Jesus' seal, nursed for His sake. And now pray chiefly for strength to suffer with courage, humility, and love. Cultivate familiar conversation with God and watchfulness over your thoughts, words, and deeds, for these bring the peace of paradise even in this life. Release the false burden that your prayer caused her death, mourn honestly, and let habitual, watchful fellowship with God carry you.

prompt: How can I be sure the second coming of Christ will be literal and visible, and not merely spiritual?
completion: The New Testament presents Christ's return in concrete, physical terms: he will come in the clouds of heaven, every eye will see him, and he will appear just as he literally ascended. The angels told the disciples that this same Jesus would come in the same manner. I am convinced of this and make it my settled commitment once for all: the coming is literal, personal, and visible, as real as the first advent. Any reading that treats it as merely spiritual—Christ reigning only in the hearts of believers, or the event already fulfilled in his saints—beclouds the whole promise and leaves no tangible ground to stand on. I do not claim strict demonstration, but the unique convergence of prophecy, the long historical preparation of Israel, and the beauty of that process furnish high corroborative evidence. Having committed, I stay put through the season of establishing and testing until hope becomes a permanent habit.

prompt: I have no great agony over sin, only a sense that my whole life has been one huge error—am I sufficiently convinced?
completion: Your sense that your life has been one huge error is a beginning, but conviction must go deeper than regret. Learn not to be troubled in tribulations, afflictions, and injuries; do not be incensed against those who inflict them, and do not entertain resentment. Sincerely believe yourself worthy of all injuries, contempt, and scorn, desiring rather to be abhorred as filthy mire than to possess the delights of earth or be honoured by men. Yet understand what sin is: it is insanity, and sickness is error, a loss of harmony. The testimony of the corporeal senses is untrue of man and his Maker, so deny it. Sin is not self-sustaining; it falls back upon itself and yields to Truth, returning to dust. You need not fight a permanent enemy—only stop believing the error, and it dissolves. That is sufficient conviction: honesty that lets error destroy itself.

prompt: How can a new planet have existed before any astronomer saw it, if nothing exists apart from mind?
completion: If nothing exists apart from mind, then the planet's existence is not independent of consciousness—but that does not mean it appears only when an astronomer looks. Mind is not one observer's private mind; it is the universal intelligence in which all things subsist. Scripture gives the pattern: with 1 Peter 1:20, Christ was foreknown before the foundation of the world and manifested for our sake. That religious thought of God directing history is the one idea of pre-existence no reason can uproot. Ground creation not in the material second account of Genesis but in the spiritual first chapter, where God creates by His word and sees it good; proclaim the Science of Mind and its formations accordingly. The senses of Mind are never lost, and matter has no sensation. What seems a loss of sense or limb is only a belief to be overcome, not a real privation.

prompt: Why do Christian nations go to war with one another and pray to the same God for victory?
completion: Christian nations go to war because men precipitate war upon themselves by wickedness. God did not design it; war is the natural penalty by which evil passions punish themselves under God's righteous constitution. It arises from lusts, covetousness, and injustice, and God's righteousness works through these ordinary laws of human nature—sin punishing itself. Praying to the same God for victory is a tragic irony: each side believes its cause is just, yet God takes no side in the slaughter. Peace will never come until mankind receives God's truth. But victory, not defeat, is God's purpose for believers; the secret is Christ himself living in the believer, entered by resting in him. When hearts rest in Christ, the passions that breed war are overcome from within.

prompt: I pray but it feels like words going nowhere—how should I really pray?
completion: Feeling that your words go nowhere is itself a summons to deeper prayer. Make prayer your main assistant in every step: before you read, work, rest, or decide, ask God to go with you and enable you to search out and discover your own heart, and to reform whatever is amiss in it. Do not doubt that he hears—God, who understands all things, hears the earnest supplication of the soul and our innermost thoughts and secret prayers, just as human invention carries messages across great distances. So ask in faith, nothing wavering. But know that prayer is not easy or flattering; it is humbling work that crucifies pride and signs your bankruptcy before God. Little praying is a deluding make-believe, a worse evil than no praying, because it pretends a relationship it does not pursue. Give yourself honestly and daily to this work, and let it search and reform your heart.

prompt: How do I draw strength from the hard things that come to me each day?
completion: Strength of character is not a temperament you either have or lack; it is the will's power to control your actions independently of your inclinations and of the opinions of men. When something hard comes each day, ask not first how you feel but what is right, and do that. Character is formed by repeated acts: each self-victory strengthens the will, each yielding to passion or human opinion weakens it, and progress is proportioned to those victories. Yet do not seek rapid progress through the letter alone or by mere effort. Study the letter, imbibe its spirit, and adhere steadfastly to the divine Principle. And before you try to help another bear his burden, cast the beam out of your own eye: first overcome your own belief and fear of disease or sin, then you will see clearly to help. Let each hard thing first search and heal your own heart.

prompt: I want to be grateful but do not know how to express it; what does gratitude require?
completion: Gratitude begins with noticing, but it does not end in words or feelings. Show it through action and daily watchfulness. Name the gifts in your life—health, relationships, daily provision—and let thankfulness shape how you live. Tell God thank you, but let prayer be more than a spoken performance: make it a life of watchful obedience, attending to what is right and doing it. The habitual struggle to be always good is the truest prayer. Do not prescribe to God what should happen or wish for particular events; bless Him for those He ordains, saying, 'Father, I am thine; do for me all that shall seem good to Thee.' And treat every special blessing as a trust to be passed on: freely give what you freely received, as a witness to others, so that gratitude flows outward rather than hoarding comfort for yourself.

prompt: How then will those subsist in the day of the last Judgment who afflict and vex the poor and deprive them of their sweat, trampling upon them as footstools?
completion: At the last Judgment, those who afflict and vex the poor will not subsist. To grind the poor and take the fruit of their sweat for your own pomp and vanity is to trample upon Christ himself, who said that what is done to the least of his brethren is done to him. It works with the Devil against the Kingdom of Christ, which consists only in Love. And mark this: the poor often pay their tithing better than the rich, for they are faithful and prompt, while the rich can hardly afford it, and many wait and wait to pay until death takes them away and they cannot pay at all. Yet let no ingratitude or ill-treatment cool your zeal; regard the wrongdoer as a patient under disease, and recommend him to God in prayer.

prompt: I love to play and be outdoors, but I'm told it's a waste of my youth. Am I wrong to enjoy it?
completion: You are not wrong to enjoy play and the outdoors. Recreation and diversion are as necessary to our well-being as the more serious pursuits of life. The Lord never commanded dancing or theater, but he permits them, and they let the body keep pace with the mind and give the mind rest. Amusements reveal character, so choose the pleasures that invigorate, brighten, and elevate body, intellect, and spirit, and refuse those that dull and deprave. And do not be ashamed of your youth: the world is old and its mirth has gone, and it needs Youth to come joyously like the wind at morning, bringing freshness, strength, and radiance, and keeping alive the hope of Spring.

prompt: Why did God allow sin to come into the world at all, if He foresaw it and could have stopped it?
completion: God gave angels and men free will, and freedom that cannot be refused is not love, so sin was permitted rather than compelled. But sin must be named for what it is: lawlessness, a fall, and a corruption of man's true nature—never a spring of progress. God foresaw it and could have stopped it, yet in His wisdom allowed it and overrules it for good. Knowing good requires knowing its opposite, but that is no license: we must not do evil that good may come, and we need not sin to learn its bitterness. Man is not made for a dark, chaotic life; he is a potential child of God, whose full nature is meant to break forth in one life, and power is given to become sons of God. The good God brings is His providence overruling evil, not evil producing good of its own nature.

prompt: Does the law make me less free, or can it make me more free?
completion: The law can make you more free, but freedom of conscience must be honored. Agency is sacred, and God does not compel anyone; he persuades by good advice and good example. Yet the law is not done away or relaxed, for it is holy and binding; the question is not whether it should be kept but how, and its righteousness is fulfilled in us by the Spirit through faith. We are called to liberty, but we must not use liberty for an occasion to the flesh. The whole law is fulfilled in loving our neighbor as ourselves, so let freedom serve love and not self.

prompt: I want to give more to missions but feel I cannot afford it—how far should I cut my own comforts?
completion: It is good that you want to give more to missions. See self-denial and economy not as a loss but as a privilege: every comfort cheerfully surrendered frees resources for the LORD and brings a fuller joy than the comfort ever gave. Set apart the firstfruits for the LORD's service, not less than a tenth of all your income, and economise in order to give more largely. And do not think the danger is only for the very rich: a moderate income brings within reach distractions that drown the voice of conscience and base comforts in whose lap duty is forgotten. Comfort makes us thoughtless, and thoughtlessness is the parent of every cruelty. So cut your comforts not merely to give, but to keep your conscience awake.

prompt: Some of my friends mock me for wearing the scapular and say it is superstition. How should I answer them?
completion: Answer your friends calmly and with charity. The scapular is not superstition: it is a devotion approved by the Church and pleasing to Mary, a mark of dedication to her, with promises and the conditions required to gain its indulgences. Three things are required: resign the will to God in humility; hate your own will and refuse to do what it drives you to; and bow under the Cross in willing submission to bear the temptations of Nature and Creature. As Elene inquired of the wise man and chose his advice, setting the nails upon the bridle as a bit for the horse of the most noble among kings, a guard invincible against stress in war and a holy sign of God, sending the bridle to her son over the sea as an offering, so let your devotion be a holy sign worn with wisdom, not a charm.

prompt: Is it wrong to grieve bitterly for those I have lost, or should faith take away all sorrow?
completion: Grief is not wrong, and faith does not ask you to pretend sorrow away. Jesus wept at the grave, yet he touched the bier and gave the dead back to their mother. So you may weep and still rest your loved one in hope of resurrection, trusting in new spring and an endless home. But do not make the removal of pain your chief aim. The saints teach us to thank God for giving, for long sparing, and for taking, and to rejoice that the departed is present with the Lord. So ask not first that the ache be taken away, but for a wise and thankful heart that yields to God's rod. Honor the real loss; let gratitude, hope, and a surrendered will stand alongside it, and let God correct and comfort you as a father does a child.

prompt: I have lost my children, and I cannot stop grieving. Is there any comfort for me?
completion: I am so sorry for your loss. Losing a child is a grief too deep for words, and you are not wrong to weep. Jesus wept at the grave, yet he touched the bier and gave the dead back to their mother. You may grieve bitterly and still rest your children in hope of resurrection, trusting in new spring and an endless home. And you are not alone: no one can see another's woe without sorrow, and the Maker himself sits by you and moans with you until your grief is fled and gone. Yet do not make the removal of pain your chief aim. Ask not first that the ache be taken away, but for a wise and thankful heart that yields to God's rod. Let God correct and comfort you as a father does a child, and let gratitude and hope stand alongside your real loss.

prompt: I'm thinking about marrying someone who isn't a member—is that a problem?
completion: Marrying someone outside your fellowship is a serious matter, and Scripture's counsel about brethren settling their own difficulties applies here too. Brethren should be reconciled and settle their troubles between them; going to the courts of the Church or the land cannot truly settle a difficulty between a man and his brother. So talk honestly with your intended spouse about faith, worship, and family, and seek counsel from wise brethren. But do not look too much to people; look away from people to God, so that in Him alone you are united. And once you marry, commit to patience, mutual compromise, and tender care. Separation should not occur without a Christian demand, and divorce warns of fundamental error. Weigh the matter prayerfully now, and let humility and forbearance guide you afterward.

prompt: I've tried to reform myself and failed repeatedly. Is there any real hope for change?
completion: Repeated failure can feel discouraging, but it does not mean change is impossible. Part of the trouble is that we imagine old habits offer lasting pleasure, yet evil holds no abiding satisfaction—it promises much and leaves us empty. Real reform comes through affection for good, as Science reveals: when the heart loves what is good, the pull of evil loosens. But do not wait until every question is settled. Cut the Gordian knot with the sword of decision, launch out into the deep with a bold plunge, and leave the speculations to Christ. And if you would help others, first cast the beam out of your own eye: overcome your own belief and fear of disease or sin before you attempt to heal another. Examine what you have clung to, turn your affection toward good, take consistent steps, and seek accountability through friends and community. Let love for good, not fear, drive your change.

prompt: My spouse and I argue constantly. How should I bear with him?
completion: Constant arguing is exhausting, and Scripture takes it seriously: contention is a disgrace before God and angels, and litigation brings poverty and ruin to a community. So do not let disagreements harden into a contest you must win. Settle differences by coming together in humility, each willing to wrong himself to make the other right. When you speak, speak plainly so your spouse can hear and understand you; say what you have to say, then stop, and do not darken counsel by many words. Above all, practice patience, mutual compromise, and tender care. Separation should not occur without a Christian demand, and divorce warns of fundamental error—so do not reach for it in the heat of conflict. Bear with your spouse as one on the same team under God, aiming for peace and mutual understanding rather than victory.

prompt: I keep drifting into spiritual laziness—how do I wake up out of sleep before it's too late?
completion: Spiritual laziness is not neutral ground: not advancing is going back, so wakefulness means resuming motion. But do not rush forward in self-will, mistaking presumption for faith. Be slow to take new steps; be willing to have no will of your own. Ascertain God's will by prayer and the Word, testing each proposed step before you take it. Then, having found it, go forward with earnest, patient, believing expectation of his help. Begin with small duties—a psalm, a short prayer, one act of self-denial—for faithfulness in early duty and self-denial leads at last to real pleasures, and recourse to Christ's grace makes every difficulty easy. When storms rise, call on the Lord present within you, whose name calms the soul, and wait on him rather than on your feelings.

prompt: I want to know why the earth was made and what my place in it is.
completion: The earth was not made for its own sake, nor is your happiness the final end. Man was created to praise, reverence, and serve God, and by this means to save his soul; other creatures were made to help him attain that end. The God who made the world is not distant from it: Christ is the Logos in whom all things consist, through whom the world was made and is upheld, who was manifest in human form and made atonement; the secret of the universe and the key to its mysteries is his cross. And the sanctuary where God dwells is a real building in heaven, the true tabernacle which the Lord pitched and not man, of which the wilderness tabernacle and temple were patterns and shadows—not the earth, nor the land, nor the saints themselves. So live as steward and pilgrim: use creatures as helps toward serving God, and read the world in the light of the Cross.

prompt: I've lost my faith in the old beautiful stories I loved—should I force myself to face the hard truth, or let myself keep dreaming?
completion: You do not have to choose between hard truth and beautiful dreams. Faith is not bound to any one theory; it uses the knowledge of each age as an instrument and readjusts as knowledge advances. But do not demand sight, certainty, or a visible path before you move. Faith trusts and goes forth, not knowing whither, steering by God's heavenly light rather than waiting for the shoreline. Nor defer to time-honored systems, cold conventionality, or material systems of thought: think independently, and seek a right apprehension of God as Life eternal. Be honest about your doubts without making certainty a precondition. The longing those stories awakened is a clue to follow, not a dream to abandon. Step forward in the dark, trusting the light that leads rather than the path you can already see.

prompt: I worry that I cannot be exalted unless my spouse is faithful too. Can a person be exalted alone?
completion: Exaltation is not an individual matter: a man cannot be exalted into God's presence alone, and the man is not without the woman, neither the woman without the man, in the Lord. So your spouse's faithfulness is not a private side issue, and your own faithfulness is not a self-contained project. Yet do not rush to separation or divorce: counsel patience, mutual compromise, and tender care, remembering that separation should not occur without a Christian demand, and that divorce warns of fundamental error. At the same time, do not demand perfect human sympathy, for each heart's bitterness is its own and God alone knows us fully. Accept hidden solitude as Heaven's will, trust God alone with your secret throbbings, and rest in the Lord who knows all yet loves us better than He knows.

prompt: I am tempted to despise this world and all bodily things as worthless; is that contempt a true piety or a despair that leads to superstition?
completion: Contempt for the world can be either piety or despair, and the difference lies in what it produces. Learn not to be troubled in tribulations, afflictions, and injuries; do not be incensed against those who inflict them, nor entertain resentment. Sincerely believe yourself worthy of all injuries, contempt, and scorn, desiring rather to be abhorred as filthy mire than to possess the delights of earth or be honoured by men. But do not mistake doubtful dread or despair for humility or meekness: that is a foul blindness and weakness against truth, coming subtly of Enmity. Distinguish it, and turn the bitterness of doubt into the sweetness of love by the knowing of love. Nor is the change mere will-power: disordered desires—for tobacco, liquor, profanity—simply left through the study of the textbook, without resolution or sacrifice. Test your contempt: does it make you grateful and free, or bitter and fearful? Receive bodily things with thanks and use them without slavery.

prompt: Is it dishonest to accept the critical position hypothetically while the questions remain unsettled?
completion: Yes, it is dishonest, and dishonesty is sin, to be confessed and forsaken. But do not demand mathematical proof before you may speak. The question is only whether the testimony is probably true; Scripture facts are proved when established by the kind and degree of evidence that would satisfy a common man in ordinary affairs. Accept what satisfies an unprejudiced mind beyond reasonable doubt, and be plain about what remains unsettled. Do not adopt a critical stance to appear fair while your convictions are otherwise. Do not, however, turn inward to inspect whether your honesty is perfect; that is curious examen. Humble yourself over faults found, and go on with simplicity and confidence, leaving the outcome to God.

prompt: How do I hand over my worries about money and daily needs to God?
completion: Handing over money worries begins with trusting God rather than securing yourself. Consider the helpers who gave themselves and their goods to God's work without salary, believing He would supply all their need; commend that spirit, offering yourself and your substance cheerfully and self-denyingly. Let your prayer be like a beggar waiting before God: keep your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, recall it gently and in tranquility, without disquiet. And beware of hoarding a reserve for future want as though it were the prudent course for one who trusts God—such stored provision can become a snare. Live from day to day upon the Lord's bounty, and make one investment in His work and the poor.

prompt: Can I be holy if I still have obvious flaws and blemishes in my life?
completion: Yes, you can be holy while flaws remain, because holiness is not attained all at once; it grows gradually, and mutual help comes by advice and especially by good example. Let others see your honest walk, receive their counsel humbly, and let your example encourage them. Yet do not settle for a love that seeks something less than perfection. Aspire constantly to the perfection of holy love, seeking nothing less than perfection in that love. And do not imagine that sin can be pardoned while it is tolerated. Sin must be forsaken and destroyed, for God's pardon is the destruction of sin, not its toleration. Acknowledge your blemishes honestly, forsake them, and let grace reform you together with the community of faith.

prompt: I am orthodox in doctrine and careful in study, yet my people seem dead. Could the problem be in me?
completion: Yes, it may well be in you. Orthodoxy and study are good, but they can become substitutes for the living Christ they describe. Confess Jesus as the only-begotten Son, God manifest in the flesh, omnipresent, omniscient, omnipotent, our living Lord and Judge, in whom all the fulness of the Godhead dwells bodily. But do not imagine that right doctrine, or the name of Christian, or the mere fact of dying to self, guarantees life. Death works no miracle; we are after death exactly as far advanced as before. The Seed of Divine love must be planted and consciously growing in us here. So pass through the dying hour and live abundantly on Christ's risen life, letting that life grow in you and be seen in your people.

prompt: I believe Jesus lived and was crucified. Isn't that all that's required?
completion: Belief that Jesus lived and was crucified is a starting point, but it is not the whole of the Christian life. The Gospels call us not merely to affirm facts but to follow Jesus and take up our cross. Yet measure your sufferings against Jesus crucified, covered with wounds and despoiled of everything; your own can in no way compare with His. Do not treat him as only a figure of the past or a hope of the future. Rest in the living Christ's continuous presence now—not 'I will be' but the unbroken presence that is with us forevermore. And do not live your own life or show forth your own excellencies. Let Christ be formed in you, living the Christ-life through you, showing forth His excellencies as a re-living of His life in your place.

prompt: How do I love God with my whole heart when I still feel attached to creatures?
completion: Love of God is not first a feeling but a rational, voluntary self-giving: you choose Him as your true good, seeking His glory and your real good, and every affection is regulated by holiness. Do not imagine your smallness makes you unnoticed—God's knowledge is undivided, and His attention rests wholly on each soul, so the ocean-tides of His love pour into even the smallest heart. So cease moaning over your unworthiness and attachments as though you must first become better before you may love Him. Rise up now and bless God with all the love you have, keeping none back; love Him from sickness as fully as in health, from weakness as in strength. Order your creaturely loves under His will, surrender what draws you from holiness, and give Him your whole heart today.

prompt: I'm not afraid of dying, but I'm afraid of what I've done—what do I do with a guilty conscience?
completion: A guilty conscience is a gift only if it leads to repentance, not despair. Name your sins honestly, make amends, confess, receive absolution, and do penance. Do not presume: unrepented sin accumulates and hardens the heart, destroying your ability to do right, so repentance must mean reformation of life. Then commit yourself and all that concerns you to the unfailing and most sure Providence of God in silence and peace, accepting all things, whatever their cause, as from the fatherly hand of Divine Providence, and rejecting the vain and wandering thoughts that weary soul and body and waste time and strength. Know that all evil of whatever kind happens by God's permission and ever for some good end; it could not be except He permitted it, and its form and measure are allowed by Him who can and will by His wisdom turn all to good. Therefore commit all things without fear to His Providence.

prompt: I want to be honest, but I wonder whether truth is just whatever God decides to command—does that make truth arbitrary?
completion: Truth is not arbitrary, because it is not first a decree but the eternal conformity of God's being and knowledge—what He knows and is, in perfect agreement, from everlasting. God's veracity toward creatures flows from that eternal truth, so His commands express truth grounded in His being and cannot be arbitrary. This is no speculation: truth is the foundation of religion and salvation, and our hope must rest wholly on it, not on error or partial guesses, for hope built on error collapses. Accept all truth from whatever source it comes—no one should refuse a fact because of who speaks it—yet insist that truth remain the foundation of religion, and that no organization, party, or authority rises above it. Let your honesty in word and deed flow from the God who is eternally true.

prompt: I have a chance at a position of honor. Should I want it?
completion: Honor is not wrong in itself, but the heart must be ordered. Offer God all your liberty, memory, understanding, and will, holding nothing back, and desire only His love and grace as your chief good. Ask whether this position helps you keep in His presence and labor for His glory and the good of souls, or whether it feeds pride and pulls you from duty. A place of honor is worth wanting only as a means of serving God and neighbor. Honor the memory of the martyrs and prophets, and delight to honor the instrument God used in the mighty work of the restoration. Let gratitude, humility, devotion, liberality, and honesty shape you: give freely, speak and act consistently and sincerely, and hold the opportunity loosely, ready to accept or decline as best serves His glory and the good of souls.

prompt: I am a minister and fear the frown of wealthy parishioners more than I should—how should I reprove sin among them?
completion: Fear of wealthy parishioners is understandable but dangerous. The message you carry is God's, and obedience is owed to it regardless of the preacher's example or weakness; the misconduct of preachers does not excuse hearers from obeying a message that comes from God. Reprove sin clearly, gently, and privately where possible, with humility about your own failings. As an officer of the Church, judge justly and promptly by the Spirit, without partiality or favor-buying, and care for every member of the Ward—especially the poor and sick. Be an example without corruption. Above all, refuse the holy table to notorious sinners: Christ will demand an account of His blood if it is given to the unworthy, and the priest's power in this is above an emperor's. So do not admit unrepentant sinners for fear of the wealthy; preach the whole counsel of God and trust His message.

prompt: I want to be a saint quickly, but I keep failing at the same sins—should I be discouraged?
completion: Feeling discouraged after repeated falls is understandable, but the saints warn that virtue is only truly great when it is constant and crowned with perseverance. You must not presume that you will automatically persevere; rather, live in fear, watchfulness, humility, and compunction to the end. Falling after a long course is not excusable but is mere negligence. Moreover, pride is the beginning of all sin, so examine whether your discouragement stems from wounded pride. Imitate the saints, who saw their own imperfections clearly and counted themselves as dust and worms. Let your failures deepen your humility, not your despair. Remember that perfection is possible in every lawful profession without leaving your state in life; you can become a saint right where you are, in your daily duties, by God's grace. Keep striving with sober watchfulness, always relying on God's grace.

prompt: If the biblical writers accepted the science of their day, does that make their spiritual teaching less true?
completion: No, the biblical writers' acceptance of the science of their day does not make their spiritual teaching less true. The Bible is not a science textbook; it uses the language and concepts of the times to communicate spiritual truths. Christian Science is not merely an intellectual or philosophical system but is fathomed by the Christian who understands best the divine Life. The spiritual teaching remains true because it comes from God, regardless of the scientific views of the human authors. The truth of the Bible lies in its message of salvation, not in its cosmological details. We must affirm one infinite Spirit and deny any real intercommunion between opposite states of consciousness. Alleged spirit communications are mortal mind's images and beliefs, not realities. So we can trust the spiritual teaching while recognizing the cultural and scientific context in which it was written, and we can understand it through the lens of divine Life. This reasoning rests on the Bible as the sole authority, showing how reason and revelation coincide in divine Science.

prompt: Is the kingdom of God something that will drop out of the sky someday, or something I help build?
completion: The kingdom of God is not merely a spiritual or inward state; it is a literal kingdom on the earth, composed of living and resurrected saints, with laws and administrators, and Christ will reign over all the earth. While it begins in the hearts of believers, it will be fully realized as a visible, earthly reign. The coming of the kingdom is the total task of humanity through the ages, realized in lives wholly under the holy Will and consecrated to making that Will prevail in society. Yet this kingdom must be revealed from heaven; an angel restores the everlasting gospel as a warning to all nations, a Zion is built up, and judgements prepare the way for Christ's reign. You help build it by participating in God's mission, but ultimately it is God who establishes it. The kingdom is both a present reality and a future hope, and we look forward to its full manifestation when Christ returns to reign.

prompt: How was Constantine able to conquer the Huns and Goths with a lesser army?
completion: Constantine was able to conquer the Huns and Goths with a lesser army not by his own strength or fortune, but by the sign of the holy rood given by the King of angels. Fear-smitten before the greater host of Huns and Goths, Constantine received a messenger of the King of angels promising aid and the token of victory. Gazing on high, the emperor beheld the beauteous tree of glory inscribed 'By this sign thou shalt overcome the foe.' Through this holy rood, the victory was made manifest as given by the King Almighty. Thus, it was not military skill but divine intervention that granted him the triumph. Similarly, the origin of the Christian Church is an insoluble mystery apart from the resurrection, which transformed weak men into conquerors for the faith. Furthermore, belief in the bodily resurrection of Christ and the admission of the flesh into heaven blocked the full development of Hellenic dualism within Christianity.

prompt: I have been taught that the world is getting better and will be converted—is that true?
completion: The idea that the world is getting better and will be converted before Christ returns is not true. The Bible indicates that evil will persist until Christ's return, and the world will not be fully converted before He comes. Our hope is not in the world's gradual improvement but in the return of the Lord Jesus. We are called to live faithfully, in purity and service, until He appears. So, while we work for good, we should not expect a utopia before He returns. Instead, we look forward to the day when He makes all things new. Moreover, to be great is to be good before the heavens and before all good men, and goodness sheds a halo of loveliness around every person who possesses it. Finally, it is our privilege and duty to be as wise in our generation as the children of this world, and even wiser, because we are privileged with superior advantages through faith and obedience to the Gospel, and we ought to know more about all matters than any other people.

prompt: I feel too unworthy to be loved by God. Why would He want anything to do with someone like me?
completion: Feeling unworthy is common, but God's love is not earned. Instead of begging God to come down, we can enter into His estate by faith and offer Him love. Faith brings us nearer to God than any sensible favor, for He is within us and should be sought there. When we turn inward in faith, we find that He is already near, and we can respond to His love with our own. The more we focus on loving God rather than on our unworthiness, the more we realize that He has always loved us. So seek Him within, not in outward signs. And remember that Christ ever loves you and approves of you tenderly; claim His sweet approval and tender regard, for He has made you worthy in Himself.

prompt: I have bitterness toward someone who wronged me and I can't forgive them. Will that affect my prayers?
completion: Bitterness can affect your prayers, but not because God is petty. Forgiveness is an inward condition of the personal life; it comes naturally to the soul that loves and forgives. If you hold bitterness, your own spirit is hardened, and that blocks your communion with God. So forgiveness depends on your own spirit as well as on God's grace. But remember: sin is forgiven only as it is destroyed by Truth and Life. Prayer cannot be a safety-valve for wrong-doing; divine Principle never pardons sins until they are corrected. And see this wrong as allowed by God's hand: all from Him, sweet or bitter, should be received equally. When afflictions are seen as from a loving Father, they become consolation. So forgive, correct your heart, and trust that God is using even this to draw you closer to Him.

prompt: Does the Bible anywhere change the Sabbath from the seventh day to the first day of the week?
completion: No, the Bible nowhere changes the Sabbath from the seventh day to the first day of the week. From creation, God blessed the seventh day and hallowed it (Genesis 2:3). The fourth commandment enjoins the seventh-day Sabbath (Exodus 20:8-11), and Jesus kept it (Luke 4:16). The apostles also kept it (Acts 17:2). The Sabbath remains for the people of God (Hebrews 4:9). No Scripture can be produced that changes the Sabbath to the first day. The seventh day is still the Sabbath of the Lord. But remember that the Sabbath is made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27). Institutions are instruments for human life; institutionalism is a danger. We must keep institutions in the secondary place, even breaking them for the sake of human welfare, as Jesus did when He healed on the Sabbath. The seventh-day Sabbath is the memorial of creation and the sign of the cross, the seal that God sanctifies His people. Trust Christ for the cost of keeping it, for He is Lord of the Sabbath.

prompt: I believe all the facts about Jesus and that He died for sinners, so am I saved?
completion: Believing the facts about Jesus is not enough. Saving faith begins with an awakened conscience. First, you must see your sin and its danger—that it separates you from God and deserves His judgment. The Bible says, 'The wages of sin is death' (Romans 6:23). Let that truth sink in. Then, turn from your sin in repentance, and believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, who died for sinners and rose again. Only when you have seen your need can you truly trust the Savior. So ask yourself: Have you been awakened to your sin? Have you repented? If not, cry out to God for mercy, and then believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved. But remember: sin is not your essential nature. You are a potential child of God, not meant for a dark chaotic life. In Christ, the full nature of God can break forth in your life, and you can receive power to become a son of God. And as you come to Christ, do not approach from a position of superiority. Identify with the sinner, confess your own faults, and point to the fountain opened for sin. Follow Christ, who took our sins and made them His own.

prompt: I feel that the world must have some one Reality behind it, but I cannot see why it should be mind rather than matter.
completion: The ultimate Reality must be Mind, not matter. Matter cannot explain mind; it cannot account for consciousness, reason, or the intelligible order of the universe. Mind, however, can explain matter, for matter is known only through mind. A Something neither mind nor matter is both unintelligible and gratuitous—it explains nothing and adds nothing. Therefore, the one Reality behind the world is Mind. This is not just a philosophical preference; it is the only coherent option. So consider that the world is the expression of a universal Mind, and that you yourself are a participant in that Mind. And realize that suffering in childbirth is not a fixed law but a false belief to be removed, for Mind controls birth without suffering. Deny sensation and intelligence to matter: nerves and brain have no feeling or thought. All pain and sickness exist in mortal mind alone, and are healed by the understanding that Mind is All.

prompt: Can the spread of Christianity as it is now preached bring about a millennium of peace?
completion: The spread of Christianity as currently preached cannot bring about a millennium of peace because the promise of peace at Christmas is conditional. The angels' song proclaimed peace and goodwill only to those who heartily submit to Christ as Saviour and King. The wars and conflicts we see are not due to any weakness in Christianity but to the grievous neglect and negation of Christianity by nominal Christians who do not truly submit to Christ. Social progress is the steady replacement of antagonism by fellowship and co-operation, the same principle by which Christ founded His Kingdom. To hasten the millennium, we must engage in patient intellectual effort to refute hostile ideas and make the rest subservient to the gospel, that Christ may rule in every department of human life. This requires discrimination and consecration, not wholesale denunciation of modern culture nor absorption in it to the neglect of the gospel.

prompt: Why does my preaching feel powerless even when I prepare well?
completion: Feeling powerless in preaching despite good preparation is a common experience. It may be due to a lack of prayer or reliance on the Holy Spirit. While preparation is important, it is not enough; the preacher must also cultivate a deep prayer life. Much prayer is necessary to keep the preacher's spirit in harmony with his calling. Sermon-making without prayer can harden and estrange the heart from God. Prevailing with God precedes pleading with men; the mightiest in the closet are the mightiest in the pulpit. In every occasion of virtue, including preaching, we should turn to God for enabling grace, asking and receiving strength more than sufficient. Therefore, ensure that you are not relying on your own efforts but are seeking God's anointing through prayer. Additionally, examine your heart for any unconfessed sin or distraction that might hinder the Spirit's work. Remember that preaching is not about eloquence but about faithfully proclaiming God's Word in reliance on Him.

prompt: I'm afraid of the tribulation times ahead—how should I prepare?
completion: Fear of tribulation is natural, but as a Christian, you should not be paralyzed by it. Instead, flee to our Lord and say in your thinking that your pain is shrewd but He is All-Mighty, All-Wisdom, and All-Goodness loving you tenderly. Abide in that beholding. Preparation involves deepening your faith and trust in God. First, stay rooted in Scripture and prayer, building a strong relationship with God. Second, live a life of obedience and holiness, so that you are ready to face trials. Third, be part of a supportive Christian community that can encourage and help you. Also, remember that God permits evil inclinations for humility. Despise the temptation while embracing the tribulation it brings. While it's wise to be prepared practically, the most important preparation is spiritual. Trust that God will give you the strength to endure, and focus on living faithfully each day rather than dwelling on fears about the future. Combine inward fellowship with Christ and outward service, avoiding morbid seclusion and living for the help of others and the preparation of the world for His appearing.

prompt: I'm trying to understand what Jesus meant by taking up the cross. What does that mean for me?
completion: Taking up the cross means denying yourself, putting to death your sinful desires, and following Jesus wholeheartedly. It involves a willingness to suffer for Christ's sake and to prioritize God's will over your own comfort. In practical terms, it means daily choosing to obey God, even when it's costly. It also means identifying with Christ's sufferings and being willing to face persecution or hardship for the gospel. The cross is no new thing but the putting of the love of God into the old fundamental pieties of the human heart—the realising by Jesus in Himself of the dearest truths about God. It reveals the infinite degree of God's interest in our life and the responsibility He assumes for its eternal issues. But the cross is also Christ's work for us—bearing our sins and wiping out our guilt. An ideal alone is a cruel mockery to those enslaved by sin. For you, it means accepting being fashioned by whatever means God pleases, desiring that the cross be wholly the cross of Jesus Christ. Examine your life, identify areas where you are not fully surrendered to God, and take steps to align your life with His will. It's a call to radical discipleship, where you put Jesus above all else and live for His glory.

prompt: How may I understand that the virtue of Love is Nothing and All Things?
completion: Love is often described as the greatest virtue, but calling it 'Nothing and All Things' is a paradox that requires unpacking. Love is 'Nothing' in the sense that it is not a tangible thing; it is not a substance or an object. It is 'All Things' because it is the underlying principle that holds everything together. Love is the virtue of Nothing and All, the principle of all principles whose power is through all things and whose height is as high as God. Whoever finds it finds Nothing and All Things. In 1 Corinthians 13, Paul says that without love, we are nothing. Love is the fulfillment of the law and the greatest of all virtues. To understand love as Nothing and All Things, we must recognize that love is not about possessing things but about self-giving. It is the essence of God's nature and the calling of every believer. When we love, we participate in the divine nature and fulfill our purpose. Love believes all things and covers others' faults, clothing them with the graces faith can claim for them, being gentle with their imperfections as God is with ours. Yet love is not a mere emotional affection, a utilitarian calculation, or the all-inclusive attribute that includes truth and holiness. God's love is rational, voluntary self-communication that seeks the true good of its object and is regulated by and subordinate to holiness.

prompt: Someone I love is suffering and I don't know how to help. What does it mean to truly share their sorrow?
completion: To truly share someone's sorrow is to love with pity, never without it. When we fall into suffering, Christ alone keeps the charge—He does not abandon us. For reverence and kindness, we should turn hastily to Him and not leave Him alone. Yet do not seek too eagerly after sensible devotion, sweetness, or tears; chiefly care to remain inwardly united to God by good will in the intellectual part of the soul, denying yourself to follow Christ, Who was poor, obedient, chaste, humble, and suffering. Recognize that God employs suffering as a remedy for moral evil, a means to cure the soul, and that His righteousness is at work even in pain. Christ's own agony was submitted to in perfect love, proving that agony is compatible with the most perfect love between God and the sufferer. Share their sorrow by turning quickly to Christ together, being present and praying, and pointing to the One who sustains.

prompt: I feel that my body is a burden and a foul thing; does God care for my body at all?
completion: Yes, God cares for your body, but He may also use bodily illness to cure your soul. Suffering with God is a paradise, while pleasure without Him is hell. Your body is not foul; it is a vessel through which God works. When illness burdens you, consider that God may be using it to draw you closer to Himself, to purify your soul. Even in pain, if you suffer with God, you are in paradise. Yet healing is not merely a touch of power upon the body; it is vital union with the risen Lord, who is for the body. Receive Christ Himself in vital union with your mortal body, knowing Him as strength, health, and full physical redemption. Remember that God chooses the poor, weak, and despised to accomplish His purposes, so do not despise your body or your weakness, but offer it to God, trusting that He can turn your burden into a blessing and your suffering into a cure for your soul, ascribing all glory to Him.

prompt: How can I forget myself?
completion: To forget yourself, wait before God like a beggar, keeping your mind in His presence. When your mind wanders, do not accept relapse as real; deny it in Truth and meet its cause mentally and courageously, conquering fear. Prayer is a humble waiting before God, not a striving. Simply place yourself in His presence and remain there, letting go of self-preoccupation. But self-denial is not merely giving up a few indulgences; it is laying the axe at the root of the tree of self. It is a voluntary self-renunciation taken up for Christ's sake, not a forced trial. Deny self-will, self-seeking, and self-glory entirely, and take up the cross willingly. This is how you forget yourself—by fixing your gaze on God, resting in His presence without anxiety, and renouncing self at its root.

prompt: I have things in my house I never use; does keeping them hinder GOD's blessing on me?
completion: Keeping unused things can hinder God's blessing. Unneeded possessions weigh you down and can prevent you from being generous. God calls us to examine what we have and to part with what others could use. This habit of mind—being ready to share—brings blessing. But also remember that nothing should go to waste. No one is wealthy enough to let a servant sweep a single kernel of wheat into the fire; no man is so rich that he can suffer a crust or a kernel to be wasted. Through carefulness and frugality, we preserve and increase the blessings God bestows. Yet blessings are conditioned on obeying God's law, paying tithing, keeping the Word of Wisdom, and building temples. So examine your possessions, share what others can use, waste nothing, and faithfully keep God's commandments, so that His blessing may rest upon you.

prompt: I want to be sure of heaven; is there any sign or pledge that I can look for?
completion: The assurance of heaven comes through faith in Jesus Christ, but our proposed end is to become the most perfect worshippers of God in this life as in eternity. The Holy Spirit is given as a pledge of our inheritance, and He works in us to make us worshippers. Look for the fruit of the Spirit—love, joy, peace—as evidence of His presence. A changed life and a desire to follow God's commands give confidence. Yet perfect resignation to God is a sure way to heaven, providing sufficient light for conduct. When you surrender your will to His, you walk in assurance. Also, affirm baptism and vicarious ordinances for the dead, for those who died without the Gospel may be brought up into glory through the living. So trust in His Word, rest in Christ, seek to become the most perfect worshipper of God, practice perfect resignation, and participate in the work of redemption for the dead.

prompt: Can I be sure my husband who died in battle is at peace with God?
completion: I am sorry for your loss. Do not look first for peace in your own reasoning, but look to the Lord of peace Himself, who gives peace of conscience, heart, and fellowship and does not change with circumstances. If your husband trusted Christ, Christ's work alone secures his peace; the manner of his death did not decide it. Scripture presents God as a God of deliverances who keeps His people in answer to prayer—yet His purposes are fulfilled in the death of some as surely as in the deliverance of others. Neither outcome contradicts His faithfulness. So bring your grief and your questions to Him, seek Him among His people, and rest not on what you can see but on His unchanging love in Christ.

prompt: I am about to cross a dangerous sea. How should I prepare my heart?
completion: Before a dangerous voyage, prepare your heart by settling your trust in God and putting your affairs in order. Pray for protection, confess known sins, and make peace with those around you. When distractions come, gently bring your heart back to its Master, laying it tenderly at His feet. Begin study with morning meditation, implore divine light in all reading, season studies with aspirations to God, and resolve doubts at the foot of a crucifix—for study without humility, simplicity, and prayer nourishes vanity and error. Cultivate purity of heart by the text's own steps: keep a strict guard over your senses, practice recollection, and be candid with a spiritual director. Watch against vanity, pride, sensuality, self-interest, and aversions, which corrupt purity of intention. Prepare practically too, and entrust the outcome to God with a steady heart.

prompt: The government has asked something hard of our community that feels unjust. Should we comply or refuse?
completion: This is a difficult situation, and your community's sense of injustice deserves to be taken seriously. Quiet your hearts and ask gently: ought this thing to be done or not? If it ought not—if it requires sin or violates what is right—then let it alone, whatever the cost. If it is merely burdensome, it may fall among the necessary things to be borne. Know whether you ought to do a thing; if not, let it alone; do the necessary things and leave the unnecessary alone. Correct your heart quietly, without harsh reprimand. Receive this trial as necessary and meet it cheerfully, examining your own obedience rather than blaming enemies alone, and trust God to overrule the efforts of those who oppose you. Seek counsel, act together, appeal through proper channels, and pray for discernment and for the officials involved.

prompt: I am a young person with questions my elders call rebellion—where can I turn?
completion: It is painful to have your questions dismissed as rebellion, but there is a better way than confrontation. Be peaceable, submit to the authorities that exist, pray for rulers, and wait patiently for the Lord to establish His own government in His own time. Learn the habits of King Cormac: listen quietly, be blind to secrets, be mild in the hall and stern only in battle, be gentle to allies. Do not deride the old, do not speak of anyone in his absence, and give rather than always asking. And hold on to an old friend; no matter how many new friends you gain, hold fast to the old, and let only wicked conduct break the thread of fellowship. Ask your questions humbly, seek trusted mentors, and let patient faithfulness, not revolt, shape your hope in the Lord.

prompt: I'm a caregiver for a sick relative and I'm exhausted—is it wrong to want a break?
completion: Wanting a break does not make you a bad caregiver, and rest is not a sin. But devotion to God sometimes means forgoing innocent, lawful pleasures so the soul takes its pleasure only with Him. Let your caregiving be shaped by that devotion: visiting and instructing the sick is a strict duty for every Christian, not the minister's business alone. Seize the time Providence affords in lingering illness, for while there is life there is hope, and do not leave the dying without gentle warning and instruction to flee from the wrath to come and turn to Christ. Arrange respite care and ask family to share the load, offering even your rest to God. And support your relative's trust in the power of Mind: tell them their strength is in proportion to their courage, not that their courage exceeds their strength.

prompt: I gossip and joke at home and then feel unclean. Does it matter what I say in my own house?
completion: It matters very much. The tongue is a fire, and being indoors does not make it harmless. Gossip and fault-finding against neighbors is slander whether spoken at your own table or in the street. The uncleanness you feel is a truthful signal, not scrupulosity. So bridle your tongue, subdue rising anger, and examine yourself before you examine your neighbor. Mind your own business and your own duties rather than judging or meddling in others' affairs, and speak of what is good in others. Yet clean talk is not enough: keep secret prayer as indispensable, for public or pleasant conversation cannot make up for closet communion with God. Pray and read the Word even when enjoyment is gone, and let that hidden fellowship season your speech at home.

prompt: I want to be found among the elect; how does election work?
completion: Election is God's gracious purpose in Christ, but it does not cancel your freedom. The authorities are set before you and you are sincerely requested to act freely and independently in voting and speaking; no one has told you how to vote, and no one has been injured for honestly stating objections. Choose the best and most capable men for office without regard to party, sustain constitutional law, and oppose corrupt administrators. Yet good men and good laws are not enough: the great need of democracy is the education of feeling and character—reverence, self-control, and sobriety of judgment—for only an educated public moral sense can rightly weigh and press upon governing classes. Look to Christ, repent, and believe, letting the fruit of election appear in a changed life; make your calling and election sure by growing in faith and holiness.

prompt: My love rules my mind completely and I feel freer than ever—is that a healthy surrender or a dangerous tyranny?
completion: What you describe may be healthy or dangerous depending on what rules. Do not turn inward and brood, nor violently resist every stirring of self-love; disavow it gently a few times a day, quietly turning toward God and the good of the other. Ask whether this love makes you more patient, generous, and prayerful, or more possessive. When dryness, sadness, terrors, or temptations arise, do not conclude your love is false or useless; serve God purely for love of his will even then, refusing that suggestion. And keep constant, patient watchfulness, for self-love, though mortified, never dies but springs up again, so vigilance must not relax.

prompt: I'm a young woman and people say women are the weaker vessel—is that true?
completion: The phrase speaks of difference in strength and a call to honor, not lesser worth; before God men and women are equal heirs of grace. But do not sink upon a bed of sloth, and do not let intoxication overcome you. Rise and begin a voyage across the clear sea, that you may reach the Land of Women. Remember that divine love is strong and concerned with character: it wields correction out of love, and there is no schism between love and justice. And know that exaltation is not an individual matter: a man cannot be exalted into God's presence alone, for the man is not without the woman, neither the woman without the man, in the Lord.

prompt: I want to know whether the creator of this world is the same God who redeemed us in Christ, or a different and lesser being.
completion: There is one God, and no lesser maker behind the world. Christ is the Logos in whom all things consist, through whom the world was made and is upheld; the Word who was in the beginning with God became flesh and made atonement. The secret of the universe and the key to its mysteries is found in his cross. This Lord is not absent now: his presence is unbroken, not merely past or promised, for he says, 'I am with you alway.' And he is not only distant lord or judge, but very Father and very Mother to us: Christ's kind Motherhood feeds and keeps us in nature and in grace, so that we may rest in his continuous, nurturing presence.

prompt: I keep reading the prophets and feel they speak of something beyond themselves, yet I cannot tell whether that is my imagination. How should I read them?
completion: Your sense that the prophets speak beyond themselves is not mere imagination, but study alone will not settle it. The Scriptures are a guide pointing to the Fountain of light, not the Fountain itself; read them prayerfully and in context, yet seek the living oracles and the Spirit of revelation, without whom the letter stays closed. Do not be troubled that God inspired writers through methods suited to an undeveloped age—dramatic composition, primitive tradition, idealizing history. These are vehicles of inspiration, not fraud. Nor is prophecy merely poetic ideal or human foresight: it is the foretelling of future events by direct communication from God, an attestation of revelation proceeding from divine knowledge. Its advantage over miracle is that the proof lies under our eyes, and every new fulfilment strengthens the argument. Read, then, watching fulfilment and seeking the Spirit who speaks.

prompt: I'm terrified I might not be saved—how should I think about this?
completion: Being terrified about salvation is a heavy burden, but do not let small faults paralyze you. Meet them without terror: humble yourself quietly before God and keep steadily on, saying, 'Courage! we have made a false step, but let us keep steadily on.' Recognize fear itself as a greater evil than the evil you fear, and refuse to let it rule your soul. It is Satan's falsehood, so answer it with trust: 'What time I am afraid, I will trust in Thee.' Cry out with St. Peter, 'Lord, save me!' and clasp the hand He extends. Trust God for goodness and mercy all the days of your life, and let trust, not terror, direct your path.

prompt: How do love and holiness fit together in a daily Christian life?
completion: Love and holiness belong together because God is both loving and holy—but holiness is the fundamental attribute, and love is normed by it. God's righteousness is fundamental in His nature; His law reflects it, and sin is an offense against Him, not merely an inconvenience. The condition of salvation is propitiation to the divine righteousness, met in Christ. Mere moral systems can show what life ought to be but provide no power to become it; Christianity alone solves that practical problem by a Divine remedy—grace through sacramental channels and the recreative work of Christ in His Church, a school of character. In daily life, true religion is a believing dependence on the unchangeable love of God joined to an affectionate walk in the unchangeable path of duty. Seek the peace of God that passes understanding rather than occasional frames, and when you fail, return to grace.

prompt: I am eloquent and earnest in the pulpit, but I see no lasting fruit. What am I missing?
completion: Eloquence and earnestness are gifts, but lasting fruit is not chiefly a matter of technique. What you may be missing is the closet. Prevailing with God precedes pleading with men; the mightiest in the closet are the mightiest in the pulpit. Before refining delivery, ask whether you wrestle with God for your hearers by name and whether your private devotion feeds your public ministry. Then subject every doctrine, custom, and practice to the one test of the word of God, willing to retract error and follow new light regardless of cost. Yet remember: the fruit of the Spirit is not manufactured behavior or forced conformity. It grows from the life of Christ in the heart, cannot be forced by human effort, and against such there is no law. Abide in Him, pray without ceasing, preach faithfully, and leave the increase to God.

prompt: How do I begin to love someone I've never seen?
completion: Loving someone you have never seen begins with turning gently away from yourself. Self-love will make its sallies; do not violently resist or brood over them—a gentle denial suffices, disavowed quietly a few times a day. When sadness or aversion rises, cease curious inquiry into its causes; patiently endure aversions and repugnances as a way of loving Him who suffered. But do not read your difficulty only as wrath or punishment. Let Love transform the afflictive circumstance into an angel entertained unawares: the unseen person, and even the resistance you feel, can become a messenger of God drawing you out of yourself. Then turn outward—learn their story, pray for them by name, serve in small ways, speak well of them. Repeated small choices of goodwill will grow genuine affection over time.

prompt: How do I pray the way Christ taught, entering into my inner chamber and shutting the door?
completion: Christ taught that we must worship God in spirit and in truth, adoring Him with an intelligence and will purified from every phantom of earth—from fear, appetite, and self-will. To pray as He taught is to enter the inmost chamber of the heart and shut the door of the senses, closing out the clamor of material sense and the pull of sin, and there to commune with the Father who sees in secret. We come with a pure heart, a free conscience, and unfeigned faith, denying sin and affirming God's allness. This prayer is our main assistant in every step of spiritual progress: we pray that God would enable us to search out and discover our own hearts and reform whatever is amiss in them. Sincerity is then proven in practice, as purified desire becomes pure living.

prompt: I feel closest to God in nature, out on a hike or by the sea—is that a real experience of Him or am I fooling myself?
completion: Feeling close to God in nature can be a genuine experience, but it is not automatic. The Holy Spirit works through the truth already revealed in nature and Scripture, not through vague impressions apart from them. Nature can awaken awe, but you must actively engage your reason and will to receive and test what you sense. Do not expect divine guidance without means; instead, let your hikes and time by the sea become occasions for conscious thanksgiving and reflection on God's revealed truth. Open your heart deliberately, appreciate His works, and test all new impressions by Scripture. Remember that the God you meet is the eternal Trinity—Father, Son, and Spirit—who before the foundation of the world existed in eternal distinctions and intercourse of love. This triune God is not merely revealed in time but is eternally Father, Son, and Spirit. So as you open the door, you are drawn into the eternal love that has always been. Then you may truly find Him, not by compulsion, but through appreciation and willing reception, with your faculties fully engaged.

prompt: I want to know whether the death of Christ on the cross has anything to do with understanding the universe as a whole.
completion: The cross is no new thing, but the putting of the love of God into the old fundamental pieties of the human heart. What the soul always trusted—that God is faithful and cares for the living and the dead—Jesus realised in Himself, revealing the infinite degree of God's interest in our life and the responsibility He assumes for its eternal issues. Scripture gives us not a theory of the universe but the moral character of God, and the cross is where that character is chiefly seen; here is the ground of hope for men and for society. Yet our consolation must rest wholly on Christ Himself—His sufferings, temptations, cross, death, resurrection, and pleading at the right hand of the Father. Looking at self clouds the view; His promises leave no room to doubt His power and will to save. To understand the whole, we must see it held by the God who in Christ took our life and its eternal issues upon Himself.

prompt: I am poor and ashamed of it. How should I see my poverty?
completion: Poverty is not simply a moral failing, but neither is it always the fault of circumstance. Much poverty comes from a want of discretion and sound calculation—spending without planning, or buying unnecessary finery a tight budget cannot bear—so examine your habits honestly and correct wasteful choices. Yet some poverty lies outside your control, and that is not your shame. If you receive help, receive it honestly and thankfully, and be frugal with what you are given; and guard your heart, for coveting another's goods is as wicked as miserly hoarding. But see your true standing: the poor are the giver's 'masters,' with great interest in the court of heaven, whose intercession makes almsgiving the wisest provision a person can make. So carry your poverty with dignity, contentment, and honest frugality, and let others give generously—for in doing so they store up the best provision for themselves.

prompt: I am dying of a consumption and my mind is sometimes clouded with doubts—how do I know my hope is not a delusion?
completion: Your fear is natural when the body weakens, but do not measure hope by the body's condition. Mind, grounded in divine strength and understanding, normally governs the body; you need not conquer doubt by will-power. Come before God like a beggar, asking nothing clever, only waiting. Keep your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, do not be disquieted—gently recall it in tranquility. And if you forget Him altogether, let that cause you no distress: forgetting is not a failure to be anxiously repaired but an occasion to return with greater trust, as one returns home. This waiting is not passivity but confidence in One who is calm. Depraved appetite and fear lose their force because Mind, sustained by divine strength, is master. A delusion would be trusting your own strength; true hope trusts Another. Even a wordless waiting is enough, for He holds you more surely than you hold Him.

prompt: I'm afraid of the future and can't sleep at night thinking about what could happen to my family—how do I stop dreading tomorrow?
completion: It's understandable to feel afraid when you love your family, but the counsel is to have no care for the morrow. Instead of forecasting what could happen, think only of doing well today: keep to your duties, be kind to those near you, and trust the eternal Father's care for tomorrow. When fear rises at night, master it rather than cultivate it—turn your thought from imagined harms toward health and Life as God, and rest in the confidence that today's work is enough. If you stumble in small faults, do not be terrified or paralyzed; humble yourself quietly before God and say to your soul: 'Courage! we have made a false step, but let us keep steadily on.'

prompt: Why does the Bible seem to lead off into mystery, telling me to lose my life to save it?
completion: The Bible does not lead you into a riddle; it calls you frankly to the path of cross-bearing, and it does not disguise its severities. The fundamental maxim of the gospel is this: die to yourself, that Christ may live in you, with all your affections and actions governed by his Spirit. We generally acknowledge this in speculation only, yet it is in the heart that this foundation must be laid. We hinder God's graces by undervaluing them, so make way for grace and redeem the time, since death is near and final. Losing your life for his sake is heroic, not easy; it costs comfort and reputation, but it brings the comradeship of God and of his people.

prompt: If I pray for daily bread, am I asking for a shortcut around hard work?
completion: Praying for daily bread is not asking for a shortcut around hard work. Prayer and honest toil are joined: we ask God for what we need, and we receive the bread of the day as God-given within the avenues of daily work—planting, tending, earning—rather than as a substitute for it. Doing our work for the love of God, with prayer for grace, makes it easy: love lightens the toil and grace supplies the strength. But we must not pray for riches; we may ask only for the means to keep ourselves and our families from want. Prayer without work becomes presumption, and work without prayer becomes self-reliance; asking for daily bread keeps us humble and grateful while we do our part.

prompt: I have won a great victory—whom should I thank for it?
completion: First, thank God, since strength, opportunity, and the abilities that made the victory possible are gifts you did not manufacture alone. Let your gratitude be devout and humble, and be liberal with credit: give freely, name specific contributions, and be consistent and sincere in word and deed. Then thank those who helped, and go further—condescend to the humor of others and bear with rude and tiresome manners, offering these victories over your own humors for the love of God. But do not stop at fading earthly memorials: seek the Saviour first, and then go to win the erring brother, giving wreaths of hope rather than fading memorials.

prompt: I am not sure whether I should break bread every Lord's day or only occasionally. What does the Scripture teach?
completion: Scripture does not give a single explicit rule like 'every Lord's day,' but several strands point that way: the early church devoted itself to the breaking of bread, and believers met on the first day of the week. The bread of the day is not a substitute for labor: prayer and honest toil are joined, and the bread comes as God-given within daily work. Set before yourself the two ways, life or death, whichsoever you shall please to choose; refuse the worse and choose the better. And when the soul is broken and stripped, do not read it as God's indifference or cruelty: it is the charring of wood before it can be limned, a painful but loving preparation, not for the soul's harms. The question is left as the text leaves it: must Thou char the wood ere Thou canst limn with it?

prompt: I look at the size of the universe and feel like a meaningless speck. Does God even notice me?
completion: It is natural to feel small before the vastness of the universe, but size is not the measure of worth. The universe and man are not recent products but are as eternal as God, their divine immortal Principle. God is not present by power only, nor by parts diffused through space, nor bound to the universe by necessity as in pantheism. In the totality of His essence He is present in every place without division or diffusion, and this presence is free, qualified by His transcendence. He counts the stars by name and knows you. If your only design is to please Him, He gives light in your doubts; He does not leave the single-hearted in darkness. Bring your smallness to Him honestly, let it become humility, and trust that the God who names the stars also names you.

prompt: Should I keep a record of the times God answers my prayers?
completion: Keeping a record can be helpful, but do not imagine that prayer times differ from other times. Adherence to God is equally required in action as in prayer; separating them is a delusion. Join prayer to every ordinary action: at work, in the shop, abroad, sitting, or lying down, keep God always before your eyes. Then a record is simply a journal of a life that prays without ceasing. Write down definite answers and give God the glory for them. For example, when I was pressed by a need I could not meet, I prayed and God supplied it in a way I could not have arranged; I wrote it down and told others, and their faith was strengthened. Keep such a record, not to exalt yourself, but to honor God and encourage faith in others.

prompt: Was the Sabbath made only for the Jews, or is it still binding on God's people?
completion: The Sabbath was given at creation, before there were any Jews: Genesis 2:2-3 says God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it. The fourth commandment stands among the Ten (Exodus 20:8-11). The seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord, blessed and hallowed at creation and remaining for the people of God (Hebrews 4:9). It is no bondage and no merely Jewish custom: it is the memorial of creation and the sign of the cross, the seal that God sanctifies His people (Exodus 31:13; Ezekiel 20:12).
