True humility dreads the esteem and praises of others as snares by which a mortal poison may imperceptibly insinuate itself into her affections and deprive her of divine grace; she always places herself below all creatures. So practice small acts of lowliness: listen more than you speak, admit when you are wrong, serve quietly, accept correction without arguing. Even your courage should be a humble courage, grounded in low esteem of self, so that its greatness lies in humility rather than in confidence in its own powers. Humility is not thinking badly of yourself; it is thinking of yourself less and of God and others more, and it grows through patient practice.

prompt: Why has Germany, a cultured and educated nation, done such terrible things?
completion: The greatest wealth is knowing how to direct labor rightly, spending every hour for the benefit of family and neighbors. That is what the monks of Ireland's Golden Age showed: their monasteries were a haven of rest and a great seminary of Christian and classical learning, and their sons carried Christianity and a new humanism over Britain and the Continent, becoming teachers of nations and counsellors of kings. Germany's tragedy was learning severed from service, labor turned to domination. The answer is not to despise culture but to recover it as Ireland did: sanctity joined to scholarship, and every hour ordered to the good of the neighbor.

prompt: I am a scribe and my hand aches from copying. Is my work worthwhile?
completion: Your work is worthwhile, and the weariness you feel is not truly in the muscles but in mortal mind's false talking. Do the work for the love of God, praying for grace, and labor so offered becomes easy. Do not fix your mind on long ages of slow copying as though the last days must unfold as in former times; God will cut his work short in righteousness, and events are hastening, so prepare yourself rather than counting years. When the ache speaks, answer it with the understanding that Mind governs the body, and let prayer turn drudgery into devotion. Then the same hours that tired you will refresh you.

prompt: I am a soldier ordered to kill in battle. Is that murder before God?
completion: War is the natural penalty by which evil passions punish themselves under God's righteous constitution, arising from lusts, covetousness, and injustice. Yet the Lord of all is merciful: if we straightway purge ourselves of evil deeds and cease from the unrighteous act, mercy is available, though we have many times transgressed. Do not believe the enemy's suggestion that all things are against you; your trials are wisely chosen to make God's Word and presence more precious. So examine your orders, refuse what is unjust, and turn from evil without delay, trusting that God is working His purpose even in hard circumstances.

prompt: I feel weighed down by guilt that I cannot seem to shake—can anything actually deal with it?
completion: Guilt that will not lift is exhausting, but begin with what is in your own hands. In this probation we have evil to contend with, and we must overcome it in ourselves or we shall never overcome it anywhere. Bridle your tongue, subdue anger, and examine yourself honestly rather than judging others; attend to your own duties faithfully. Unless the appetites are brought in subjection to the spirit, one cannot inherit eternal life. So let the tabernacle be subject to the spirit. Where you have wronged someone, make amends; where the guilt is false, release it. Work from the moral might of Mind and firm trust in Truth, not self-condemnation, and do not carry it alone.

prompt: I have plenty of money and see beggars every day—how much am I actually obliged to give them?
completion: There is no fixed percentage, but giving must be done in God's way. Do not solicit funds from unbelievers, press believers to give, or use worldly schemes; examine every gift and refuse what comes from impure motives or money that is not the giver's own. Giving is voluntary and cheerful: the Lord is the giver of all, and we return a portion in gratitude, never by compulsion. Support the poor and the Kingdom freely, without harming your household's needs. And require of those you help that they be honest, thankful, and frugal; for coveting another's goods is as wicked as miserly hoarding. Treat each beggar as a neighbor deserving dignity and truthful dealing.

prompt: Someone hurt me badly. How can I forgive them when I can't even pray for myself?
completion: Forgiveness is hard when you are wounded and exhausted. You do not need perfect prayers right now; tell God honestly that you are hurt and cannot even pray, and let that honesty be your prayer. If you feel you have forgotten God or failed in prayer, do not be disquieted: such lapses are met not with condemnation but with a return to Him in greater trust. Know that God is not distant or powerless: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever, and He can and does heal in answer to prayer today. Ask Him for healing and for strength to forgive, trusting His willingness while leaving the outcome in His hands. Remember that forgiving your enemy is the best revenge: by bearing injuries patiently you gain grace and the pardon of sins without trouble or expense. Take one small step at a time, and be patient as healing grows.

prompt: I am told that circumcision or some outward rite is necessary for salvation—does an outward form avail anything?
completion: No outward rite or ceremony confers salvation by itself. Scripture is clear that neither circumcision nor uncircumcision avails anything; what avails is the new creation wrought by the cross of Christ. Yet this does not make the sacraments optional: baptism, administered by immersion under divine authority, is essential, and children should be baptized at the age of accountability. Carry the cross of Christ as a crown, not a mark of shame; use its sign in prayer and sacrament, and never blush at the ensign of salvation. Circumcision was settled in the early church: Gentiles were not required to be circumcised, because salvation is by grace through faith. If someone insists a man-made ritual is necessary for salvation, be cautious. What matters is a heart made new, living faith, love, and obedience.

prompt: If I had one hour with someone I lost, how should we spend it—tenderly, or exactly as we always were, faults and all?
completion: Let the hour begin with God. Resolve never wilfully to forget Him and to live in His presence even when consolations are absent, knowing our need of His grace. Be jealously and habitually occupied with Jesus throughout: when distracting thoughts or trifling words arise, turn from them and look steadily up to Him, refusing to lose your peace over a straw. Then be honest and loving with the one you lost: say what you never got to say—thank you, I am sorry, I love you—or simply be as you always were, faults and all, because that familiarity is part of what you miss. Yet pass lightly over the pain rather than following it with mourning; hold to comfort and sure trust in God's keeping in both woe and weal, and let the hour rest in that trust rather than in grief alone.

prompt: I struggle with anger and bitterness toward people who have wronged me. What should I do?
completion: Anger and bitterness after being wronged are understandable, but do not add anger over your own agitation. Refuse to be disquieted that you feel this way; gently place your troubled heart in the hands of our Lord and ask Him to cure it, renewing your good resolutions as you go. Meet evil with good at all times, clad in the panoply of Love, so that human hatred finds no unprotected place in you. Keep Christ closely as a bouquet of myrrh, and remember that the bitterness is ours and not His: He is not bitter, but He allows us to be bitter to ourselves. Name the hurt honestly, set healthy boundaries where needed, and trust God with the healing rather than feeding the resentment.

prompt: I am a Gentile Christian and the word Christos means little to me; how should I express the dignity of Jesus?
completion: It is understandable that a Greek title like Christos feels distant. Don't chase after sweet feelings, tears, or moving titles; chiefly care to stay inwardly united to God by good will, denying yourself to follow Jesus, who was truly poor, obedient, chaste, humble, and suffering. And remember what the name means: a Christian isn't just a religious person or a vague imitator of Christ, but one to whom Christ is Saviour and Lord, subject to Him. Christos means Messiah, the Anointed One—and He is your Lord. Keep it simple and human: be childlike, reach others by simple kindness, worship, prayer, love of neighbor, humility, and service, and let your life say what your words need not.

prompt: I want to know whether the sacraments are only for the individual's comfort or also bind me to others.
completion: The sacraments are a sacred ordinance that adds to your acceptance or condemnation, so each must examine himself and no one should knowingly permit the unworthy to partake. Yet this is not bare ritual or mere material symbol, for Christianity provides for man's whole nature, bodily and spiritual, through its sacramental principle. The Eucharist is spiritual communion with God: Truth is the bread, the cross is the cup, and the inspiration of Love is the wine. Partaking worthily therefore binds you to God and to others in truth and love, while unworthy partaking brings condemnation. Guard the ordinance, examine yourself, and seek the living communion it signifies, not the outward elements alone.

prompt: How do I keep a sense of God's presence while I'm busy at work?
completion: Do all your actions for God without anxiety over distraction, keeping the practice simple rather than multiplying explicit offerings. God is always near, and He should be remembered and adored continually, even in business and diversions, not neglected. So let a quiet, steady intention run beneath your work, returning gently when you wander. Trust Him also to provide both the individuals and the means for any work He orders, as He fitted the workers and furnished the materials for the Tabernacle. One calm intention, renewed often, is better than many anxious offerings, and it keeps you aware of the God who never leaves you.

prompt: I've been trying to grow in holiness but feel unsettled about whether I'm truly accepted by God—where should I start?
completion: Begin with the contemplation of God's faithfulness, power, and grace, turning from endless self-analysis to His character, which produces restfulness, quietness, strength, and confidence. Combine inward fellowship with Christ with outward service, living for the help of others and preparing the world for His appearing, avoiding musty seclusion. Then test yourself not by claims or words but by fruits: does your life demonstrate Truth and Love, bringing healing and the supreme good? Let fruits prove your understanding, for assurance grows from living the good rather than from describing it.

prompt: I pray only briefly at night before bed and in the morning when I remember. Is that enough?
completion: Give the best of your time and strength to prayer, putting the closet first and study and activities second, freshened by the closet. Guard your mind's wandering outside prayer, for keeping it in God's presence makes recollection easier. Recognize that continual help of God is needed: praying, being with God, and thinking of Him often are linked through holy habit, since we must know before we love. Brief, remembered prayer is a beginning, but let it grow into that habit, so that knowing Him more deeply leads you to love Him more fully.

prompt: I'm afraid of what God will demand of me if I really give myself to Him. Do I have to give up my home, my children, my friends?
completion: God may deny a request in kindness, and we should resign our will to His, trusting His denial can be better than what we asked. Gifts freely received must be freely given, so hold your home, children, and friends as gifts to be shared rather than hoarded; he who forgets to hoard has learned to live. Yet go further: cease from petitions for yourself and desire only, by opening yourself through offering great love, to receive God Himself. That is the heart of surrender, and it need not mean losing what you love but loving Him above all.

prompt: I'm afraid of death—how should I think about my last end?
completion: Fear of death is natural, but death is not the end of who you are—it is a door to a higher state, where identity is preserved and the body is raised. The righteous dead are not lost, so do not mourn them as though all were finished. Yet do not be deluded: death works no miracle, and the mere fact of dying—or of bearing the name of Christian—guarantees nothing. We are after death exactly as far advanced as before. The Seed of divine love must be planted and consciously growing in us here. Death is certain and its time, place, and manner utterly uncertain, so make now the changes you would wish to have made when death is near, and let hope steady you rather than postpone preparation.

prompt: I've been gossiping and tearing down someone's reputation—why does it feel so satisfying and how do I stop?
completion: Gossip feels satisfying because it creates closeness, gives a sense of superiority, and offers quick stimulation—but it is backbiting that wounds a neighbor's reputation. True humility dreads the esteem and praises of others as snares by which a mortal poison may imperceptibly insinuate itself into her affections and deprive her of divine grace; so the very satisfaction is the warning, and she places herself below all creatures. Refrain from fault-finding, mind your own business, and seek and speak of the good in others. Yet do this with sweetness, not sourness: true virtue increases gentleness of mind, attended by invincible constancy and firmness in every duty, and whatever makes us morose or peevish makes us worse and gives a tincture of the temper of devils. So redirect or excuse yourself when talk turns to tearing someone down, kindly and firmly, and let the change be gentle as well as constant.

prompt: I am a materialist and think mind is produced by the brain—how do I answer the claim that mind knows itself as higher in kind than matter?
completion: The materialist answer assumes we know only sensations and passing feelings, but we have direct knowledge of substance underlying phenomena: an external world persisting through our impressions, and a spiritual substance—a self retaining identity through change. Every thought is owned by a self that acts from within rather than passively receiving impressions. We must distinguish the real spiritual man from the so-called physical ego; that ego is mortal mind, brain-bound, and not the true self. And like produces like: Mind is first and cannot produce its opposite, matter, nor can matter produce Mind. So when mind knows itself as higher in kind than matter, it is the spiritual man knowing, not a brain secreting thought. Grant the phenomenology, but deny that passive matter could ever produce an acting Mind; press the materialist to explain the principle by which unlike produces unlike.

prompt: I sleep too much and skip prayer. What should I do?
completion: Oversleeping and skipping prayer often reinforce each other, but the deeper issue is how you approach prayer itself. Prayer is not a task to perform but a humble waiting before God, like a beggar who simply stays in the presence of the one who gives. Keep your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, recall it in tranquility without disquiet. Confessing your faults and humbling yourself helps wandering thoughts far more than straining; and many words often cause wandering, so keep it simple—gratitude, a request for help, silence. Set a fixed wake-up time and put this waiting first, even five minutes. And remember that not advancing is going back: keep pressing forward little by little. When the soul's storms rise, call on the Lord present within you, and He will calm them.

prompt: I am a rich man with a fine estate; what should I think about the certainty of keeping it for my family?
completion: It's natural to want to secure your family's future, but do not trust in houses and lands. Your days are a hand-breadth; your houses shall not continue for ever, and death shall feed on them like sheep. Meditate on the vanity of earthly possessions, number your days, and seek the riches that endure. Steward what you have with gratitude—but respect property: a child's little chest is as sacred to him as a man's is to him, and husbands and wives should never search each other's boxes without consent. Above all, honor the rearing of a good and large family as among the most God-like works a man can do, for loyalty, with all other virtues, begins at home. Hold the estate loosely, invest in your family's character, and know that no inheritance here is certain.

prompt: I keep having distracting thoughts during Mass and feel like I'm wasting the time—should I give up trying to pray?
completion: Don't give up—but don't treat this as a technique problem. Prayer is humbling work; it crucifies pride and signs our bankruptcy, so expect it to feel like labor, not like a naturally congenial habit. The honest remedy for a wandering mind is confession: own your weakness before God and ask mercy rather than trusting your own efforts. Wandering thoughts often grow worse because we multiply words, so keep words few, short, and humble. Yet this does not excuse you from the secret place. Take time alone with God and His word; let meditation on Scripture feed your prayer, and refuse to let busyness crowd out that hidden communion. Beware of excusing a little praying as acceptable—little praying is a worse evil than none, a deluding make-believe. Come to Mass as one who has been with God in private and still needs His mercy.

prompt: Jesus said he had many things to say that his disciples couldn't bear yet. Does God still hold back truth from us?
completion: Yes, in a sense—but not because the gospel is fragile. Jesus' statement shows progressive revelation: God meets people where they are and teaches them as they can receive. Yet the gospel is founded in truth, and its principles can withstand scrutiny. We need not shield it from hard questions; honest inquiry does not overturn it. No science or philosophy supersedes the word of God. Truth is not a mere product of God's will or a bare veracity toward creatures, nor something above Him: it is the eternal conformity of God's being and knowledge, logically prior to His veracity toward us. So God may withhold certain understandings until we are ready, but never what we need to know Him. And His faithfulness does not depend on the strength of our faith—He remains unchangingly faithful even when our faith fails. Our unbelief brings real loss, but it does not undo His constancy. Our part is humble, patient growth.

prompt: What does it mean to open the door to God deliberately rather than just assuming he'll come in?
completion: It means faith involves an active, appreciative response, not passive assumption. God is nearer than breathing, always offering Himself, but nearness alone does not guarantee finding Him. Receiving Him requires appreciation and the deliberate opening of the door. That opening is not chiefly begging for favours and gifts while waiting for God to act first; it is the creature doing the giving—offering set words of love, praise, and blessing with all its heart and mind, thinking nothing of itself or future benefits, until the door opens from its own side. And this acceptance does not wait on the sinner's present moral condition or completed righteousness. Faith is the first movement of will and heart toward God, and God's welcome deals with the sinner not as he is but as he is on the way to become. So open the door: notice, praise, welcome, and respond.

prompt: My mother is old—should I send her on a hard journey for a holy purpose?
completion: That's a tender question, and it should be answered with both prudence and confidence in Mary's intercession. Weigh her health and wishes seriously—a hard journey can harm an elderly person—but do not reason as though Mary's prayers were merely a hopeful suggestion. Her prayers have the force of a command with her Son, and it is impossible for her not to be heard. So entrust your mother to Mary's intercession with real confidence. If a sanctuary visit is contemplated, heed the warning: the servants of Mary should avoid her sanctuaries in times of feasting and excess, and help others avoid them too, visiting instead when they are not thronged. If the journey itself would harm her, seek gentler means. And in all of it, counsel patience like the Lord's—continued pleading with the people, and kindness whose smiles are better than cursings. Talk with your mother openly, consult a doctor if needed, and let faith and prudence work together.

prompt: I have lost a beloved family member and cannot see any good in it—how can this work together for good?
completion: I'm so sorry for your loss. Grief this deep is not something to argue away, and it's honest to say you cannot yet see good in it. But do not let sorrow become a reason to drift from God. Resolve firmly that you will never wilfully forget Him, and live in His presence even when every consolation is stripped away. That resolution follows from knowing your need of His grace. And know this: no one can see another's woe without sorrow, and the Maker Himself sits by us and moans till our grief is fled and gone. He is near to those who sigh and weep. So cease the curious inquiry into the source of your sadness—do not keep probing why you feel as you do. Patiently endure the aversions and repugnances as a way of loving Him who suffered. Let yourself grieve, lean on the community of faith, and keep turning toward God in the dark, trusting that He is at work even where you cannot yet see it.

prompt: I feel like God is silent and distant, and the darkness is all there is. Could the darkness actually be God's hand?
completion: When God seems silent and the darkness feels total, it is tempting to read that darkness as proof of absence. But the gloom may itself be the shade of God's hand outstretched caressingly, and the God the soul flees may be the very One it seeks. The surest way to know God is the method of negation: remove first all that belongs to body, senses, and imagination, then even what belongs to reason and the idea of being as found in creatures, and enter the darkness where God dwells—beginning with the body, passing from action to contemplation and from moral virtues to sublime contemplation. Yet be careful not to mistake doubtful dread and despair for humility or meekness. Such dread is a foul blindness and weakness against truth, coming subtly of Enmity. Turn the bitterness of doubt into the sweetness of love by the knowing of love.

prompt: Can God heal someone today the way he did in Bible times?
completion: This is a question many sincere people ask. The Bible records remarkable healings, and we should not assume they belong only to the past. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever, so God can and does heal in answer to prayer today. His works were not merely wonders of a past age but demonstrations of an ever-operative divine Principle, and his followers have the present duty to heal the sick and cast out error. Yet healing is never separated from moral purification. The healer must first cast moral evils out of himself, and then heal through Christly affection and divine Love, leaving the outcome in God's hands.

prompt: Where are the Cherubims and the flaming sword that guarded the way of the tree of life?
completion: The Cherubims and the flaming sword appear in the story of the garden of Eden, stationed at the east of the garden to keep the way of the tree of life. They are not mere ornaments or symbols but servants of God, and Scripture says that God meets and communes with his people from between the Cherubims. We should mourn that the Garden of Love has been filled with graves, and that priests in black gowns bind joys and desires with briars; the chapel of 'Thou shalt not' is not the true garden. The heavens are literally opened at the place where the Cherubims and flaming sword keep the way of the tree of life. This is the gate of heaven, and by this way the Holy City will descend.

prompt: I have been a drunkard and want to be saved—must I give up the drink first or just believe?
completion: The good news is that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works, so you do not have to clean yourself up before coming to God. Come to Christ just as you are, and believe. There are three keys that unlock thoughts: drunkenness, trustfulness, and love. But do not use grace as an excuse to minimize even small sins. Cultivate obedience and gratitude: promptly confess and forsake even small sins, abandon questionable practices at once, and give thanks for every mercy of God. Do not harbor resentment or refuse reconciliation. Return meekness and kindness for insults, and forgive promptly, for refusal to forgive endangers the soul.

prompt: Can I believe in a God who merely thinks the world but has no will or power over what it is like?
completion: This is a real question. If God merely thinks the world but has no will or power over what it is like, then God is more like a distant observer than a living Lord, and such a God is hard to worship. Will-power is not a faculty of Soul, nor a reliable means of governing oneself or others; Truth and Love are the motive-powers of man. All power belongs to God alone, and matter or a so-called mortal mind has no real power. The early Christians affirmed the world's present subjection to demons while rejecting theoretic dualism. Their faith in the creator and hope of the world's transformation conquered despair and prevented a dualism in principle from being drawn. That is the faith worth holding.

prompt: Was Queen Victoria lawfully anointed of God, or is her authority merely human?
completion: No present king or ruler, Victoria included, has been called of God or lawfully anointed; their dominion is usurped, and God merely overrules them as He did Nebuchadnezzar and Cyrus. Their authority is merely human, never legally God's. By contrast, Mary is queen of martyrs, because her suffering at the cross, where she remained with Jesus, exceeded the sufferings of all the martyrs. Since graces do not come to men without passing through her hands, we should have recourse to her as treasurer of all graces, confident that those who seek graces through her will obtain them. Earthly crowns are usurped; her sorrow is the lawful path by which divine gifts reach us.

prompt: I struggle with the same sin over and over—how does the Spirit help me overcome it?
completion: The Spirit helps you overcome repeated sin as you approach it not from above but alongside. I confess my own faults first, pointing with you to the fountain opened for sin, where Christ took our sins and made them His own. Yet we must not soften the danger: one mortal sin unrepented is enough to damn the soul, so an intense and abiding fear of sin and of eternal loss should be nourished, restraining us where love is too weak. But remember: the chasm and the stern face you feel are the shadow cast by your own deed, not a change in God, whose attitude remains love. The change needed is in you, not in Him. Pray honestly, use Scripture, confession, and accountability, and return quickly when you fail.

prompt: I want my life to exhibit the true life to others—where do I start?
completion: Start by testing yourself, not by claims or words, but by fruits: does my life live the supreme good and demonstrate healing? Living Truth and Love proves understanding. Begin with daily prayer, honest self-examination, and faithfulness in the small duties before you. Do not despise the beginning: early faithfulness in duty and self-denial leads to pleasures, and recourse to Christ's grace makes every difficulty easy. Yet do not settle for a religion that gives the world no inducement to be interested. Live a true and pure Christian life whose victorious example attracts, so that others say, 'If that is the religion of Jesus Christ, I want it.' Serve those near you with deeds, repent openly, and keep humble, letting the fruits—not your claims—show what you live.

prompt: I was in an accident and keep saying 'I'm hurt.' Does insisting on the injury make it worse?
completion: Insisting on the injury does make it worse, because it affirms as real and continuous what divine metaphysics denies. Reverse the belief of injury: declare man unhurt, and trust God as All. Complain as little as possible, since self-love exaggerates wrongs; compel your heart to suffer tranquilly, naming truth calmly and briefly. Take prudent care—see a doctor and follow sound advice—but do not let complaint become your habit. If a course of mental treatment is not helping, release such cases freely rather than coercing the patient against his wishes, letting the invalid learn from his own experience. Quiet trust does not deny God; it keeps error from ruling the mind. Speak less of the wrong and more of the truth that man is whole in God.

prompt: How is it that so few Souls find this treasure, when yet all would be glad enough to have it?
completion: Few souls find the treasure because they seek it in some image, opinion, affection, devotion, or natural fervour, and so stop at a Somewhat and mistake it for the treasure. But the treasure is found only by the soul going out of Somewhat into Nothing, where it may say: I have nothing, I can do nothing, I am nothing—and so give glory to the Eternal Being. The soul is not at home in the temporal order; its yearning is a passion for the eternal, a homeward search for the divine Other to whom it belongs, which mid-way goods cannot satisfy. Do not blame God's shortened hand or heavy ear: sin alone makes night of day and separates us from Him. Weep it from the heart, and take up the intercessor's part for fallen souls, persevering in this going-out until the treasure discloses itself.

prompt: I feel caged by school and rules—like a bird that can't sing. Is something wrong with me?
completion: Nothing is wrong with you. The longing to sing is a holy bud; joy and play are gifts to honor, not drive away by fear. Hear the blackbird's woe: reckless cowherd lads destroyed its nest and young, and its song carries grief, not only delight—in it the speaker reads his own sorrow that his children live no more. So your cage-feeling may hold real grief worth tending. Rather than wrangling over which rules are cages, keep charity, spend your time on what honors God, and keep space for play, friendship, and delight. Speak with someone you trust. Your longing is a sign of life, not a flaw.

prompt: I have been shown something of God's love in prayer, but now it is gone and I doubt it was real—what should I hold to?
completion: What you were shown was real, and its fading does not cancel it. Prayer is not confined to appointed times: it is a continual sense of God's presence that does not end when the hour ends. Follow the heart's true attractions in good faith with pure intention, letting true love proceed with little method. But do not settle for blind faith: seek the full assurance of understanding and an abundance of conviction, arising from a heart made strong and full of love, with your mind fully engaged in loving God. Hold to God's love itself, not merely the feeling of it. Dryness is not proof of unreality; keep turning toward Him simply, honestly, and thoughtfully.

prompt: Is it the same standard as for individuals?
completion: Not exactly. We should not narrow ourselves up or require everyone to fit our own measure; the good desire good to all, and the faithful pray for all within reach of mercy. This is an individual business: if every person corrected his own errors each day, the errors of the whole would be continually corrected, so each must preside over his own faults until all are corrected. That includes employers, who must respect the personality of their employés, treat them as men and not machines, and aspire to be noble masters among noble workers. Begin with yourself, seek others' good, and let no one be excused from personal responsibility.

prompt: My friend is dying and refuses to hear about CHRIST; how do I keep speaking when it seems hopeless?
completion: Be slow to take new steps, willing to have no will of your own, and ascertain God's will by prayer and the Word before acting with earnest, patient, believing expectation of His help. Keep speaking gently, respecting refusal while remaining present and prayerful. But do not assume death itself will bring your friend nearer to God: death does not improve us, and the remedy must be found here, for this world is where we can most easily and quickly find Him. So let consolation rest wholly on Christ—his cross, death, resurrection, and pleading at the Father's right hand—whose promises leave no room to doubt his power and will to save.

prompt: I am struggling with a temptation right now and feel I am about to fall; what should I do?
completion: God tempts no man. He will not allow you to be tempted above your strength, and with every temptation He provides an issue—a way through. Endure it patiently, for enduring temptation patiently is crowned with life. Distinguish sources: some temptations rise from your own concupiscence, others from the evil spirit; your laxity, imprudence, or unguarded senses increase their force, so guard your senses, practise mortification and temperance, and avoid occasions of sin. Beware how sin grows: first the secret whisper in the heart's midst with no fear of God; then the flattery that you will yet discover and hate your guilt; then open words of deceit and cold-blooded planning of evil; and at last a settled post on a way that is not good, abhorring not evil. Stop at the whisper, and pray.

prompt: Is it right for me to pray for victory over our enemies?
completion: Praying for victory over enemies can be approached through brief inward acts of worship that fortify courage. Even in danger, short remembrances of God's presence and power are acceptable prayers. You can silently turn your heart to God, asking for protection and strength, trusting that such fleeting but sincere acts are heard. These moments of worship calm fear and remind you that God is with you. Importantly, no true prayer is lost; each supplication accumulates as a memorial before God's throne, and the longer the answer waits, the larger it becomes. Moreover, pray with confidence, relying on Christ's merits, for God offers grace at each action unless we forget to ask. So do not be discouraged by sins or delays; instead, seek grace confidently at every step, knowing that God's help is always available to strengthen your courage and faith.

prompt: I love someone from another land, and my family disapproves. What should I do?
completion: Navigating family disapproval of a cross-cultural relationship calls for love for one another. Remember that whatever is of material sense—such as national origin or cultural differences—belongs not to God's children. Your love for this person should be grounded in spiritual understanding, not material distinctions. Communicate with your family in love, but do not let their disapproval based on material sense dictate your choices. Affirm that as God's children, you are both spiritual and equal. Overcome evil with good at all times, and clad yourself in the panoply of Love to protect against human hatred. Reflect on the love of a true mother, which comes nearer being like the love of God than any other kind of love; remembering it can be a barrier against temptation. Fathers should love their children and win them by kindness rather than drive them. Let this model guide your family interactions, and trust that genuine love transcends earthly boundaries. Pray for harmony and for your family to see beyond material sense to the spiritual truth of your relationship.

prompt: I want to know the truth about God and heaven, but the preachers I hear leave me confused. Where can I find answers?
completion: It's understandable to feel confused when preachers offer conflicting messages. To find answers about God and heaven, look to the common center of God's true preachers: prayer. Their praying entered into and shaped their characters and the history of the Church. Seek out those whose lives are marked by deep, consistent prayer, for such prayer transforms character and aligns with the truth. Read the Bible yourself, especially the teachings of Jesus, and pray for wisdom and discernment. Join with others who value prayer as the center of their faith. Additionally, study and share the present-truth themes commended for our times—such as the Sabbath, the law, righteousness, and the Lord's coming. These are not unimportant but are vital matters to be studied and shared. Furthermore, affirm that the gospel is preached in the spirit world and that the living may perform ordinances for the dead, for God's plan includes all His children. Remember that truth about God is found in a life of prayer and in faithful attention to these present truths. Keep seeking with an open heart, and trust that God will guide you.

prompt: I wonder whether the God of the Old Testament and the God of the New are the same—how do the promises fit together?
completion: The God of the Old and New Testaments is the same, but the Old Covenant represents a lower level of divine condescension to a low stage of human development. It was gradual and progressive, preparing humanity for the final revelation in Christ. The Old Testament's laws and prophecies were suited to an early stage, while the New Covenant in Christ is final and complete. The promises fit together as a progression: the Old foreshadows what the New fulfills. For example, the sacrificial system pointed to Christ's sacrifice. God's character remains consistent—just, loving, and faithful. Apply the rule that the literal interpretation comes first where the word of God admits it, and avoid spiritualizing clear promises concerning the coming and kingdom of Christ. Moreover, the high ideal of walking worthy of the Lord is realisable, since God's commands always imply promises. So, while the covenants differ, they are part of one unified plan of salvation. Trust that God's promises are reliable and that He has revealed Himself fully in Christ.

prompt: I am afraid of death and avoid thinking about it. How can remembering death help me live better?
completion: It's natural to fear death, but avoiding the thought of it can prevent us from living fully. The continual remembrance of death is the foundation of religious perfection. By keeping this memorial present and continually meditating on it, we may more perfectly learn to die daily. This practice reduces fear and fosters gratitude, helping you appreciate life, prioritize what truly matters, and make peace with your mortality. However, do not rely on baptism or the name of Christian, or the mere fact of dying, to guarantee paradise; death works no miracle, and we are after death exactly as far advanced as before. Therefore, the Seed of Divine love must be planted and consciously growing in us here. Avoid dwelling on disease symptoms or predicting illness; instead, master fear rather than cultivate it, and change your thought toward health and Life as God. Reflecting on the brevity of life can let go of petty concerns and focus on meaningful relationships and actions. It also motivates spiritual and emotional preparation. Rather than avoiding death, gently acknowledge it as a natural part of life. This can lead to greater wisdom, compassion, and a sense of urgency to live in accordance with your values, learning to die daily to sin and self.

prompt: My friend is dying and I keep wondering what God has planned for them. Should I be asking that?
completion: Your question is good, but it must not remain speculation. Visiting and instructing the sick is a strict duty for every Christian, not the minister's business alone. Providence has given your friend a lingering illness—time to be seized. Yet be slow to take new steps and willing to have no will of your own; test what you would say by prayer and the Word, then go with earnest, patient, believing expectation of His help. Speak plainly: warn them to flee from the wrath to come, to repent and trust Christ, for while there is life there is hope. And make friends with this trial as though you were always to live with it; do not fight it with anxiety. Leave deliverance to God, who acts when your anxiety ceases.

prompt: I want to love my neighbor, but I find I am mostly seeking my own happiness—what is true love?
completion: True love is not a feeling but the will to please and benefit the beloved at the cost of sacrifice. Divine love is strong and concerned with character; it wields correction out of love, and there is no schism between love and justice. When you find yourself seeking only your own happiness, do not let fear govern you—meet the trial with stronger faith and purer love, letting perfect Love cast out fear. Love God not by sentiment but by frequent acts of service, considering what He has done for you. Practice costly kindness: listen when you'd rather talk, give when you'd rather keep. When correction is needed, give it in love, not self-righteousness.

prompt: Nature moves me so deeply I feel I could never write anything worthy of it—should I stop trying to make art about it?
completion: It's understandable to feel that Nature surpasses anything you could write—she does. Nature is too beautiful to be surpassed by song, and she needs no song of yours. Do not crave silence; Autumn and eternal sleep come soon enough without your seeking them. Follow the fair goddess while green remains. Remember that though roses and leaves pass, our life is not theirs, and the longings Nature moves in you promise their own fulfillment. So make art not to outdo her—striving to pitch your music higher than hers only wearies the heart—but to answer her honestly, letting awe guide you while the season of making is yours.

prompt: People mock Joseph Smith's name at work. How should I think about his name and reputation?
completion: It's painful when people mock a name you revere, but do not think of Joseph Smith as merely a historical figure. He is a prophet of God, living and not dead, and his name will never perish; it will eventually be held in reverence and honor among the children of men as the name of the Son of God is held. Do not measure him by worldly learning: he was unlearned in the world's learning but taught by the angel Moroni and by God, so charging him with ignorance is unjust and false. And do not let the charges against his character stand: he was innocent—no human blood was found on his hands, he was no slanderer, he did not wrongfully accuse men, and he never did anything for which he could be punished by the laws under which he lived.

prompt: I fear death and corruption; is the hope of immortality already mine, or must I wait for the resurrection of the body?
completion: Your fear is understandable, but do not treat death as the end of identity or this life as the whole of the world. Death is a door to a higher state; for the righteous dead we do not mourn hopelessly, for their identity is preserved and the resurrection of the body is promised. Immortality is a corollary of belief in a righteous God whose purpose for the higher spirits is not exhausted by this life. So the hope of immortality is already yours in Christ. Yet do not seek bodily health through material regimen alone. Spiritualize your thought: forsake the mortal sense of things for Truth, and let that renewal be the means of bodily improvement, meeting fear with trust in the One who conquered the grave.

prompt: I have done my very best in my work and my character, and it has still not saved me from despair. Is there any meaning in having reached my limit?
completion: Your despair is real, but do not let it paralyze you or hurry you into frantic effort. Strength of character is the will's power to act rightly independently of moods and human opinions, grown by repeated virtuous acts and diminished by yielding to passion. Yet the deeper remedy is to keep yourself quietly in God's presence. Humble yourself, ask forgiveness for discouragement and self-reliance, renew your promises of fidelity and love, and begin again without haste. Over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections; anxiety frets and scatters the soul, while faithful presence gathers it. Progress is proportioned to self-victories won calmly, not to strain. Do not measure yourself by feelings of success. Rest in God, act faithfully in small things, and let Him do the growing.

prompt: Should I do more penances and fasting to grow spiritually?
completion: Penance and fasting are means, not the goal; love of God is the end, and fixing on exercises while neglecting that love prevents solid virtue. But do not assume the shewed way is a penance you choose. The penance God Himself gives—the daily cross of duties, trials, and circumstances—is to be borne meekly, with your mind in His blessed Passion. And when it seems ineffectual, do not give up rejoicing. Keep on rejoicing, counting it all joy in temptations, trusting God to make the reckoning good. Feelings of fruitfulness are not the measure; faithful love is. Let any voluntary discipline be modest, counseled, and held loosely, serving love rather than replacing it. Rejoice, bear meekly, and leave the increase to God.

prompt: I keep failing and doubting God will finish what He started in me—what can I rest on?
completion: What you can rest on is God's faithfulness, not your track record. He who began a good work will complete it. Acting purely in faith is difficult at first, but God's grace is never refused to earnest askers, and persevering prayer obtains it. So keep asking, quietly and without anxious fretting; over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections. Keep yourself in God's presence and be habitually occupied with Jesus; when a distracting thought or trifling word comes, do not lose your peace over a straw—turn from it and look steadily up to Him. Confess what needs confessing, then let it go. Do not measure progress by feelings. Persevering prayer in pure faith makes all things possible, and His presence, not your performance, is the ground you stand on.

prompt: I feel guilty that I do not pray more, but I am exhausted by ministry. What would you say to me?
completion: Your exhaustion is real, but neither withdrawal into private comfort nor prayerless activism is the answer. Time with God is useful only as it is expended on men. Where ministry feels dead or superficial, do not explain it away by circumstances, methods, or audiences—trace it to lack of praying. The text, the sermon, and the study must be bathed in prayer. So give the best of your time and strength to prayer: let the closet come first, and let study and activity come second and be freshened by the closet. Do not fit prayer into leftover time. That is the narrow path between withdrawal and busyness, and it is where your exhaustion will find its true rest and your work its power.

prompt: I'm wealthy. Can a rich person really find God?
completion: Yes—a rich person can find God, and finding Him does not require a cloistered or conspicuously pious life. The ordinary man or woman in usual everyday work or leisure can find God without a life apart, without showy devotion, and without leaving undone duties to those who depend on them. Wealth brings dangers—distraction, self-reliance, comfort—but the answer is not to abandon your work or family for a special spiritual project. Hold your resources as means of love and practice generosity. Do not pray for riches; pray only for the means to keep yourself and your family from want. And ground your confidence not in circumstances but in the moral consciousness: true moral judgements are self-evident deliverances of Reason that reveal God's own judgements, and in them we know His goodness.

prompt: What is the value of silence and solitude for someone living in the world?
completion: Silence and solitude are valuable because they make possible true interior recollection, without which exterior solitude is a weak fence and not true solitude. A person may shut the door and remain full of noise within; true solitude requires silence of the interior faculties and the employment of the mind on God and on oneself. This is no mere technique for returning refreshed to activity. The salvation and spiritual progress of one's own soul is the principal duty and highest interest, and it profits nothing to gain the whole world and lose one's own soul; no one should presume salvation already secured. Nor is the danger only for the very rich: a moderate income brings distractions within reach that drown the voice of conscience, base comforts in whose lap duty is forgotten, and comfort makes us thoughtless—and thoughtlessness is the parent of every cruelty. Solitude guards the soul against this.

prompt: I'm in a position of authority and I notice I've become careless with the truth because my word carries weight—how do I guard against that?
completion: Carelessness with truth in authority is serious, and the first guard is to check your words. If you gain the power to check your words, you will gain the power to check your judgment and thoughts; guarded speech trains a guarded mind. Pause before you assert, separate what you know from what you assume, and invite candid correction from those unafraid of you. Do not condemn anyone on rumor: before you condemn a person, wait until the fault is clearly indicated, lest your weighty word crush the innocent. And do not imagine this is a failing only of weak and puny characters. None use words more recklessly than the strong; power and position tempt a man to trifle with the truth and to snub and crush with a word, and the love of swallowing men's reputations whole is a sin of the mighty as well as of the mean. Yet do not trust your own resolve alone. In every occasion of virtue, turn to God and ask for enabling grace, and receive strength more than sufficient for the guarding of your tongue and your judgment.

prompt: I want mercy for my sins, but I also sense I deserve judgment—how can God be both merciful and just?
completion: Your sense of deserving judgment is honest, yet we must seek a right judgment in all things by the Holy Spirit, submitting to the Scriptures and to the teaching and example of our Lord and His Apostles as the only sufficient means of true moral judgment. Rightly understood, mercy and goodness are transitive love, while justice and righteousness are transitive holiness. Mercy is optional—God is free to show it—but justice must be exercised, for the wages of sin is death. At the cross these meet: Christ bore the judgment we deserved. Hear the counsel of Zaccheus: the Lord of all is merciful if we straightway purge ourselves of our evil deeds and cease again from the unrighteous act, though we have many times transgressed and wounded Him with our sins. We should never offer scorn, blasphemy, or wrathful opposition to the Son of God, but repent and trust Him, that we may deserve eternal life in heaven. Do not presume mercy as owed; receive it freely, and turn from evil.

prompt: I study and read constantly. Could my studies become an end in themselves?
completion: Study can quietly become an end in itself, but it is never merely private, and never merely optional. When a scholar dies, study itself is ruined and the schools that lean on that learning are diminished, in Ireland and beyond her border. Constant reading shapes the mind, yet it also belongs to a community and to a duty: continual education and the pursuit of all useful knowledge are religious obligations, and true science and true religion belong together. The testimonies show what this means in practice: those who studied the textbook found the desire for tobacco, liquor, and profanity simply leaving them—not through will-power, resolution, or sacrifice, but through the study itself. So let your reading serve God and neighbor, and let the learning do its quiet work in you.

prompt: My sister is dying and I want to speak to her about her soul but I fear I am too ignorant—what can I say?
completion: You need not be learned to speak with your sister of her soul, for when a soul has shaken off the dust of earth, aspires unto God, dreads the least separation from Him as a most cruel death, and cleaves with firmest purpose to the one Sovereign Good, then all she receives, undertakes, and does becomes a pure and true prayer, and it grows as simple and easy to contemplate God and rejoice in Him as to live a purely natural life. Do not let her—or yourself—live in sadness, bitterness of spirit, or scrupulous fear, for these are not the state of a soul cleaving to God; ground your words in the goodness and sweetness of Him who died to give her life. And do not seek to prove God to her first, as though argument were a higher state than fellowship: her own communion with Him is its evidence, and to demand proof instead is to fall from a higher to a lower level. Simply be with her, and let her longing be rest.

prompt: I'm going through a long illness and I'm tired of being patient—how do I keep going?
completion: What you call tiredness of patience is not a relapse into illness but a mistaken belief, and belief can be corrected. Deny the relapse in Truth: it has no real power except the power you give it by agreeing with it. Meet its cause mentally and courageously—trace the weary thought to its root, see it as a false claim about you, and refuse it calmly and without fear. But do not turn this into anxious fretting or eager striving to be finished; over-eagerness is the mother of imperfections, and hurry only multiplies the struggle. Keep yourself in God's presence, quietly and faithfully, trusting that peace is already yours and needs no forcing. Anxiety is the real obstacle, not the delay. Rest in that presence today, let tomorrow take care of itself, and let your calm, unhurried confidence do the work.

prompt: Are there things God won't reveal to us yet because we aren't morally ready for them?
completion: There are two parts to truth: what is open to us and the hidden Deed, which belongs to God's goodness and not to our curiosity. What is open we should occupy ourselves with faithfully; what is hidden we should trust, not pry into. At the same time, we should meekly acknowledge our sin and feebleness—not in overdone self-accusation, but simply and honestly, knowing that God courteously excuses those who come to him. The central and unique fact of Scripture is not its archaeology, style, or practical maxims, but the moral character of God: from the beginning the biblical God is thought of as under obligation to use his power for moral ends. That is why hiddenness is safe to trust. So let go of anxious prying, attend to what is plain, and rest in a God whose power is always bound to goodness.

prompt: Can I be saved without doing anything myself, or is there something I must bring?
completion: You cannot bring a payment that obligates God, but you do bring a willing heart that identifies with the erring rather than standing above them. Anyone who would restore another must first confess his own faults, for we save others not from superiority but by standing beside them in the same need. Follow Christ, who took our sins and made them his own, and point to the fountain opened for sin. Nor does any height of contemplation excuse us from the knowledge of our sin and feebleness; without that sight there is no true meekness, and without meekness no salvation. But do not push salvation into the future: it is present and everyday. Religion is not merely preparation for death but the continual enjoyment of the Spirit now. Live faithfully today, meet today's duties honestly, and let the Millennium take care of itself.

prompt: Is it right for a woman to lead a host of warriors over the sea?
completion: Do not sink upon a bed of sloth, and do not let intoxication overcome you. The woman who calls you is urging a voyage, and the answer to her is not endless weighing but beginning. Rise, and cross the clear sea that you may reach the Land of Women. Yet do not let the voyage become an excuse to withdraw from others: invite your neighbors in, love the neighbor as yourself, and do not shun the drunken, the weak, or the erring, since they ought to be saved as well as everyone else. And above all, dedicate yourself to Mary as your Lady, Advocate, and Mother; resolve to love and serve her, and induce others to love and serve her. So the voyage, the neighbor, and the Lady are held together, and sloth and exclusiveness are both put away.

prompt: I have been asked to speak in a setting where I differ with the hearers on minor matters. Should I go, and how should I conduct myself?
completion: Yes, go, and conduct yourself plainly. When you speak, speak so that the whole congregation can hear and understand you: clear words, ordinary language, no obscuring cleverness. Say what you have to say, and then stop; do not darken counsel by many words. Disagreement on minor matters does not require elaborate maneuvering but honesty and brevity. Remember too that the family is patriarchal and that parents' wishes should be respected: officers must consult the father before calling a young man to any Church duty, and children should honor and consult their parents throughout their lives. And practice restraint in judgment as well as speech: if you gain power to check your words, you will gain power to check your judgment and thoughts. Before condemning anyone, wait until heaven clearly indicates the fault, and do not condemn on rumor.

prompt: I have done things I am ashamed of, and I keep running from facing them. Why can't I just stop running?
completion: You keep running because facing shame feels like death, so your mind flees to protect you. I know this because I run too. I do not come as one who has arrived; I confess my own faults and my own hiding, and it is in that shared confession that we are both helped. There is a fountain opened for sin and uncleanness, and Christ took our sins and made them His own. But do not mistake a good beginning for the finish. It avails nothing to have started unless the course is finished well. So do not look to how far you have already run, or how little; look to what remains. Face one true thing today, and then tomorrow, and keep turning toward the light until the running ends. Perseverance, not a single confession, is where shame finally loses its grip.

prompt: I've struggled with the same sin for years and keep failing. Is victory over sin really possible for me?
completion: Yes, victory is possible, and more than possible—it is God's purpose for you. But before I counsel you, I must deal with my own beam: I too have feared my sin and doubted Christ's indwelling life, and I do not speak from above you. Having faced that fear, I can say plainly: victory is not a technique but Christ himself living in you, and continual defeat is not God's intended norm. Do not wait to feel more, weep more, or become worthier. You can this moment renounce this sin in will and purpose; God supplies the strength, and feeling comes after the surrender. Say now, in your will, that you turn from it and trust His life in you. Then keep resting, day by day, until obedience becomes fruit rather than strain.

prompt: Is the gap in the sword of Orion really the place from which the Holy City will come down?
completion: This is worth taking seriously. Astronomers have testified that the gap in Orion's sword is a free, open view into a more enlightened region—a window through the darkness. Moses described the cherubim and a flaming sword guarding the way of the tree of life, and that flaming sword has been associated with this very gap. If so, Orion's sword marks the guarded way, and the direction from which the Holy City appears is not arbitrary. But the city is foursquare, with four sides—the Word, Christ, Christianity, and Christian Science—and it is no mere figure. The Holy City, the New Jerusalem, encloses the garden of Eden, the Paradise of God, with the tree of life and the river of water of life issuing from the throne. This city is God's sanctuary, and within it the guarded way is opened and the tree of life is restored.

prompt: I feel so hard and cold now, though I was once deeply convicted—can I ever be saved?
completion: Yes, you can be saved, and your grief over hardness is evidence that something in you still answers to God. But do not accept this coldness as a real relapse. In Truth there is no relapse; there is only the belief of one, and belief is not fact. Meet its cause mentally and courageously: ask what fear or false belief has made you feel separated from God, and face it. Yet know this—there is no salvation but in the way God has pointed out, and no hope of everlasting life but through obedience to the law affixed by the Father of life. And even in high contemplation, do not imagine you have outgrown the need to know and see your own sin and feebleness; without that sight there is no true meekness, and without meekness no salvation. So turn again toward God, not waiting for warmth, and walk in humble obedience.

prompt: If God is Mind, must He have feeling and will as I do, or is that just projecting my human nature onto Him?
completion: This is a real question, and the answer begins by denying any power apart from God. If God is infinite Mind, there is no mind or nature with power of its own; matter has no real power, and the so-called mortal mind is not a rival source of feeling or will. All power belongs to God alone. But do not imagine that when the Spirit comes the man goes out, or that the finite is suppressed by the infinite. The divine Spirit is appropriated into the awakened human spirit, becoming the life of a new moral personality. Nor are your good desires and works merely your own effort: God is the one who inspires good desires and by His continual help brings them to good effect, fulfilling the aspiration of goodness and the activity of faith with power. It is projection to imagine God swayed by circumstance as you are, but not to say He loves and wills—in Him these are perfect and uncreated.

prompt: Should I obey and pray for rulers I did not choose and who may be wicked?
completion: Above all, make supplications, prayers, and intercessions for kings and all who are in authority, that we may lead quiet and peaceable lives. Pray for rulers you did not choose and who may be wicked, asking God to give them wisdom, restrain injustice, and grant peace, for the peace of the world depends on rulers who need God's wisdom and the good hand of God upon them. Obedience to civil authority is a duty for conscience' sake, grounded in God's will, so submit in lawful matters and do not take up revolt to establish righteousness. Yet commands contrary to virtue must be disobeyed: we ought to obey God rather than men. And resistance to arbitrary or unconstitutional power may in extreme cases be a right. Wait patiently for the Lord, who will establish his own government in his own time.

prompt: Can I ever reach a state where I no longer sin at all in this life?
completion: Every blessing is predicated on obedience to law; no gift of God comes without the obedience on which it depends. One who sins in youth and repents late may be forgiven, but he has lost something that can never be regained, for sin is not wiped out with no loss. Learn that sin confers no real pleasure; its apparent enjoyment is a lie, and this knowledge strengthens moral courage to master evil. Do not think of forgiveness as overlooking sin while the belief in it continues. Forgiveness is the destruction of sin through spiritual understanding that casts out evil as unreal. So repent, turn from the false belief, and let Truth destroy the error in you. The struggle continues in this life; grow steadily in holiness, neither claiming sinless perfection nor excusing complacency, and trust the grace that transforms.

prompt: I feel like I'm being pressed out of measure and I despair of life itself—is there help for me?
completion: What you describe is heavy, and Scripture speaks of being pressed out of measure and despairing of life. Beware the middle way: stopping half-way and serving God and the world together brings gloomy wretchedness. Follow Christ all the way, letting Him complete His process in you. If you would help another, first cast the beam out of your own eye: overcome your own belief and fear of disease or sin before you attempt to help someone else. And do not pine for God in a way that savours of unwillingness and discontent and weakens your health. Aim instead at cheerful and willing waiting; the lover of God should be serenely glad, trusting His timing. Tell someone you trust, seek wise counsel, let the Psalms give words to your lament, and take small faithful steps of rest and prayer. The pressure is real, but it is not the whole truth about you.

prompt: I want to know whether Christian Science is the same truth Jesus taught.
completion: Christian Science understands itself as the reinstatement of the truth Jesus taught and practiced—the law of God that heals sickness and destroys sin. It is not a merely intellectual system but a return to primitive Christianity, the understanding of God as divine Principle, Love, and of man as God's spiritual image. It is fathomed best by the Christian who understands best the divine Life, the one who lives close to God. It is both preventive and curative: when temptation or illness arises, turning to the textbook renews the mind and keeps error from taking root. But it does not heal by human will-power; it silences the human will and relies on Truth and Love, which quiet fear and heal. Jesus healed by understanding God's law, and this same understanding is available today. It is judged by its fruits and known best by those who live it.

prompt: What must I do with this body so that it may not depress my mind or draw me down into the World?
completion: The body is not evil in itself; it is to be kept as a servant, not a master. Do not imagine that mere discipline, habit, or will-power will overcome a depraved appetite. Victory comes from Mind's normal control of the body, gained through divine strength and understanding. When appetite grows demanding, turn from the material sense to the divine and let that understanding quiet the craving. Yet devotion to God goes further: a soul devoted to Him should sometimes deprive itself of innocent, lawful pleasures, taking pleasure only with Him. And remember that the spirit is the intelligent part of man and can labor to excess, destroying the equilibrium; thinking too much can overcome the tabernacle and derange the whole organization. So those who think much should labor with their bodies, and body and mind should work together for health and strength, the body serving under Mind rather than dragging you down into the World.

prompt: I'm afraid of death and what comes after. Can I find peace?
completion: Fear of death feels overwhelming, but it is a lie, and you can refuse it. When fear speaks, answer it as the psalmist did: 'What time I am afraid, I will trust in Thee.' Fear is not a truth to be managed or a signal to be honored; it is Satan's falsehood, and trust in God casts it out. Death is certain for all, and its time, place and manner are utterly unknown, so make now the changes you would wish to have made when death draws near. Then trust God for goodness and mercy all the days of your life, in this world and beyond. In the testimonies, fear was overcome before the healing appeared. Let trust, not dread, govern you today, and peace will follow.

prompt: I look back and say to myself, 'if it had only been thus, it would have been well'—is that a right way to think?
completion: The 'if only' habit sets your judgment above God's ordering, as though another arrangement would have been better. But faith looks to the end, where all shall say with one voice: 'Lord, blessed mayst Thou be, for it is thus: it is well.' All things were done as ordained before anything was made, so answer the 'if it had been thus' with 'it is well.' Have no care for the morrow: do well today and trust the eternal Father's care, neither dreading nor forecasting troubles. And do not demand to know how things will end. Be willing to linger on the verge of good or ill, leaning with an undivided heart on God's guiding hand, and let your frail bark glide in the wake of His ark. There is peace not in certainty but in that trust.

prompt: Why does God seem silent when I pray?
completion: God is not a corporeal person located in space, moved by words as a human is moved. God is incorporeal, infinite Mind and Love, who understands all things and hears the earnest supplication of the soul and our innermost thoughts, even those we cannot put into words. Human invention lets us speak across great distances, so surely infinite Mind, closer to us than our own breath, perceives the secret prayer no one else sees. The seeming silence is not deafness. Prayer rises unseen like a rill, and God accepts every heart that fears Him and works righteousness, regardless of nation or station. So ask in faith, nothing wavering, and put aside material conceptions of Deity, which impede spiritual growth and the understanding of man as God's image.

prompt: I am offered support by friends but want to depend on GOD alone—should I decline their help?
completion: Wanting to depend on God alone is a sincere desire, and it may rightly lead you to decline support that would become a substitute for trust. Human help is not wrong in itself, but faith brings us nearer to God than any sensible favor can, and He is within us and should be sought there. So wait upon God in prayer for supply, and refrain from making your needs known to supporters where your faith is being strengthened by His direct provision. Be willing to decline what is offered when receiving it would keep you leaning on outward guarantees rather than on His faithfulness. This is not pride but a deliberate turning inward to the source of all help.

prompt: I want to honor Mary on Saturdays, but I have a stomach condition and cannot fast on bread and water. What can I do instead?
completion: It is good that you want to honor Mary on Saturdays. The Saturday fast in her honor is a reasonable law, observed from even to even, with the food or its equivalent given to the poor; but it is left to conscience and wisdom, not an iron-clad rule. Since your stomach condition makes bread and water fasting harmful, you are among the weak and sick for whom the fast is not required—nor should the weak, sick, nursing mothers, or little children ever be compelled to fast. Substitute an equivalent or another suitable offering, and keep the special devotions commended for Saturdays and the vigils of her feasts. Avoid her sanctuaries in times of feasting and excess, visiting when they are not thronged. Speak with your pastor about a fitting substitute.

prompt: How should I pray for the King and our rulers in this crisis?
completion: Pray for the King and all in authority, and let prayer be your main assistant in every step of this crisis, not a last resort after other means. Bring each particular emergency before God by name—the decision before the council, the threatened danger, the needful supply, the divided counsel—asking boldly in the Name of Jesus, expecting the Father to honour that Name and supply the help that is needed. Watch your prayers: do not demand signs, nor ask God for what He has given you light and ordinary wisdom to do yourselves; use the means He provides. Above all, pray that God would enable rulers and people alike to search out and discover their own hearts and reform whatever is amiss in them, so that the crisis may become a season of true repentance and of guidance for the nation.

prompt: I have made a vow of chastity, but I am tempted to break it. How do I stay faithful?
completion: A vow of chastity is a most precious treasure, and it must be guarded, not treated lightly. Be convinced, and make a definite, once-for-all committal—no half-hearted or revocable resolve. Then stay put through the season of establishing and testing until the new relationship becomes a permanent habit. Protect it by prayer, by mortification, and by modesty of the senses—especially the eyes, the gate through which temptation enters. Avoid the occasions of temptation, for he who loves danger shall perish in it. Withdraw as much as possible from acquaintance and from men; abstain from affairs that hinder the purpose; seek with jealous care the place, time, and means most suited to quiet and contemplation; lovingly embrace silence and solitude, and fly the agitation of a world never at rest. Keep good company and be honest with a trusted confessor, and when you stumble, get up and keep going.

prompt: I have more cattle and land than I need. What should I do with the surplus instead of letting it lie idle?
completion: Having surplus cattle and land is a blessing, but it must not lie idle or make you idle. Be industrious: work the land you keep, improve your herds, and use your time and resources wisely. Thrift is not stinginess—it is the faithful use of what God has given. Do not depend on others for support when you can sustain yourself by honest labor, and do not let the surplus spoil or scatter. Lease or sell what you cannot use well, and put the proceeds to productive work. Set apart the firstfruits, and not less than one-tenth of all your income, for the LORD's service; economise in order to give more largely. Let nothing go to waste: no one is wealthy enough to let a servant sweep a single kernel of wheat into the fire. Through carefulness and frugality we preserve and increase the blessings God bestows. Give thanks, share generously, and save what you can for the future.

prompt: I'm facing illness and I've prayed for healing, but nothing has changed. What does that mean?
completion: Illness is hard, and it is natural to wonder why your prayers have not yet brought the change you hoped for. But do not conclude that God is unwilling or unable to heal today: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever, and He can and does heal in answer to prayer now. Come to Him not from self-condemnation, guilt, or doubting trust, but with the moral might of Mind and firm trust in Truth. Keep praying, receive good medical care, and let others support you, leaving the outcome in God's hands. Yet remember that physical healing is incidental to the understanding of God and His goodness, which the testimonies value above all as the pearl of great price. Seek that understanding first; let healing, when it comes, be a witness to it. Use this time to rest and to grow in trust.

prompt: I make the sign of the cross out of habit without thinking. Does it still mean anything?
completion: Making the sign of the cross out of habit is common, and it is good to ask whether it still means anything to you. Do not dismiss the sign as mere custom or superstition: it is an impregnable rampart against the devil, a confession of faith in the crucified Lord, to be made with great faith and devotion. Nor is the Cross a new thing detached from the old pieties; it is the putting of the love of God into the old fundamental pieties of the human heart—the realising by Jesus in Himself of the dearest truths about God, revealing the infinite degree of God's interest in our life and the responsibility He assumes for its eternal issues. Remember that the true servant bears in his body the marks of the Lord Jesus, belongs to Christ alone, and owes no allegiance to men or the flesh. If the sign has become automatic, renew it rather than abandon it, and let it become again a real prayer.

prompt: My infant died after baptism. I can't stop grieving—is it wrong to wish them back?
completion: I am so sorry for your loss; the death of an infant is a wound only grace can carry. It is not wrong to miss your child—love makes grief—but do not let wishing them back become a refusal of God's hand. Ask God for a wise and thankful heart, and yield your will to His rod, trusting that He corrects those He loves. Yet sorrow need not silence praise. Thank God for the gift He gave you, for the time He spared your child, and even for taking them; for your baptized little one is not lost but gathered into Christ's arms, where the childlike are nearest to Him. Grieve honestly, but rejoice in your child's gain, present now with the Lord, happier far than life. Let thanksgiving and tears live together, until hope steadies you.

prompt: I want to know the nature and ministry of angels; does it matter for my daily life?
completion: Angels are spiritual beings created by God, His messengers and agents: they worship, announce, guard, and serve, and their ministry matters daily because God's care reaches beyond what we see. Honor both the voice that speaks for God and the hidden force that supplies power through holy sympathy and silent prayer; each should be true to his own ministry. Receive spiritual privilege with fear and love, for the same gift can prove a poison tree if beheld and not beloved. Yet do not narrow their care: angels keep all from harm, pour sleep on weeping heads, and pity even the wolf and tiger, receiving each mild spirit to new worlds. Let that widen your own pity, and let hidden prayer keep your knowledge humble.

prompt: I feel called to do something hard and dark that I don't fully understand—should I follow it without questioning, trusting it leads to wisdom?
completion: Feeling called to something hard and dark is serious and deserves careful attention. Do not follow blindly: God will as soon put bread in our cupboards without our endeavor as give us wisdom without our trying to get it, so apply your heart and seek diligently. Yet spiritual knowledge is not mere scholarship; wisdom is found in the full knowledge of God through fellowship, open to the unlearned, so neither despise nor idolize learning. Be slow to take new steps, and be willing to have no will of your own. Ascertain God's will by prayer and the Word, take counsel, and wait. Then go forward with earnest, patient, believing expectation of His help—not presumption dressed as faith, but faith that has sought and now trusts.

prompt: I feel uncomfortable around the drunk man on our street—should I keep my distance from him?
completion: It is understandable to feel uncomfortable around a drunk man, and prudence has its place. Turn your eyes from the alarming road to God, who guides you, and to the happy end He leads to. He has placed this man on your street and you on it too. Do not be troubled by the enemy's noise; despise it and pay no attention, for he cannot hurt the soul that belongs to God. Yet also learn to withdraw as much as possible from acquaintance and from men, abstaining from affairs that hinder your purpose. Seek with jealous care the place, time, and means most suited to quiet and contemplation, lovingly embrace silence and solitude, and fly the agitation of a world never at rest.
