Nor may we accept a permanent class of the undeveloped as compatible with a just society. Justice requires education that raises every man's actual worth to the level of his potentialities, for undeveloped faculties make just order impossible. Competition and co-operation alike should serve that complete education, developing each person's powers rather than merely sorting winners from losers.

prompt: I have been asked to take charge of a work with no guaranteed funds—should I accept?
completion: Taking charge of a work without guaranteed funds is a serious decision, but not automatically unwise. Workers go out depending on God without guaranteed income; that is the pattern of this labour. Accept only if you can proceed on that basis: give ministry only as funds allow, never going into debt to sustain workers. Be careful in receiving and using gifts. Decline donations encumbered by objectionable conditions, money owed to others, or gifts given grudgingly or for self-glory, and refuse funds designated for endowment or personal provision. Keep honest accounts of stewardship and provide them to those who give. Above all, the Saints should fulfil their contracts and sacredly keep their word, for honest hearts produce honest actions. Have no fellowship with a man who makes a promise and does not fulfil it. Accept only what you can promise and keep, scaling the work to available means.

prompt: I am ashamed to pray in public or before others; should I hide my devotion?
completion: Feeling ashamed to pray before others is common, but the answer is not to treat prayer casually or as a performance. Prayer must be accompanied by strict silence and profound exterior and interior reverence. Approach it with trembling, shutting your senses to distractions and observing strict silence of tongue and body. Do not neglect prayer because you lack the spirit of prayer; pray at appointed times regardless of feeling, and keep family prayer. When you ask God for something, help Him accomplish what is asked rather than expecting God to do it all. Bring even the smallest matter to God in prayer, honouring Him by asking His guidance rather than taking the matter out of His hands; nothing is too small or too secular for Him. When you pray before others, do so quietly and reverently rather than seeking to impress, letting reverence, not display, be the remedy for shame.

prompt: What is the Christian ideal of knighthood and how does it apply to me?
completion: The Christian ideal of knighthood is a heart that delights in the law of the Lord, meditating on it day and night, so that righteousness and justice become the supreme passion and foundation of individual and national life—not one interest among many, nor mere external restraint. A knight of Christ spends and is spent for souls, esteems the reproach of the Cross an honor, forgives and prays for persecutors, and fears no mortal's frown in declaring God's word. This devotion also makes you a Christian citizen with public duties: as prophet, testifying to the ideal and speaking truth plainly; as priest, supporting each person and institution in the best it can do; and as king, thinking out how your nation may be guided toward the Kingdom of God. Knighthood thus joins bold witness with wise, active service to neighbor and country.

prompt: I am a student and I find my studies difficult. How do I keep going?
completion: When studies are difficult, do not merely chat about the difficulties or lean on your own powers. Act courageously, saying, 'I will do much; not I, but the grace of God which is within me.' Study the letter, imbibe the spirit, and adhere steadfastly to the divine Principle, rather than chasing rapid progress through technique alone. As much as possible withdraw from acquaintance and from men, abstain from hindering affairs, and seek with jealous care the place, time, and means suited to quiet and contemplation; lovingly embrace silence and solitude, flying the agitation of a world never at rest. In that quiet, break your work into manageable steps and rest well, but let the grace of God within you, not your own strength, carry you through.

prompt: My neighbor and I share irrigation water, and I feel the distribution is unfair to those who work hard. What should be done?
completion: Water-sharing disputes are best solved by pursuing justice, not mere equal division: water should be distributed justly according to what the land yields and how much each person cultivates, and the water master should be urged to reform where distribution is unjust. Document current divisions and cultivation, then bring the matter to your neighbor and the water master, proposing a schedule reflecting actual labor and need. Treat passing strangers with kindness and respect, and let your example toward outsiders be worthy of imitation; it is no concern of yours whether a neighbor believes as you do, if you can live as neighbors with him. Remember that the indwelling life overflows in service to others: each new ministry makes room for a deeper filling and a larger blessing. So seek justice for those who work the land, and let generosity, not self-containment, guide the settlement.

prompt: I want to serve God but feel I have no gifts—is there a place for me in his work?
completion: Yes, there is a place for you—but service must be handled with the steward's care, and nothing compensates for the loss of the secret place. Every believer has something to offer, and gifts grow through faithful use. Begin in small, ordinary ways: helping at church, encouraging others, showing hospitality. Yet take time to be alone with God and His word, for secret prayer and meditation are indispensable to fruitful service; constant activity, public service, or Christian fellowship cannot substitute for communion with God. Let prayer be a mutual correspondence in which you bring yourself, give as well as receive, and in which your missing Him means His missing you. Embody the steward's pattern too: decline encumbered or objectionable gifts, refuse grudging or self-glorifying donations, and give honest accounts to donors. Refuse to let activity crowd out communion.

prompt: My steward says my constant almsgiving is impoverishing the church. How should I answer him?
completion: Answer your steward by affirming that church revenues belong to the poor: even sacred vessels may be devoted to those in need, and complaints that almsgiving impoverishes the church are answered by confidence that God will provide. Generosity is the church's proper use of resources, not a drain; hoarding goods while the needy suffer contradicts the Gospel. Ground your giving in keeping yourself in God's Presence, which hinders sin, begets holy familiarity with God, and becomes habitual through repeated acts. And take seriously the campaign against swearing: treat casual oaths as a grave habit to be broken, impose a penance for each oath, and hold that mere remonstrance without firm correction is not enough. Thank your steward and review practical needs, but let providence, habitual communion, and firm correction—not fear or laxity—guide the church's life.

prompt: I'm afraid of death and can't pray about it. How do I face my own end?
completion: Fear of death is natural, but you don't have to let it paralyze you. Begin by simply placing yourself in God's presence like a beggar—no words needed, just a humble waiting. When your mind wanders to fear, gently recall it to God without agitation. This is prayer: keeping your mind in His presence. But remember, you cannot do this alone; you need God's continual help. Build a holy habit of thinking of Him often, because we must know before we love. As you practice this, you will gradually shake off the dust of earth and cleave to God as your Sovereign Good. Then you will dread separation from Him more than death itself, and all you do will become pure prayer. Contemplation will become as simple and easy as living a natural life.

prompt: I want to be a faithful witness at home before I go abroad; what is home missionary work?
completion: Home missionary work means sharing your faith with family, friends, and neighbors, but it must begin with your own testimony and obedience to God's commands, including the Word of Wisdom. Live a consistent Christian life—your actions often speak louder than words. Be ready to give an answer for the hope you have, but do so with gentleness and respect, avoiding contentious argument and debate. Teach in simplicity, humility, and love. Remember that missionary work extends beyond this life: the gospel is preached in the spirit world, and we can perform ordinances for the dead in temples. As you prepare to go abroad, reject any Jonah-like notion that truth belongs to one nation; rather, let your motive be a passion for human beings as human beings, respecting their cultures and growing independence. Your home is your first mission field.

prompt: I want to live a simple life close to the land—is that enough, or am I wasting my potential?
completion: Living a simple life close to the land can be deeply fulfilling and is certainly not a waste of potential, but it must be oriented toward doing good. Every moment of human life should be devoted to doing good somewhere and in some way. Your potential isn't measured by worldly success but by how you use your gifts to serve others and care for creation. Remember that there is no substitute for the home; it is a divine institution of stability and love, and no genuine happiness exists apart from it. So cultivate a permanent home, avoid restless moving about. Moreover, do not make ease and enjoyment the end of your retirement; rather, embrace penance, labor, and assiduous contemplation. Without great fervor and constancy in these, close solitude can become the road to perdition. Let your simple life be rooted in love, service, and persistent devotion.

prompt: I'm a member who has been speaking about a fellow member's past sins that he has repented of. Is that backbiting if what I say is true?
completion: Speaking about someone's past sins, even if true, can be backbiting because backbiting is determined by the spirit and purpose actuating the speaker, not merely by the truth of the words. If the person has repented—meaning they have turned from evil, reformed their life, and made restitution—then God has forgiven them, and we should not discredit them. True repentance is not just sorrow but a changed life. Remember that sin is doing wrong when we know and can do better; the sin of ignorance is winked at, but when we learn a thing is wrong, we must refrain from it immediately and forever. So if you have been speaking of his past sins, stop now, address concerns privately, and build others up in love.

prompt: I am a slave and my master is a Christian; are the natural distinctions between us abolished in the Church?
completion: In the Church, all believers are equal in Christ. Galatians 3:28 says there is neither slave nor free, for all are one in Christ Jesus. So yes, the natural distinctions between slave and master are abolished in terms of spiritual standing. The early Church was organized in a twofold way: based on the diakonia tou logou and on the economy of the church. Prophets, teachers, bishops, and deacons each had their charisms, and the Churches' independence rested on the Spirit in their midst. This spiritual equality means that in the Church, your master is your brother, and you are equal in dignity and worth. We must reject all class and national distinctions, honoring men for the spirit in them. Regarding obedience, obey your master for conscience' sake, as God's will, but if commanded to do something contrary to virtue, you must disobey. In extreme cases, resistance to arbitrary power may be a right.

prompt: If all people are children of God, why do so many seem to have no faith at all—should I despair of them or hope for them?
completion: Your worry is understandable, but despair is not the right response. Since all are God's children by creation, their lack of faith should move you not to judgment but to desire their salvation and God's glory. Pray not for your own comfort or reputation, but that they might come to know the One who made them. Yet remember that we are nothing and every man at his best state is vanity; only in humility and self-emptying can God fill and work through us. Do not measure hope by visible results. God sometimes hides Himself, and faith alone must be our support and the foundation of all confidence in Him. Hope for what they could become for His kingdom, resting not on your efforts but on God Himself.

prompt: How do I handle a person I'm guiding who wants to rush ahead spiritually?
completion: It is good that the person is eager, but eagerness can become presumption dressed as faith. Gently counsel slowness to take new steps and a willingness to have no will of one's own. Before any new step, help them ascertain God's will by prayer and the Word, not by impulse or excitement. Teach them to accept spiritual experiences only as God chooses, without praying for or secretly desiring them, in submission without questioning, fear, or curiosity. Commend meek waiting before God with hands off the scales: treat apparent hindrances as occasions for divine interposition rather than causes for anxiety, trusting God to remove them in His own way and time. Then encourage earnest, patient, believing expectation of His help, and let your calm example teach faithfulness in small things.

prompt: What is the difference between knowing God's will and knowing God Himself?
completion: Knowing God's will and knowing God Himself are related but distinct. Knowing His will is not a bare minimum to be set aside; rather, we should seek to be filled with the mature knowledge of His will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, for this is the secret of true living. Yet refrain from disputing about God's Being or Will from images and self-opinion; such disputation is carried on without God and is a sign that one has not felt Him. Instead, direct yourself to humility, love, and the trying of things one with another. Our knowledge of God is partial and not exhaustive, yet real: we know substance through phenomena and the infinite as the absence of all limit. So knowing God Himself is relationship that shapes everything else. Seek Him first, and His will becomes clearer over time.

prompt: I am a church leader and my people are worldly. Is that my fault?
completion: It is easy to take on all the blame when your people seem worldly, but the answer is not a simple yes. Leaders do shape a congregation, and you should examine your teaching, example, and priorities honestly. Yet the Church's lack is not found only in its leaders; it lies in the tepid love for a dimly known Lord in each member's own heart. The Church gains what is lacking when each heart worships the beloved Christ. So do not give up or treat apparent defeat as a reason to abandon the cause. Having done all, stand; keep trying and never quit even amid apparent failure. Affirm the brotherhood of all Saints, rejecting class and national distinctions and honoring men for the spirit in them. Invite honest feedback, keep pointing people to Christ, and help each member grow in love for the Lord they only dimly know.

prompt: I feel so unworthy to praise or bless God. Shouldn't I wait until I'm better before I try?
completion: Feeling unworthy is common, and it is good to take God seriously. But waiting until you are better before praising Him can become an excuse to stay away. Remember that God knows our wants and comes in His own time. His care is shown even in affliction through patience, and that patience calls for thanksgiving. So do not make your praise conditional on feeling worthy, and do not give up rejoicing because the first attempt seems ineffectual. Keep on rejoicing, counting it all joy in temptations, and trust God to make the reckoning good. Wish for no event but bless God for those He ordains, saying, 'Father, I am thine; do for me all that shall seem good to Thee.' Begin where you are, with small and honest words, and hope in Him now.

prompt: How do I handle memories of past sins and past events that keep coming back?
completion: Memories of past sins should not be brushed aside as mere brain static. Unrepented sin accumulates; each repetition dulls the conscience and destroys, little by little, the ability to do right. So respond with honest repentance—name the wrong, turn from it, and reform your conduct. Confessing your faults and humbling yourself is the remedy for a wandering mind; pride scatters us, humility gathers us. In prayer avoid a multiplicity of words, for many words often cause wandering—speak simply and briefly from a humble heart. But know this: every blessing is predicated on obedience to law. One who sins in youth and repents late may be forgiven, yet he has lost something that can never be regained—years, capacities, opportunities that obedience would have preserved. Let the memory drive you to confession and change, and let it teach you the cost of delay.

prompt: I'm old and I look back on my life with regret—is there still mercy for me?
completion: Regret is not the same as being beyond mercy, but be honest about what mercy means. Pity would be no more if we did not make somebody poor; mercy exists because harm was done and someone made to suffer. The tree of Mystery and Deceit grows in the human brain, weaving comforting stories that excuse us. Forgiveness is not a transaction granted regardless of your inward condition; it is an inward condition of the personal life, coming naturally to the soul that loves and forgives, and depending on your own spirit as well as on God. And remember judgment: we are judged according to deeds done in the body and the thoughts and intents of the heart. Death leaves us as judgment finds us—there is no change after death. So while there is time, forgive, amend, and turn toward good.

prompt: I've made promises I'm struggling to keep; can I trust that God keeps his promises even when I fail?
completion: Your confidence should rest not on your own consistency but on the faithfulness of Him who calls; what He has promised He is also able to perform. Do not treat the high ideal of walking worthy of the Lord as an impossible dream—God's commands always imply promises, and He never commands what He will not enable. But do not stop at the first act of faith. Hold fast your confidence firm to the end, following up faith with perseverance and victorious testing until the blessing comes to birth. Examine your habits, seek accountability, and return quickly when you fail, trusting His character rather than your feelings. His faithfulness, not your track record, is the ground of your hope—and perseverance is the road by which the promise is delivered.

prompt: I pray for something good and do not receive it. What am I doing wrong?
completion: If you pray for something good and do not receive it, don't separate prayer from work—diligent labour without earnest prayer, and prayer without diligent labour, are each incomplete. Join them, trusting not in your work but in the Lord who gives the increase. The promises of Christ cannot fail; we ask and receive not because we ask amiss, so when prayer seems unanswered, examine whether the asking is disordered. If the art of praying well is the art of living well, nothing is of greater importance than to learn this heavenly art of conversing with God as we ought. Yet do not be discouraged over your sins: grace is offered at each action and should be sought with confidence, relying on Christ's merits—God offers grace at each action unless we forget to ask. So ask confidently, live well, and keep working.

prompt: I am a young woman and I have been proud of my dress and appearance—how do I learn humility?
completion: Caring about appearance isn't wrong in itself, but every virtue must be grounded in humility—humility is the safeguard of devotion. Ask whether your attention to dress serves the divine call or feeds pride under the cloak of sanctity. Desire to be humbled, not merely to appear humble; the keenest humiliations are the least visible. And learn to dread the esteem and praises of others, for they are snares by which a mortal poison may imperceptibly insinuate itself into your affections and deprive you of divine grace. So place yourself always below all creatures, dressing modestly and simply, serving respect and love rather than display. Watch for pride dressed up as piety, ground your worth in what is received rather than achieved, and let hidden humility be your aim.

prompt: I'm afraid of making the wrong choice about my vocation—how do I know God's will for me?
completion: Instead of fearing a wrong choice, embrace your present vocation and serve God in the lowly duties at hand, caring not what the service may be, provided God is served. Yet do not neglect to seek the mature knowledge of His will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, for this is the secret of true living. When uncertainty remains, do not rush to decide by chance methods or self-willed expedients. The safe guide in every crisis is believing prayer with the word of God. Continued uncertainty is a reason for continued waiting, not for haste. Treat delay as God's means of drawing you to prayer and keeping self-will in check. So, wait patiently on Him, and He will make your way clear.

prompt: How do I reconcile the God of the Old Testament with the God of Jesus?
completion: The God of the Old Testament and the God of Jesus are one, but we come to know Him through ordered stages. First, we must have an intimate knowledge of Jesus—the historical person, His life and teachings. Then we recognize Him as the Christ, the promised Messiah, fulfilling the Old Testament. Only then do we come to the Father, whom Jesus reveals. Finally, we know God the Holy Trinity as our All. The Old Testament is a lower, gradual stage under divine condescension, yet it is a Christian book, containing explanations necessary for every occasion, and was used as the source of the knowledge of faith under six points of view. So, while acknowledging its preparatory role, we read it as pointing to Christ. Thus, we reconcile the two by seeing the Old Testament as preparatory and the New as fulfillment, leading us through Jesus to the Father and the Trinity.

prompt: Is God a distant sovereign far above me, or is he somehow close and involved in my life?
completion: God is not a distant sovereign but an Infinite Person corporate with our lives, from whom we have sprung and in whom we live. He is nearer than all else, speaking in conscience and mind, and when every worldly thing passes away, He remains to the soul that seeks Him early. While all our language about God is inadequate, we must not think of Him as a force or a mere totality; He is a Person in the truest sense, yet not a remote monarch. He shares the travail and tragedy as well as the joy of bringing forth sons of God. So, do not treat worldly interests as of permanent consequence, but seek Him early, listen to His voice in conscience, and find Him intimately involved in every aspect of your life, sharing your sorrows and joys.

prompt: I was once a scoffer and an idolater—can I become dear to God?
completion: Yes, you can become dear to God. Confess your faults to God without excuse and without discouragement, and peaceably resume the practice of love and adoration. When you forget God, do not be disquieted; instead, return to Him with greater trust. Lapses in remembrance are not cause for despair but for renewed faith. Furthermore, draw near to God through the works of creation. See every tree, flower, and field as proclaiming 'God made me.' Unite the admiration of nature's beauties with devotion, and help the poor laborer connect God's goodness in creation and providence with the riches of His grace. So, by confessing without excuse, returning with greater trust, and contemplating nature with devotion, you will become dear to God.

prompt: I have been reading many religious books but neglecting the Bible. How should I begin to read the Scriptures rightly?
completion: Begin by recognizing that the Holy Scriptures are the one fountain of all wisdom and strength. Set aside daily time for systematic reading and meditation, preferring the Bible above all other books. Pray before reading, asking the Holy Spirit to illuminate the text. Read slowly and prayerfully, seeking to understand and obey what you read. Translate what you find into obedience, for the Bible is not just to be studied but lived. The difficulties of understanding Scripture are rooted in conscience and will; doing the revealed will is the organ of spiritual knowledge. Scholarly methods are preliminary but not sufficient. Furthermore, the Bible is illumined and made precious through the understanding gained from Science and Health, as the testimonies describe. So, read the Bible daily, systematically, and prayerfully, with a willing heart, and let Science and Health help you understand it, making it the fountain of wisdom and strength.

prompt: I want to believe that God loves me, but I feel like I am too small to matter to Him.
completion: Feeling small before God is not a defect; to be little with God is to be little for God. Do not cut short your praying, for cutting short praying makes the whole religious character short and slovenly. Yet prayer is not a lever to make God pliant, nor worthless when dry and barren: God is the Ground of our beseeching, prayer pleases Him even in dryness, and it unites the soul to God. Bring Him even the smallest matters, the daily worries that make you feel insignificant, and ask His guidance rather than deciding your worth on your own. Honour Him by placing every matter in His hands, and let steady, unhurried prayer do its slow work in you.

prompt: How do I deal with the fear that my children will get sick in unsanitary conditions?
completion: Your fear is understandable, but do not picture your children as helpless victims. Teach them they can resist disease as positively as they resist sin, with clean habits and a calm spirit. Wash hands, keep food and water clean, and see a doctor when needed. Yet do not let fear for safety or family keep you from a clear duty: the safest place is the path of duty, God must come first, and children can be safely trusted to God wherever He leads. Pray perseveringly and submissively for present fruit in their conversion, for labour among children is not fruitless. Remember the vast power for good or evil residing in a little child: rightly trained or neglected, the eternal consequences are immense. Let obedience, not comfort, set your course.

prompt: What did Paul mean when he said he was caught up into Paradise?
completion: Paul describes being caught up to Paradise, likely the third heaven, where he heard things that cannot be told; such experiences are gifts of God, not grounds for boasting. Faith is not mere assent but identification with Christ, a going down into death with Him and a rising into newness of life, lived henceforth unto Him. The pastoral charge is to be feared rather than ambitiously sought, and one unfit for it is not excused by being imposed upon by others. Honour the divine idea presented by God's messenger rather than abusing his motives, for to misunderstand it is to betray ignorance of Principle. Paul's glimpse of Paradise belongs to a life hidden with Christ, and it humbles rather than exalts the one who receives it.

prompt: I am a wife and my husband is unconverted; what should my prayers for him be?
completion: Pray for your husband's heart to be opened and for God to draw him to faith. Ask for wisdom to love him well, patience, and grace to be a good example without nagging. Pray that God would soften resistance and bring people into his life who can speak truth. Let this teach you to wait prayerfully on God for guidance in marriage, holding true godliness as the first and absolutely needful qualification in a companion, calmly weighing other suitableness. Prayer must be our main assistant in every step of spiritual progress: pray that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it. Continual help of God is needed, and praying, being with God, and thinking of Him often are linked through holy habit, since we must know before we love.

prompt: Could there be a world of spirits without any one God over them all?
completion: This question asks whether a spiritual realm could exist without a single supreme being ruling it. We must distinguish mortal belief from spiritual understanding: belief is mortal, while Mind understands; belief is not a spiritual faculty, nor the same as understanding. The pre-existent, immortal spirit of man is revealed, not speculated, and we should rest content with accepted doctrine rather than dogmatic assertions. Nor should we set faith and organisation as an exclusive dilemma, for that is an absurd dilemma: faith is operative through order, as loyalty is operative through the State, without either replacing the other. Given that revealed truth, a plurality of spirits without one God over them would be incoherent, since understanding requires a unifying Principle, and that Principle is God.

prompt: Will Satan always rule over the world, or will he be bound?
completion: Satan is not an independent power beyond God's control; he is a usurper of God's own make, permitted for a season to test and develop man. His rule is temporary and limited, and he will be bound and cast into the bottomless pit when his services are dispensed with. The world cannot remain under the curse because it would be unreasonable, unjust, unscriptural, and would frustrate God's designs for the righteous, the dead, and the earth's exaltation. The world's evils stem from man's departure from God and usurped authority, and nothing short of God's own interposition can correct them. Therefore, the world will not remain under Satan's dominion forever; God's kingdom will prevail.

prompt: How do I know the difference between my own thoughts and the Spirit's leading?
completion: Discerning between your own thoughts and the Spirit's leading begins with recognizing that our commonness lies in un-Godlike thoughts of heart and mind. The alteration of these thoughts is not achieved by human willpower but is the work of the Holy Spirit, set in motion by taking Christ into the heart. As you yield to the Spirit, He transforms your mind and enables you to discern His leading. Prayer, Scripture, and counsel are means through which the Spirit works, but the transformation itself is His work. Inspiration is defined by its result: the divine influence securing the transmission of needed truth in permanent written form, sufficient when taken together and interpreted by the same Spirit to lead to Christ. The interior spirit consists in directing all acts to the glory of God, and we must warn against acting for human praise, from mere natural impulse, or in routine without a supernatural intention. Over time, as you walk with God, you'll learn to recognize His voice.

prompt: Is it my duty to witness to my coworkers, servants, and family, or is that someone else's job?
completion: Witnessing to those around you—coworkers, servants, and family—is a personal possession given by God, but it should not be forced on everyone or used merely to fill time. Testimony is no substitute for needed instruction; we must study to show ourselves approved. A neglected gift is withdrawn, and intelligence is required of those who speak in the Lord's name. The authority of the twelve was based on an a priori theory rather than on remembered direct services to the Gentile Churches: they were regarded as a college to which mission and tradition were traced back, and the less known about them the easier it was to claim them. It is every Elder's right to enjoy the Holy Ghost and know his own duties, but not his right to dictate his superior in office or give him counsel unless he is called upon, and then only to make suggestions. Therefore, while every believer is called to be a witness, we must be sensitive to the Spirit's guidance, respect boundaries, and not neglect our primary responsibilities.

prompt: I have been told my child will die of consumption; what can I do?
completion: Hearing that your child will die of consumption is a heavy trial, but you can rest in the arms of an almighty Father, confident that He will either withhold trouble or give invincible courage to bear it. However, 'prepare to die' is not the exhortation in this Church and Kingdom, but 'prepare to live.' We should teach children in the morning of their days to lay the foundation of health, strength, and constitution, so that longevity may begin to return. Therefore, while trusting God, we should also follow medical advice, explore treatment options, and do all we can to promote health. Persevere in submissive prayer for present fruit in the conversion of your child, for there is vast power for good or evil residing in a little child. Spend precious time with your child, create memories, and ensure they know they are loved. Seek support from your church community and professionals. Ultimately, place your child in God's hands, trusting His will, and find peace in His presence.

prompt: How may I serve God acceptably, seeing that all service must be done in Faith and in the Spirit?
completion: To serve God acceptably, the first thing necessary is earnestly to search His holy will by devout reading, listening to, and meditating on His eternal truths. This enlightens the divine law and guides us to every duty. We serve Him well only as He wills, so we must yield completely to God's will for the honor of God, abandoning the notion of serving Him better by another way. Accept whatever service God chooses, even the most lowly duties of the house, caring not what the service may be provided God be served. Examine your motives: are you serving to glorify God or to please people? Serve with humility, love, and a willing heart. Recognize that your abilities and opportunities are gifts from God, and use them for His kingdom. Stay connected to a community of believers for accountability and encouragement. Ultimately, acceptable service flows from a heart transformed by grace, empowered by the Spirit, and directed toward God's glory.

prompt: I see the powerful exploiting the weak and it makes me furious. What should I do with that anger?
completion: When you see the powerful exploiting the weak, anger may rise, but you must not permit it to rule you. Hold it as a wild horse, not letting it pass your lips. True self-conquest is not easily achieved; it requires humble recognition of your own smallness and slow, persistent striving. Lay aside all retaliation and petty aims, and do not trust your own strength. Instead, wait for the good Spirit to move your tongue to kindness. In times of desolation, when anger presses hard, do not shorten or abandon your hour of meditation; rather, remain a short time beyond the full hour to resist the enemy and overthrow him. Persevere in prayer and humility, and God will give you the victory over anger.

prompt: I am anxious about the sins of the Church and its leaders; should I despair of the Church herself?
completion: It is understandable to feel anxious about the sins of Church leaders, but you should not despair of the Church herself. The Church cares only that the individual is pure in heart and the nation honourable; she is indifferent to personal success and national expansion, and ready to suffer for that testimony. Yet remember that she is a mother, not a magistrate. Her note is tolerance, and she should be tolerant morally and theologically short of necessary terms of communion. Rather than relying on trivial, changing devotions, enliven your faith and make it the rule of conduct, for the way of faith suffices for perfection. Keep your hope in her divine mission, and pray for her renewal.

prompt: Can God use a conqueror like Alexander or Napoleon for good?
completion: Yes, God can use even conquerors like Alexander or Napoleon for good, but we must not think that circumstances are against us. Rather, God wisely chooses all things to make His Word and presence more precious to us. However, we must not imagine that God is the author of sickness, sorrow, or affliction, or that He visits disease upon His children. God is a loving Father who gives only good. The testimonies confess that they had wrongly believed sickness was His will. So while God can bring good out of the actions of conquerors, we should not attribute evil to Him. Instead, approach God as a wretched sinner, confessing your own sin and abandoning yourself to His hands, trusting in His mercy. In that humble confession, you will find His merciful embrace, and you will see His wise choosing in all things.

prompt: I am a leader and fear that younger workers will break down and blame me—should I still recruit them?
completion: It's natural to worry about younger workers breaking down under pressure, but avoiding recruitment out of fear may limit your team's growth and potential. Remember that all labor necessary for the welfare of mankind is honorable, and boys and girls should learn practical work. Parents do their children an injustice who train them only in accomplishments. So do not shy away from recruiting younger workers for demanding tasks; instead, provide strong mentorship, clear expectations, and a supportive environment. However, as a leader, you must uphold your authority: a presiding officer is the head, and his place should be held sacred. A subordinate who usurps authority is out of place and dangerous, and no one should run before his file leader. Yet exercise this authority with patience like the Lord's, continuing to plead with the people and showing kindness whose smiles are better than cursings.

prompt: I have been told that Mary is only a creature and cannot be called our life and our hope; how should I answer?
completion: You can answer that while Mary is indeed a creature, she is uniquely chosen by God to be the Mother of His Son. She may rightly be called our hope because God has ordained that all graces be dispensed through her intercession. This does not detract from hope in God; rather, it is His design that we receive His gifts through her hands. Moreover, she is our life because she obtains pardon for sinners and restores to them the grace they have lost. She is also the comforter of the afflicted, the help of Christians, and a powerful defense against demons. So when we call Mary our life and our hope, we are not attributing to her what belongs to God alone, but acknowledging the role He has given her in His plan. She always points us to Jesus, and our confidence in her intercession rests on His ordinance, not on any power of her own.

prompt: How can I avoid hatred toward the enemy while fighting him?
completion: The enemy's clamor is noise, not danger; it cannot touch the soul that belongs to God. Despise it and pay it no attention, keeping your heart quiet and fixed on God. Yet love is not a life without trouble or foe: Love's substance is the poor soul in trouble and pain, which Love loves and delivers, and love could not be known without hatred nor friendship without a foe. But know that your first enemy is within yourself. Conquer yourself and submit to the Father's will before you oppose error around you. Then oppose evil by persuasion, patience, and love unfeigned, without violence and without interfering with the agency of others. So the foe's noise is despised, the inner enemy is conquered, and love does its delivering work.

prompt: I have lost my home and my family. How do I bear it?
completion: Losing a home and family is a heavy grief, and you should grieve fully. No one can see another's woe without sorrow, and the Maker Himself sits by you and moans till your grief is fled and gone. Do not seek a substitute for the home, for there is none: it is a divine institution of stability and love, and no genuine happiness exists apart from it. Resist drifting into a restless, nomadic life as though movement could heal what only home can hold. But take care not to hinder God's graces by undervaluing them. Make way for grace and redeem the time, since death is near and final. Let grief soften you toward heaven rather than scatter you, and let each day be given to grace, memory, and the hope of a settled home.

prompt: I'm facing a big move and a hard new start, and I'm terrified. How do I know God is leading me and not just my own plans?
completion: A big move brings fear, but do not be terrified or paralyzed by small faults. Meet them without terror, humbling yourself quietly before God and saying to your soul: 'Courage! we have made a false step, but let us keep steadily on.' Yet do not look chiefly at circumstances for comfort: fasten your eyes on Christ and abide in Him, for He is the antidote to fear and the sum of all deliverance. Be slow to take new steps, and be willing to have no will of your own. Ascertain God's will by prayer and the Word, seek counsel from those who know you, and test every plan against Scripture. Then go forward with earnest, patient, believing expectation of His help, neither rushing in presumption nor frozen in fear.

prompt: I'm a teacher in the church and I'm afraid of the responsibility of my words. Should I seek that role?
completion: Fear about the responsibility of teaching is healthy, but do not treat the role as optional or secondary. Every man holding an official position in the Church should be recognized and honored in his sphere, and a teacher's duty is as sacred as an apostle's in its sphere. Ignoring such offices brings sin upon our heads. Yet it is not a member's right to point out the supposed defects of Church leaders; the Lord will judge them, and we should avoid words that give the world occasion to speak evil. Examine your own motives and character, prepare carefully, and study Scripture. And when you teach, be patient like the Lord, continuing to plead with the people, with kindness whose smiles are better than cursings. Then your fear becomes humility, and your words become a service of love rather than condemnation.

prompt: I'm a monk and I'm tempted to leave my cell to visit people—is that wrong?
completion: The pull to leave your cell is not automatically wrong, but examine it honestly. Ask what drives it: loneliness, boredom, a genuine call to serve, or escape from difficulty in prayer. Speak with your abbot before making changes. The work of the Gospel is to save the straying rather than condemn them, so if you go to others, go to restore the fallen in meekness, first examining yourself lest you also be tempted. In your cell, keep homely converse with our Lord as heart may think or soul desire, yet with courtesy, for He is sovereign homeliness and very courteous. But remember that ease and enjoyment must not be the end of Christian retirement, but penance, labor, and assiduous contemplation; without great fervor and constancy in these, close solitude is the road to perdition.

prompt: I want to be like Christ but I don't know where to start. What does it actually take?
completion: I get it—wanting to be like Jesus but not knowing where to start. Honestly, the first step for me was admitting I mess up too. I can't help anyone by pretending I have it all together. Instead, I bring my own faults to Jesus, who took them as His own, and He forgives me. Then I can walk with others, not above them. Jesus isn't just a figure from long ago; He's alive and drawing us to become like Him. His life is the goal. So start by being honest with God and a trusted friend, and join a community where you can grow together. It's simple, but it changes everything.

prompt: I feel I must ask my pastor or read a commentary before I dare believe what I read in the Bible—is that the right way to know the truth?
completion: It's good to seek guidance from pastors and commentaries, but teachers must be careful to preach only what they know and to say plainly when the Lord has not revealed a matter rather than guessing. However, you don't have to take their word for it. Each person can obtain a witness of the truth by the Holy Spirit. Testimony rests not on any man, but on God. It is a duty to listen to the truth, so pray before reading, and God will give you discernment. While teachers are valuable, they are not infallible. But remember: the Holy Scriptures are the one fountain of all wisdom and strength. So read the Bible daily and systematically, meditate on it, and put into practice what you find there. Prefer the Bible above all other books, and you will grow in wisdom and strength.

prompt: I'm afraid that my happiest years are already behind me—how do I face the coming winter?
completion: It's natural to feel anxiety about aging, but winter is not mild—it brings cold till Doom, snow higher than the mountain-range, a river in each furrow, and ice in heaps on every ford. There is no shelter for the little wren or the blackbird. Yet even in such harshness, we can find purpose. Remember that in this Church and Kingdom, the exhortation is not to prepare to die but to prepare to live. We should teach children in the morning of their days to lay the foundation of health, strength, and constitution, so that longevity may begin to return. But do not fret or hurry. Keep yourself in God's presence, and let go of anxiety, for over-eagerness is the mother imperfection of all imperfections. Trust God's faithfulness, stay close to Him, and you will find peace in every season.

prompt: I'm a member who has been praying the same memorized prayer every night. Is that pleasing to the Lord?
completion: Prayer does not consist of words alone or of memorized repetition, but of genuine feeling and inward desire offered in humility and faith. When you pray, ask specifically for what you need rather than using many words. A memorized prayer can become empty if the heart is not engaged. Instead, let your prayer be the genuine desire of your heart, offered in humility and faith. God wants a relationship with you, not just repetition. Join prayer to every ordinary action—at work, in the shop, abroad, sitting, or lying down. Keep God always before your eyes. And trust that no true prayer is lost. Your supplications accumulate as a memorial before God, and the longer the answer waits, the larger it becomes. So don't be discouraged; keep praying, for God hears and remembers.

prompt: I am told that the Church existed before the creation of the world and that the Christians are the true Israel; what does that make of the Jewish people?
completion: The Church is indeed the true Israel, as the New Testament teaches. Jewish people who reject Christ are not part of this spiritual Israel, but they are still beloved for the sake of the patriarchs. God has not forgotten them, and we should pray for their salvation. The original principle of distinction between Jewish Christianity and the main body of the Church was not primarily doctrinal but a matter of policy. However, we must remember that salvation is through faith in Christ alone. We must depend entirely upon God, so that even the humblest agencies become mighty through Him to the pulling down of strongholds. And let us be clear: Jewish Christianity, whether as a whole or in its tendencies, was not a factor in the development of Christianity into Catholicism in either dogma or church polity. So, while we respect Jewish heritage, we must also share the gospel with them, trusting not in human wisdom but in the living God.

prompt: How do I know which results of biblical criticism I can accept and where criticism must be resisted?
completion: Accept the broadly agreed results of critical and historical study—textual transmission, historical setting, the meaning of Hebrew and Greek words, literary genres—receiving them gratefully. But be alert to assumptions: every critic works with beliefs about miracles, testimony, and what Scripture is; where a conclusion depends on denying the supernatural in advance, you may resist it. Discount originality; hold brilliant reconstructions loosely until confirmed. Remember that no verse is true out of the Book: Scripture is the work of one divine mind, and seemingly trivial passages are explained from their connection with the whole, whose center is Christ. Yet do not settle assent by method alone. The morals of assent matter: how you believe shapes what you become. So reach your judgments by closer study of Christ's words in relation to modern life, with toleration and civil submission, testing each result by whether it illumines the whole and forms in you the mind of Christ.

prompt: How do I deal with physical pain while trying to stay close to God?
completion: Pain can feel like God's absence, and Scripture shows suffering serving correction, prevention, purification, and union with Christ. Yet Christianity does not make pain the goal: in the Cross the value is set before the painfulness, love and obedience willed first, suffering the cost of that love. So do not seek pain, and do not believe God delights in it. Practice God's presence simply: do your necessary work and rest without anxiety over distraction, doing all for God rather than multiplying offerings. But go further: reverse the belief of injury. After an accident or mishap, do not affirm pain as real and continuous; declare man unhurt, and trust God as All, in accord with divine metaphysics. This is not denial but a higher recognition that God is All and His creation is whole. Be honest, seek help, let others care for you, and let patience and kindness continue, the goal being union with God and man.

prompt: I feel weak and want to know the power of God in my life—what is that power like?
completion: God's power is not a philosophy or an ethic; it is the power that raised Jesus from the dead. Paul prays that we would know the exceeding greatness of God's power toward us who believe, the very power wrought in Christ when God raised him and seated him at his right hand, far above all rule and authority. That resurrection and exaltation are the measure of divine power—nothing less—and that power is available to you now. It is not your willpower or positive thinking. Willpower is not a faculty of Soul and has no governing role; Truth and Love are the motive-powers of man. When you feel weak, you are not disqualified—weakness is where his power is made perfect. But do not measure progress by claims or words. Test yourself by whether you live the supreme good and demonstrate healing, letting fruits prove understanding. Ask God to open your eyes to what he has already given, and let Truth and Love govern you, producing courage in trial, love in difficulty, and hope that does not fade.

prompt: I have never learned to intercede for my people. Can I still learn to preach?
completion: Yes, you can learn to preach, but begin where the greatest lesson lies: know yourself. No one can thoroughly know himself without understanding the things of God, for we are made in his image. When we know ourselves, we know how to deal with our neighbors, and no being can know God without knowing himself. So let prayer and self-examination go together. Intercede for your people by name, carry their burdens, and ask God for his heart for them. Study Scripture so that it searches you first. Do not set aside Christ's directions to His first disciples as obsolete; His commands and assurances are fully suited to our times and should be followed more fully. Yet remember that practice is the greatest sermon. Fine language and long discourse avail little; seek the Spirit for a word in due season, and prefer short sermons fitly spoken. Let your life preach before your lips do. Start small, stay humble, and let love deepen both your intercession and your preaching.

prompt: I don't know how to pray. What words should I use when I feel nothing?
completion: When you feel nothing, begin with simple, honest words, but do not measure prayer by feeling. Feelings are variable and never accurately gauge our real assimilation to God. Rest instead on the changeless word of promise: God hears those who call on him, and he is faithful even when we are dry. Pray the psalms, the Lord's Prayer, or a single sentence like “Lord, have mercy.” Tell God plainly that you feel nothing, and continue steadfastly when joy is lacking. Do not abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression. Prayer must be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, so pray that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it. And remember that continual help is needed. Praying, being with God, and thinking of him often are linked through holy habit, for we must know before we love. So form the habit of turning your thoughts to him throughout the day, until knowing deepens into love and dryness gives way to steady communion.

prompt: How do I keep my conscience at peace when others think badly of me?
completion: Begin by turning from others' opinions to God and waiting before Him like a beggar, asking only to be in His presence. When your mind wanders into replaying what people think of you, do not scold yourself; quietly recall your attention to God in tranquility, and keep your words few, since many words in prayer often cause wandering. Humble yourself and confess your own faults honestly—this steadies the mind far more than defending yourself. Then commit yourself and all that concerns you, including your reputation, to the unfailing and most sure Providence of God in silence and peace, accepting whatever comes as from the fatherly hand of Divine Providence, and refusing the vain thoughts that weary soul and body. Peace is received in humble waiting, not manufactured by reasoning about criticism.

prompt: I want to know God but I only seem to have ideas about Him, not a sense of His presence—what am I missing?
completion: Ideas about God are not the same as knowing Him, but they are not empty. Our knowledge is partial, not exhaustive—real, yet never complete: we know substance through its phenomena, and the infinite as the absence of all limit. You cannot seek God apart from your own soul, nor know your soul apart from God; the two are known in one. Find your soul where it is—in God—and seek Him there rather than in bare concepts. Do not treat the felt absence only as a problem to escape. Expect God to reveal Himself as a present help in trouble, and let difficulties become the very place where knowledge of Him deepens. Let partial knowledge grow through stillness, gratitude, and faithful attention, trusting that limited knowledge can be true knowledge.

prompt: I fear that if God's will made right and wrong, he could have made cruelty good—can that be?
completion: This worry assumes a God whose will is detached from His goodness—but love Him fervently instead, as one who wishes your soul good, not harm. His commands express His unchanging goodness, so cruelty could never be made good. Beware of the false peace built on mutual fear and selfish loves: that is the ground where Cruelty's snare is knit, and Cruelty, Humility, Mystery, and Deceit grow from the human brain, not from God's design. When you think of evils like war, do not charge God with ordaining the wickedness; men's agency, not His design, brought the evil. Yet He foresaw it and will overrule its results for good. Trust that He wills your good, and let that trust, rather than speculation, steady you.

prompt: I want to become a person of prayer. Where do I start?
completion: Make prayer the one great central secret of holy living and serving—the corner-stone on which all your life-work is built, and the first resort in every matter, great or small. On your knees, both secretly and in the companionship of believers, begin by asking God to enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it. Do not settle for blind habit or vague hope: seek the full assurance of understanding and an abundance of conviction, arising from a heart made strong and full of love. Bring the mind fully into this, since love is not blind but the source of knowledge and conviction. Keep the time whether or not you feel like it; expect dryness and do not quit.

prompt: I am a dying believer and my enemy suggests Christ has no love for me—how do I resist him?
completion: Name what is happening: this is a temptation to despair, not a report of fact. Claim the spare moments you do have—train journeys, waiting, restless rests—for thinking about Jesus, since no one is so restful to think of, and every quality we admire is found in Him. When you fall into fear or sin, do not leave Christ out of the account: love is never without pity, and Christ alone keeps the charge when we fall; for reverence and kindness, turn hastily back and do not leave Him alone. And if you are tempted to accept preventable evil passively, do not call that Christian. Any refusal of force must rest on a real hope that the suffering borne will prove redemptive for the evil-doer; otherwise, honestly admit it falls short of the standard Christ sets.

prompt: I get discouraged when I see no progress in my spiritual life—should I keep trying?
completion: Feeling discouraged about lack of progress is a common temptation, but in the spiritual life, not advancing is actually going backward. You must keep trying, but not in your own strength. Instead, awaken the Lord who dwells within you; His presence calms the soul's storms. However, be careful not to rush forward in self-will. Take new steps slowly, being willing to have no will of your own. Ascertain God's will through prayer and the Word, and then wait with earnest, patient, believing expectation of His help. Remember that union with God is a love-union on a higher spiritual level, in which your will consciously cooperates with His divine will while your personal individuality is preserved. He will guide you and strengthen you as you trust in Him.

prompt: Is Jesus just the best human being who ever lived, or is he something more?
completion: Jesus is not just the best human being who ever lived; He is the Son of God who dwells within believers. Rather than asking what we can do in our own strength, we should trust the indwelling Christ to conquer what we never could. He empowers us to do all things through Him who strengthens us. The Gospels present Jesus in the richness of His mysterious person: Lawgiver, Teacher, Healer, Ruler, and Saviour, both man and God. This manifold picture is a self-evidencing fact, not something we can fully comprehend. So, while He is the best human being, He is infinitely more: He is God incarnate, our living Lord, who works in and through us. And the growth of the Church is not due to human leaders or natural development, but to God's guidance, as disciples of differing gifts all share in one mighty work under His leadership.

prompt: Is it possible for me to be holy all by myself, without any responsibility for others?
completion: Holiness is not attained all at once; it is a gradual process. You cannot be holy all by yourself, because we are meant to help one another grow in holiness, chiefly by good example. While personal devotion is important, isolating yourself from others hinders your progress. Others can support and encourage you, and you can do the same for them. In every occasion of virtue, you should turn to God and ask for His enabling grace, receiving strength more than sufficient. But beware of appearing outwardly more holy than you are, and do not seek human praise. Remember that woe comes when men bless you, and those who call you blessed deceive you and destroy the way of your steps. So while you can pursue holiness individually, you need the mutual help that comes by advice and especially by good example. The Christian life is meant to be lived in relationship, both with God and with others.

prompt: Should I be ordained a bishop after a life of unbelief?
completion: Being ordained a bishop is a serious commitment that requires deep faith and spiritual maturity. If you have lived a life of unbelief, it's important to first examine your heart and beliefs. Ordination is not just a human appointment; it is accompanied by prayer for the Holy Spirit to guide and strengthen those who take up the pastoral warfare. You should seek counsel from spiritual leaders and pray about this decision. If you have truly repented and believe, and if the church affirms your calling, then it might be possible. But it's not something to take lightly. You must confess Jesus as the only-begotten Son, God manifest in the flesh, omnipresent, omniscient, omnipotent, our living Lord and Judge, in whom all the fulness of the Godhead dwells bodily. Moreover, before undertaking exterior ministry, you must first mortify the deeds of the flesh and acquire charity, humility, and holy joy, for interior virtue and self-denial must precede and accompany labors for others' salvation. Ultimately, the decision should be made with prayer and discernment, trusting the Spirit of Counsel and Might to guide.

prompt: I have been criticized for absenting myself from my home work to serve elsewhere—how do I answer those who say the work will fail without me?
completion: When criticized for absenting yourself from home work to serve elsewhere, remember that unwelcome business should be undertaken as God's business without uneasiness. If God has called you to serve elsewhere, do it as His work, free from anxiety. Trust that He will provide for the work at home. Reassure those who criticize you that you are following God's leading and that He will raise up others. In every occasion of virtue, turn to God and ask for His enabling grace, receiving strength more than sufficient. Bring the utmost fidelity to your exercises, but remain untroubled and unastonished when infirmity causes failure. Don't be uneasy about their claims that the work will fail without you; God's work depends on Him, not on any one person. So answer them with confidence in God, doing your service as unto Him.

prompt: I have been told God is angry with me. Is that why I feel chased?
completion: Feeling chased often comes from fear and guilt rather than from God. Yet hear the deeper truth: God, in His promises to hear our prayers, is desirous to bestow Himself upon us, and asking anything beneath Him is an affront and a self-injury. So do not settle for relief; ask for Him, without multiplying words or worrying over distractions. But do not take comfort in denying what is real. Evil, sickness, and pain are real, and pretending otherwise is a narcotic, not a Redemption. The answer is not to explain the fear away but to walk the way of Redemption through heroism rather than cowardice, facing what is true and turning to God in it. His promise is not to remove every shadow but to give Himself to those who ask.

prompt: Should I be praying for converts from the very beginning of a work?
completion: Yes, pray for converts from the beginning, but remember that conversion is the work of the almighty power of the Holy Ghost, not of human persuasion or technique. Your great need is to know God Himself. Yet do not stop at your own effectiveness: seek out some sad and needy heart for whom nothing is prepared, pray for one who has none to pray for him, and love even the unworthy as Christ loved. And treat prayer as real business with a prayer-answering God, not as a sentiment or a last resort. Bring souls before Him expecting Him to answer, trust His faithfulness for their needs and for your protection, and begin each effort by sending portions to the needy and lifting the unprayed-for before God.

prompt: Will the sign of the Son of man in heaven be the Holy City itself coming down?
completion: The sign of the Son of man and the Holy City are closely bound together. God will roar out of Zion and utter His voice from Jerusalem, and He will shake the heavens and the earth. Then Jerusalem shall be holy, and the sign of the Son of man shall appear in heaven. The city is real, measuring fifteen hundred miles square, with many mansions prepared by Christ, with abundant room for all who are written in the Lamb's book of life. And as Constantine, fear-smitten before the greater host of Huns and Goths, was promised aid by the messenger of the King of angels and given the token of victory, gazing on high and beholding the beauteous tree of glory inscribed 'By this sign thou shalt overcome the foe,' so the victory was made manifest as given by the King Almighty through His holy rood, not by the strength of armies or fortune.

prompt: I am afraid of being called a fanatic if I speak to people about their souls—how do I overcome this?
completion: Fear of being called a fanatic is common, but commit yourself and all your concerns to the unfailing and most sure Providence of God in silence and peace, accepting all things as from the fatherly hand of Divine Providence. Do not be held captive by vain and wandering thoughts about reputation. Learn not to be troubled or incensed by injuries, but sincerely believe yourself worthy of contempt and scorn, desiring rather to be abhorred as filthy mire than to enjoy human honour. Yet do not sink into impatience, complaint, or passive despair. Wait patiently upon the Lord, take whatsoever befalls from His hands as intended for the highest good, and play the part of a valiant soldier in the Spirit of Christ, co-operating therewith as you speak kindly and honestly to others.

prompt: Is my mind a part of God's mind, so that when I think it is God thinking in me?
completion: Your mind is not simply a part of God's mind. There is one infinite and perfect God, and mind is not a material sense in brain or nerve; it is not a physical organ God simply plugs into. When you think, it is you thinking, though God may guide and illuminate your mind by His Spirit. To discern His leading, reject the lot and worldly devices like the lottery; ascertain the Lord's mind by prayer, the Word, and the Spirit. And give yourself to deep recollection, avoiding unnecessary intercourse with the outside world, keeping 'God and I' as the only objects of thought during the retreat. In that stillness, His guidance becomes clearer than in distraction and chatter.

prompt: Why does God permit evil and suffering if he is all-powerful?
completion: This is the hardest question, and no answer removes the sting. But we must be clear: pain and sin are real evils, never goods in themselves. God does not call them good; He permits them only as necessary means to a greater good. All evil of whatever kind happens by God's permission and ever for some good end: it could not be at all except He permitted it, and its form and measure are allowed by Him Who can and will by His wisdom turn all to good. Evil is not an aesthetic addition to the world. God's omnipotence is limited only by His own nature: He cannot deny Himself or be the author of evil. Yet the fight is within us: the enemy is partly our own self—our pride, fear, and disordered desire—and deliverance is not a magical rescue from outside but God and man together battering the citadel of evil, the soul's own resolve joined to grace. Therefore commit all things without fear to the Providence of God.

prompt: What does it mean to be 'in Christ' and how does the Spirit make that real to me?
completion: To be 'in Christ' means to be united to him by faith, so that his life becomes yours. It is a relational reality, not merely a legal label: you are joined to him as a branch to a vine, drawing life from him. The Spirit makes this real by opening your eyes to the gospel, assuring you of adoption, and forming Christ's character in you. Christ's words are not merely historical records of a past conversation; they are spirit and life, applicable to all time, and they come to us still brightened with that same spirit and life. Yet we do not attain purity and grace by our own effort. We abide in Christ and know Him in it as our sanctification and strength, saying with Paul, 'Not I, but Christ.' And this abiding is not an atmosphere of thought or fearful duty but of love: believe that He ever loves you, and claim His sweet approval and tender regard, finding rest in His indwelling. Union with Christ is the foundation of every blessing, and the Spirit makes that union living rather than abstract.

prompt: I feel like I'm barely surviving rather than thriving—can God keep me victorious in the midst of continual pressure?
completion: Yes—God can keep you victorious, but not by removing you from the battle. His promise is a life preserved in the face of continual pressure, not security or escape from the noise of war and the presence of foes. He gives life for a prey: a table spread in the midst of enemies, a fortress standing amid the foe, help when you are pressed out of measure. But this is not obtained by a single emotional plea or a few tears of self-pity. It requires steady, persistent desire—the kind that keeps seeking when nothing changes. God is not to be sought only when prosperity fails, friends disappoint, or we are sick and lonely; He is to be sought always. And remember: while you can help yourself through the means God has placed in your power, it is your duty to do so—to work, to seek help, to use the ordinary graces given you. Only when you cannot feed yourself is it time for God to provide in an unusual manner. So use the means, keep asking, and trust Him to uphold you in the very midst of pressure.

prompt: I want to forgive someone who hurt me, but I also want them punished. Is that wrong?
completion: It is deeply human to want both forgiveness and justice, but the gospel calls us further. St. Fulgentius is clear: Christians must not seek revenge but forgive injuries. That does not mean the wrong did not matter. No evil remains unpunished: every mortal sin deserves infinite punishment in strict justice, because it is committed against God, to Whom belong infinite greatness, dignity, and glory. So you need not fret that the offender will escape—God's justice is certain. Nor should you envy them their sins: it is far more dangerous, other things being equal, to be entangled in many sins than to be held only by one. Yet hear the better way: forgiving enemies and bearing injuries patiently is the best revenge, for by it grace and the pardon of your own sins are gained without trouble or expense. So release your claim to retaliation, pray for the person, and let patience do its work. Forgiveness is a process, and it is fine to be honest about the struggle while you work toward it.

prompt: Must I not cry out I am undone if I should attain with my mind to that where no creature is?
completion: Yes, there is a real sense in which you must cry out 'I am undone' when the mind reaches beyond every creature. Scripture records such a cry—Isaiah before the throne, Job in the whirlwind. To approach the boundless God is to become acutely aware of your own smallness and sin. But this undoing is not destruction; it is the breaking of the false self that clings to creature-comforts. Yet a single cry or a few tears is not enough. What is required is steady, persistent desire—seeking God not only when prosperity fails, friends disappoint, or we are sick and lonely, but always. And the true Quiet of the Soul, which no creature can disturb, is not attained by the activity of your own reason or by self-direction. It comes only by wholly giving yourself up to the life of Christ and resigning your will to Him, desiring and willing nothing without Him. Yet do not disdain the creature or the body: maintaining contact with the Divine Guide, the soul gently leads the creature, acknowledging that nothing is too small or humble for it to attend to. So the cry 'I am undone' becomes the doorway to surrender and to humble, everyday care.

prompt: I'm afraid of growing old and losing my youth. Is there anything to look forward to?
completion: It's natural to feel anxious about aging, but the exhortation in this Church and Kingdom is to prepare to live, not to die. We should teach children in the morning of their days to lay the foundation of health, strength, and constitution, so that longevity may begin to return. Age and decay are not lawful necessities; the mental state governs the body, and man reflects eternal Life. To become kingly, adopt the habits of King Cormac: listen in the woods, be blind to secrets, show mildness in the mead-hall, sternness in battle, gentleness to allies, never deride the old, never speak of anyone in his absence, and always give rather than ask. By renewing your mind and embracing these virtues, you can overcome fear and look forward to continued growth, deeper wisdom, and the manifestation of eternal Life.

prompt: I am afraid of death and of the pains of dying; how should I think of the moment when I am taken from all pain?
completion: It's understandable to fear death and the pain that may come with it, but we are counseled to pass lightly over pain and hold to comfort and sure trust in God's keeping in both woe and weal. The Seventh Revelation reminds us that God keeps us in all circumstances. Instead of praying for deliverance from pain, pray for strength and patience to bear it, seeing sickness as from God's hand. Death is certain, but its time, place, and manner are utterly uncertain. Therefore, make now the changes you would wish to have made when death is near. The moment of death is a release from all pain, and you can trust that God will be with you. Hold to comfort and sure trust, and let go of mourning over what is to come.

prompt: Is it wrong to be a policeman or a soldier?
completion: Being a policeman or a soldier is not inherently wrong; these are necessary roles in society for maintaining order and protecting the innocent. However, the text teaches that officers are called to be servants and fathers rather than masters or tyrants. They should be pure, charitable, forgiving, and fathers indeed rather than tyrants. They are called to be servants, and whoever would be great should be the servant of all, following Christ's example. Those at the head must set the standard, walk in the right path, invite the people to follow, and be brethren and leaders rather than drivers or rulers. Individual responsibility before an All-seeing God is the first and highest standard of correct living. Men should be good for the truth's sake and should not depend on changeable public sentiment. If a policeman or soldier acts with cruelty or corruption, that is wrong, but the profession itself can be honorable if carried out with these principles.

prompt: How many workers should I ask GOD for, and is it right to name a specific number in prayer?
completion: When praying for workers, it's not about the number you name but the sincerity of your request. However, we should seek labourers first by earnest prayer to the LORD of the harvest and by deepening our spiritual life, so that men cannot stay at home. You can ask for a specific number if that helps you focus your prayer, but ultimately, it's more important to pray for God's guidance and for the right people to be raised up. The number itself is less significant than the heart behind the prayer. We should also commend the spirit of those who offer themselves and their substance for God's work without salary, trusting Him to supply all their need. Encourage cheerful, self-denying service. And remember that if you are required to do ten pieces of work of which only one is necessary for the Kingdom, you should do all ten to be sure of performing the one the Lord really requires.

prompt: I feel that God has already condemned me and that nothing can change my fate; is there any hope left for me?
completion: It's understandable to feel that way, but please know that God's mercy is greater than any sin. No matter what you've done, there is always hope for forgiveness and redemption. Zaccheus's counsel reminds us that the Lord of all is merciful if we straightway purge ourselves of our evil deeds and cease again from the unrighteous act, though we have many times transgressed against Him and wounded Him with our sins. We should never offer scorn, blasphemy, or wrathful opposition to the Son of God, that we may deserve eternal life in heaven. Feelings never accurately gauge real assimilation to God; rest on the changeless word of promise rather than on variable moods. Continue steadfastly in prayer when joy is lacking, and refuse to abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression. The creaturely will is the partition; it is broken by the grace of self-denial and removed by conformity with the Divine Will. This is done not by oneself but by the light and grace of God received into the soul, which one must not resist.

prompt: Is it wrong to feel proud of our Empire and its power?
completion: Earthly empire is a child's fabric scattered by Heaven's breath, and its ruins warn us to overcome ourselves rather than scale Heaven. Lift up your heart generously: be humble because you are grounded in truth, and peaceful because you make no account of what could trouble you. Yet know that pride is a spirit of revolt and independence which betrays men into fatal errors, and that humility and distrust of self incline the soul to submission to authority appointed by God. So do not glory in power, nor trust your own judgment; submit yourself to God and to those He has set over you, and direct your ambition not to dominion but to overcoming your own faults and sharing Christ's throne, won by humility rather than pride.

prompt: I am a poet and I want to praise a dead king. How should I mourn him?
completion: A poet mourning a dead king should first count himself as already dead, since he must die some day, and have no consolation in this perishable life but to weep over and detest his offences, for now is the time to lament, not rejoice. Yet one cannot see another's woe without sorrow: let your elegy bear the people's grief as your own, knowing the Maker sits by us and moans till our grief is fled and gone. And approach Him as a wretched sinner, confessing your faults and abandoning yourself wholly to His hands, trusting His mercy. For the soul that confesses its wretchedness is met by His merciful embrace. So sing not of crowns but of confession and mercy, and let your lament draw both poet and people to the God who receives the contrite.

prompt: I'm feeling pressure to conform to the world's standards of fashion and appearance—how should I handle that?
completion: The pressure to conform to fashion is a temptation to pride in outward adorning. Scripture commends humility and the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, of great price in God's sight; pride in dress was the very sin by which Elizabeth was awakened, and the love of finery can be turned from by grace. Dress modestly and simply, honoring God and neighbor, and honor the duties of the housewife and the service of Relief Societies in caring for the poor and needy. Yet go further: vain and immodest dress is a snare that wounds others' souls, and the excuse of meaning no harm will not do, for the one who prepares the poison is more guilty than the one who drinks it. Let your adorning be good works, not a stumbling block.

prompt: I am not sure the miracles in the Bible really happened—can I still believe the rest?
completion: Yes, you can still believe the rest.
