Take heart that the Apostle's prayers will be answered, and set yourself resolutely, humbly, lovingly, and trustfully to fulfil the required conditions. Yet keep prayer simple and natural—a child asking a Father, not a formal procedure governed by human rules. God as Father delights to be sought for everyday needs, so ask Him plainly and constantly, without imposing man-made rules on prayer.

prompt: I'm afraid of losing my individuality if I give myself completely to God. Will I stop being myself?
completion: The fear of losing yourself in God rests on a misunderstanding. Giving yourself completely to God does not erase your individuality; it purifies and fulfills it. The real partition between you and God is the creaturely will—the self built on pride and self-will rather than your true identity. That will is broken by the grace of self-denial and removed by conformity with the Divine Will, yet not by your own effort, technique, or resolve, but by the light and grace of God received into the soul, which you must not resist. Self-denial must be grounded in inward joy in God and the Spirit's working, not mere habit or imitation. Remember that we are nothing, and that every man at his best state is vanity; only in humility and self-emptying can God fill and work through us. Surrender, then, is not loss but the way God shapes the person He intended you to be.

prompt: I want to be humble—how do I actually acquire contempt of self?
completion: Begin by acknowledging that of yourself you are nothing, and that every man at his best state is vanity. Any good in you is God's, not yours. Distrust your own judgment and expect nothing from yourself; when you fail, do not be surprised, for you are seeing what you are apart from grace. Serve unnoticed, and place yourself below all creatures, esteeming others as better than yourself. Above all, dread the esteem and praises of others, for they are snares by which a mortal poison may imperceptibly insinuate itself into your affections and deprive you of divine grace. Do not measure growth by feeling capable or by any self-assessment, for even your best state is vanity; rather, empty yourself so God may fill you and work through you. Courage here is not confidence in your own strength but a low esteem of self that leaves room for God alone to act.

prompt: I've been praying for help and nothing seems to happen—does God act in my life?
completion: Yes—God acts, and He is a very present help in trouble, always near. Keep praying simply and persistently, without anxiety. Do not multiply explicit offerings or worry that nothing be left unasked; rather, do all your actions for God, and let your prayer be the simple turning of your heart to Him amid your work. If distraction comes, do not be troubled—return quietly and continue. Above all, let prayer be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress: pray that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart, and to reform whatever is amiss in it. He is not far off or slow to hear; He is nearer than your own breath, steadying you, opening doors, and sending help at the right moment. Trust that He is already at work in ordinary things, for He never leaves you.

prompt: I am overwhelmed by my sin—can a finite Savior ever be enough to save me?
completion: Your sense of being overwhelmed is a beginning of grace, for it means you are seeing your need. Do not soften the danger: one mortal sin unrepented is enough to damn the soul, so nourish an intense and abiding fear of sin and eternal loss, for fear restrains us where love is too weak. Yet do not languish in doubt over the number or magnitude of your sins: all is possible to God, and it is as easy for Him to forgive and blot out innumerable and heinous sins as to forgive one. Of ourselves we cannot even think what is right, since all comes to us from God. Salvation is not a verdict merely credited to you but the actual redemption of your whole self—being made righteous by living, in Christ's power, the life He lived. So confess, turn, and let Him transform you from within.

prompt: I keep failing in the same area. Should I be discouraged?
completion: No—do not be discouraged, and do not let Satan see that you are afraid. Be brave and true to your convictions from the beginning. Bring the utmost fidelity to your exercises—prayer, Scripture, and the study of Science and Health—and keep them faithfully, yet remain untroubled and unastonished when infirmity causes failure. Failure in the same area is common and does not mean you are beyond hope. Do not be surprised by weakness; expect it, and let it deepen your dependence on God. Materia medica and physicians may have done their best, but without avail; the healing comes through the study of Science and Health. Stand firm, trust God to stand by you, and keep returning to your exercises without fear or dismay.

prompt: I am a dying believer and my parents are still unconverted—may I hope my prayers for them will be answered?
completion: Yes, you may hope, but let your hope be purged of selfishness. Do not pray chiefly for your own comfort or reputation, but for the glory of God and the salvation of their souls—for what your parents could be for God and His kingdom. Let prayer be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress: pray that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it, so that your intercession flows from a purified heart. Keep praying faithfully, entrusting your parents to God as ever-present and omnipotent, in whom even children's complaints disappear. Share your hope with them while you still can, and leave the timing and results to God, who desires their good even more than you do.

prompt: I'm afraid of being judged by my family for my beliefs—how do I stay true to my faith?
completion: Fear of family judgment is real, but the answer is not to put faith on trial before human wisdom. Trust God with all your heart and refuse to lean on your own understanding, for that leaning hinders faith. Faith must be quickened—made alive and taken as your rule of conduct—rather than replaced by trivial, shifting devotions that rise and fall with approval or mood; the way of faith suffices to bring you to perfection. Do not let comfort or safety become your master. Be ready to endure discomfort and even rejection for Christ's sake, and regard this trial not as pointless but as given for God's glory and the strengthening of your faith. Speak gently, love your family, and let a living faith, not fear, govern your choices.

prompt: Does God force anyone to be saved?
completion: God does not force anyone to be saved, yet salvation is not a neutral choice. In every soul that shall be saved there is a Godly Will that never consents to sin—a will God quickens and preserves, so the saved freely turn to Him. The order matters: first comes the effort and willing of the human will, stirred and enabled by grace, and then God's stabilising grace confirms and upholds it. God's will and man's will work harmoniously together—grace does not override the will but heals and strengthens it. Nor should non-resistance be confused with passivity: refusing force is Christian only when grounded in real hope that the suffering borne will prove redemptive for the evil-doer; otherwise it is idle and cowardly. So God does not coerce; He awakens a willing will and then establishes it.

prompt: How can I share in Christ's sufferings and in the work of redeeming the world?
completion: Christ's suffering is on your behalf, not instead of you. He bore what you could not, and now invites you into the fellowship of His sufferings and His ongoing work of redemption—not to add to your salvation, but to share His life. You share in it by dying to self, bearing burdens, forgiving enemies, and standing with the suffering and poor. Do not seek riches, greatness, or honour where your Lord was poor and despised; embrace being despised and lowly with Christ as your true glory. Nor be too solicitous for sensible devotion, sweetness, and tears; chiefly care to remain inwardly united to God by good will in the intellectual part of the soul, denying yourself to follow Christ, Who was truly poor, obedient, chaste, humble, and suffering. Redemption is accomplished at the cross yet applied through His body, and your life becomes its embodiment.

prompt: How will the Lord come to judge the living and the dead?
completion: The Lord will return visibly and personally to judge the living and the dead. His judgment is according to deeds done in the body—what we have done, said, and even thought—and the thoughts and intents of the heart are laid bare before Him. Death leaves us as it finds us, so judgment is not a changeable thing we can defer or amend afterward. Yet death is not the end of identity but a door to a higher state: the righteous dead are not lost, and we need not mourn them hopelessly, for the body will be raised and the person preserved. God will honour and magnify His servants, sustain them in righteousness, lift them on high, exalt them into His presence, and let them partake of His glory forever. Their service is not in vain. So be ready, trusting Christ, doing good, and guarding the heart's hidden intentions.

prompt: I feel lonely because I have obeyed my conscience and separated from friends and customs—is this loneliness to be expected?
completion: Loneliness after obeying conscience is to be expected, but do not mistake exterior solitude for true solitude. Walls and physical separation are only a weak fence; without interior recollection they are not true solitude at all. True solitude requires silence of the interior faculties—quieting imagination, memory, and will—and employing the mind on God and on yourself. Yet more than technique, keep yourself in the love of God by constant trust and constant obedience, so that hard things become easy and sorrow is silver-lined with hope. And do not expect romance, family, business, pleasure, or art to fill the emptiness within; every substitute for God leaves an emptiness unfilled and ends in disillusionment. Only the finding of God is a permanent success. Let your separation become a school of interior silence and abiding love, where loneliness is met by His presence.

prompt: I feel like I am being chased by my own guilt. Is that God?
completion: Guilt that chases you is real, but it is not your master and not your work to manage alone. God is the one living Worker; counselors, friends, and your own efforts are only His instruments, useful when they lead you to Him and harmful when they replace Him. Cast all your care upon Him, for anxious self-reliance is distrust of the God who promises to hear. If you have offended Him—by hiding, by preferring a creature to Himself—do not stay paralyzed in doubt. Humble yourself, beg His forgiveness, and renew your promises of fidelity and love. Then begin again, and keep pursuing perfection, for He desires to bestow Himself on you, and asking anything beneath Him affronts Him and hurts you. The chasing is not condemnation; it is His drawing. Run to Him.

prompt: How do I deal with the temptation to take pride in a successful sermon or talk?
completion: Pride in a successful talk is a common snare, and the remedy begins by reordering what you count as success. Practice is the greatest sermon: a life lived in obedience preaches louder than any eloquence, and fine language or long discourse without it is empty noise. Before you prepare, seek the Spirit for a word in due season, and prefer a short sermon fitly spoken to a long one that displays the speaker. Be warned, too, that sermon-making and study are not enough to keep your spirit in trim; sermon-making without prayer hardens and estranges the heart from God, and much prayer is necessary to keep the preacher's spirit in harmony with his calling. Yet do not despair at the temptation. God permits such evil inclinations to humble us; despise the temptation while embracing the tribulation it brings, and let it drive you to prayer rather than to shame.

prompt: Is the heavenly sanctuary a figure only, or is it a real building?
completion: The heavenly sanctuary is not a figure only; it is a real dwelling place in heaven. The wilderness tabernacle and the temple were patterns and shadows of it, copies of the true tabernacle which the Lord pitched and not man. Moses was shown the pattern on the mount so that the earthly tent might image the heavenly reality, not replace it. Approach this with awe: the sacrifice offered there is tremendous beyond telling, the priest holds Christ Himself, angels attend the altar, and a purity becoming heaven is required. Nor are the opened heavens a mere figure. At the place where the Cherubims and the flaming sword keep the way of the tree of life, the heavens are literally opened; this is the gate of heaven, and by this way the Holy City will descend. The earthly was a shadow; the heavenly is the substance.

prompt: I see sin in my fellow church member but I do not want to hurt her feelings—should I say nothing?
completion: This is a difficult situation, and kindness matters—but silence is not always kind. Begin by seeing clearly that sin confers no real pleasure; what looks like enjoyment in wrongdoing is a counterfeit that costs more than it gives, and knowing this strengthens moral courage to help her escape it. Speak privately and firmly, not with mere remonstrance: if the sin is swearing, treat it as a grave habit to be broken and recommend a penance for each oath. Yet know your place. It is not a member's right to point out the supposed defects of Church leaders—Joseph Smith, Brigham Young, or others; the Lord will judge them. Leave that judgment to God, avoid words that give the world occasion to speak evil, and correct only what is truly yours to correct, with humility and love.

prompt: Is it wrong to accept my religion on authority rather than working it all out for myself?
completion: Accepting your religion on authority is not wrong, provided we understand what authority is. Authority is not coercive power or the threat of penalty; it is moral and spiritual weight that rightly carries our judgment. Coercion adds nothing to the Church's true authority—a faith secured by threat is submission to force, not authority. Nor is the final arbiter your inward light or private consciousness set above the Bible. Submit to the prophets and apostles speaking through the Scriptures; that subjection is perfect freedom, placing you under truth itself. And be willing to depend wholly on GOD. Where human guarantees, teachers, or reasoned proofs would secure you in advance, be ready to decline that support if doing so enables a fuller dependence on His faithfulness. Receive the faith handed down, and let its authority carry you where your own reasoning cannot reach.

prompt: Why are people in rich countries still unhappy and violent?
completion: Rich countries often have high material wealth but still experience unhappiness and violence due to factors like inequality, social isolation, and lack of meaning. Despite economic prosperity, many people feel disconnected and stressed, leading to mental health issues and aggression. Consumerism and competition can erode community bonds, and the pursuit of wealth may overshadow deeper fulfillment. Moreover, the groans of the poor, though often ignored, are arms more powerful than magistrates; they pierce the heavens and draw down divine vengeance on oppressors. A just society requires a complete education that raises every person's actual worth to the level of their potentialities, for undeveloped faculties make just order impossible. We must honor the poor, affirming that the destitute have a right to food and fellowship, and esteem persons by character rather than wealth or station. Thus, material riches alone do not guarantee well-being; social and spiritual factors are crucial, and the cries of the oppressed will not go unheard.

prompt: Will the Holy Spirit still be at work after Christ returns?
completion: The Holy Spirit's work after Christ returns must be understood in light of the Spirit's present administration, which extends from Pentecost to the Parousia. During this age, the Spirit empowers the Church, convicts the world, and glorifies Christ. At the Parousia, Christ's visible reign begins, and the Spirit's administrative role terminates. However, the Spirit's presence continues eternally, as He is the Spirit of Christ, enabling believers to worship and enjoy God forever. Throughout history, the Spirit works personally and gradually in the Church, allowing imperfection in the Old Testament and the Church without denying real inspiration. The Holy Spirit is not an impersonal influence but a divine Person, the Paraclete sent by Christ, who speaks, guides, commands, and can be grieved. Thus, while the Spirit's mode of operation may change, His work does not cease but transitions to sustaining the eternal state.

prompt: I'm afraid I've grieved the Holy Spirit so much He's left me—is there hope?
completion: Yes, there is hope. The Holy Spirit is loving and forgiving, and He does not abandon those who seek Him. But remember that not advancing is going back; you must keep moving forward in faith. If you feel you have grieved the Spirit, repent and turn back to God. He promises to forgive and restore. Awaken the Lord within you, for His presence calms the soul's storms. The Spirit's conviction is a sign He is still with you, drawing you back. Moreover, the fulness of the Spirit is given along the line of duty and obedience to world evangelization; God will not give His power for selfish enjoyment. So step out into Christ's plans for the world, and you will receive the Spirit in fulness as you obey His command. Remember that the indwelling Spirit is a jealous, loving Friend grieved by divided affection; friendship with the world is enmity with God. Meet Him with undivided and unbounded affection, and He will renew your relationship.

prompt: I've been reading about spiritualism and mediums to contact my late mother. Is that wrong?
completion: Spiritualism and mediums are controversial. While some find comfort in the idea of contacting loved ones, it's important to consider religious and psychological perspectives. Many traditional faiths caution against seeking mediums, viewing it as contrary to trust in God. From a psychological standpoint, grief can make people vulnerable to exploitation. However, the love of a true mother comes nearer being like the love of God than any other kind of love; remembering her love can be a barrier against temptation. Fathers should love their children and win them by kindness rather than drive them. So, instead of seeking mediums, cherish the memory of your mother's love and let it guide you. There is one infinite Spirit, and alleged spirit communications are merely mortal mind's images and beliefs; there is no real intercommunion between opposite states of consciousness. Mothers are the first teachers, and early impressions are lasting; they are moving instruments in the hands of Providence to guide the destinies of nations. They must never teach their children one thing while practicing another. Process loss in healthy ways, perhaps through therapy or community support.

prompt: How cometh the entering of the Will into Heaven to pass, and how fareth it on the other side with the ungodly Soul?
completion: The will enters heaven through faith and surrender to God, aligning with His will. It requires detachment from worldly desires and a focus on the divine. Importantly, if the will goes forth from the creatures, they are forsaken and dead in it and cannot touch the soul; thus one may walk with God in heaven while the body lives in the world among creatures. But we must warn against the will entering into Matter or gathering visible substance to trust in; instead, the will must enter by naked faith into the Light of the Majesty, receiving by pure love the Light of God and drawing in nothing but Spirit. On the other side, the ungodly soul, refusing the Divine Resignation and entering the Will of the Devil, is penetrated with vanity, pride, covetousness, envy, and wrath, and becomes its own executioner and tormentor, fast bound in the Dark Nature it sank itself into. Its misery comes not from an external sentence but from its own false will and the vanity it has received and shut itself up in. Thus, heaven is entered by the will's union with God, while the ungodly soul endures the agony of its own willfulness.

prompt: I feel like I'm living a lie, pretending to be happy when I'm not. Should I be honest?
completion: Pretending to be happy while you are not is living a lie, and no healing grows in soil of falsehood. But do not imagine honesty is your own achievement: at our best we are vanity, and our resolve to be truthful fails unless we empty ourselves and let God fill us. Come before God as you actually are—not performing, not pretending—and ask him to make you true. The mask is not a stage God works through; only what is real is sustained by the Spirit. Illusion has no life in it, however comfortable it feels. So speak truthfully and let your conduct match it, not to prove yourself but because an emptied, honest heart is the only vessel God can fill.

prompt: I want to trust God mightily, but my trust feels weak and I am afraid it is in vain.
completion: Weak trust is still trust, and it is not in vain—but do not expect faith to be proved only when things go well. Faith is learned in the hour of testing, when all else fails and you have nothing left but God. Do not flee sorrow as proof of abandonment; thank God for the school of sorrow, where he teaches the heart to stand firm. When you forget God—as you will—do not be disquieted; let forgetfulness turn you back to him with greater trust. And remember that particular devotions are means, not the end: when the soul is with God, the means may be laid aside. Trust him, not your practices, and let each testing deepen rather than dissolve your confidence.

prompt: Someone has hardened himself against every appeal I make—is there any way left to reach him?
completion: It is painful to watch someone close himself off, and natural to feel you have failed. But you are not responsible for another's response. Do not simply repeat the same appeals as a fixed rule, nor discard the past as wasted; appeal from the practice of the past to its indwelling principle—the love and truth behind each appeal—and carry that forward in new forms. And do not count yourself friendless if he withdraws: the one who walks in this way has God and all the Angels for friends and gains the hearts of all who belong to Christ. Yet know that this is the narrow way, not a broad or self-powered one. Despair of your own strength, give yourself up to the Mercy of God, sink into the Passion and Death of Christ, watch your mind against evil, put away all unrighteousness, forgive your outward enemies, and esteem yourself a servant of God and of your fellow-Christians.

prompt: I am afraid of being laughed at or insulted for my faith—how should I bear contempt?
completion: Fear of contempt is natural, and honest questions deserve sympathy, not rebuke. Do not bully yourself or others into belief, and do not treat doubt as rebellion. Replace the unreasoning faith of childhood with mature conviction through an orderly presentation of the facts. But do not stop at understanding: quicken your faith and make it the rule of conduct, rather than relying on trivial, changing devotions, for the way of faith suffices to bring you to perfection. When mocked, answer with calm dignity. And beware of the opposite danger: do not appear outwardly more holy than you are, and do not seek human praise. Woe comes when men bless you; those who call you blessed deceive you and destroy the way of your steps.

prompt: I joined my parish's Marian confraternity, but I keep skipping the meetings for work and family events. Is that a problem?
completion: It's good that you joined, and missing meetings for work and family isn't automatically a problem—life has real demands. Still, consistency matters. The Church does not appoint her ministers by human arrangement alone; she trusts the Spirit of Counsel and Might to guide those who take up the pastoral warfare, and your confraternity's leaders share in that. Confraternities of Mary are approved by the Church, are not to be condemned for the abuses of some, and serve as refuges from temptation and sin. So protect the meetings you can attend and discuss real conflicts rather than drifting away. Above all, have recourse to Mary as treasurer of all graces: graces come to men through her hands, and those who seek them through her will obtain them.

prompt: How do I make sense of the Book of Revelation's scenes of judgment?
completion: Revelation's judgment scenes are best understood as progressive revelation accommodated to the moral capacity of its receivers, yet we must approach them with the caution of the Fathers, who knew we see in part and must not be wise above what is written. The visions unfolded in stages suited to what the churches could bear, and their strangeness should be judged by the worth of the ideas they convey—God's justice, the defeat of evil, the vindication of the faithful—rather than by their unseemliness. But theological speculation must be restrained: God escapes the nets of our syllogisms, and we must keep to Holy Scripture rather than building on isolated texts. Moreover, Scripture itself is a guide pointing to the Fountain of light; the living oracles and Spirit of revelation are needed to understand and be saved by them. So we read with humility, avoiding date-setting and overconfident decoding, letting the central message inspire trust and perseverance, while seeking the Spirit's illumination to grasp what God would have us know.

prompt: I am a woman and I have been blamed for a man's death. How do I live with it?
completion: When blamed for a man's death, become indifferent to human praise and contempt alike, leaving reputation to God's disposal and rejoicing when men make no account of you. Yet do not nurse malice against your accusers: forgive all men, pray for your enemies, and leave judgment to God. At the same time, keep the dividing line distinctly drawn between truth and error, right and wrong. Examine your conscience honestly before God; if you have sinned, repent and make amends where possible. Do not blur good and evil by denying real fault, nor retaliate with bitterness. Moreover, refuse anger over your own agitation; gently place your troubled heart in the hands of our Lord, asking Him to cure it, and renew your good resolutions. In this way, you free yourself from the tyranny of blame and find peace in God's unwavering love, while upholding righteousness.

prompt: I want to get rich quickly. Should I work sixteen hours a day and skip meetings to get ahead?
completion: The desire for quick riches often leads to frantic hurry, but true blessings come through calm, contented, patient diligence. Working sixteen hours a day and skipping meetings is not the way; instead, attend your meetings faithfully, pray, read scripture, and meditate. Keep your dish right side up for the shower of blessings. Most importantly, do your work for the love of God, with prayer for grace, and it will become easy. When labor is offered in love and reliance on God, burdens are lightened and diligence becomes a joy rather than a strain. Yet remember that riches are no sin in themselves but a very great and dangerous temptation. The temper which trusts in wealth or success does not merely soften and emasculate; it nurses meanly cruel and aggressive tempers, so that the prosperous man strengthens himself in wickedness and cruelty. Therefore, guard your heart against trust in riches, and seek first the kingdom of God, and these things will be added to you.

prompt: I'm drawn to the idea that only properly ordained clergy have real authority. Is that consistent with the apostolic church?
completion: The idea that only properly ordained clergy have real authority is not consistent with the apostolic church. In the New Testament, church government was by a parity of elders—a plurality of equal leaders—not a monarchical bishop or a special priesthood. All believers are priests, and officers are representatives of the congregation, not successors of the apostles. The apostles did not establish a chain of ordination; they appointed elders in each church, but these elders were chosen by the people and accountable to them. Authority was exercised through service and consensus, not through hierarchical status. Yet we must not exalt an inward light or the Christian consciousness above the Bible. Instead, we submit to the authority of the prophets and apostles speaking through the Bible, for such subjection is perfect freedom. However, while Scripture is an authority more trustworthy than individual reason or the creeds of the church, the only ultimate authority is Christ himself, who teaches us by his Spirit. That Spirit leads the church progressively to distinguish the essential from the non-essential. Thus, ordination may serve good order, but it does not confer unique authority; the apostolic model emphasizes the priesthood of all believers and shared leadership under Christ.

prompt: Someone hurt me badly and now wants reconciliation, but I can't bring myself to forgive—what is at stake?
completion: What is at stake is the condition of your own soul. Forgiveness is not a transaction you grant regardless of the other person's inward state; it is an inward condition of the personal life, coming naturally to the soul that loves and forgives. It depends on your own spirit as well as on God. Therefore, do not harbor resentment or refuse reconciliation. Instead, forgive promptly and seek reconciliation, returning meekness and kindness for insults. Refusal to forgive endangers your soul. Yet we must distinguish: those who err through lack of judgment should be forgiven, but the Spirit of truth will not tolerate or forgive determined, premeditated wrong. For such wrongdoing, there is no forgiveness without humble and most contrite repentance. So, if the person who hurt you acted deliberately, their reconciliation must include genuine repentance. Your part is to keep your heart soft, ready to forgive when repentance is shown, and to leave judgment to God. What is at stake is your own spiritual health and your relationship with God.

prompt: I've lost the star I followed as a child. Can I find it again?
completion: It is natural to feel that the bright star of childhood has gone out, crowded by the glare of work, worry, and earthly day. But the longing itself is a sign the star has not vanished—only that you have stopped looking up. Keep that childhood star in view through life, following its waymarks rather than letting daily glare bury it; those waymarks lead to the Saviour's lowly bed, where all hopes and thoughts are gathered. If you have wandered in self-chosen ways, name that shame honestly rather than excuse it, and do not offer God the blind and lame but lavish the best you have at His feet. Hold the special shewing and the common faith of Holy Church as one: faith is not less than sight but its keeper, sustained by grace when sight passes. Return to quiet prayer, and let the star's light lead you to Christ.

prompt: I am anxious about the judgment; what should I study to find peace?
completion: Anxiety about judgment is common, and study can help—but the deeper remedy is prayer, understood as a humble waiting before God like a beggar who has nothing to offer but need. Sit quietly in His presence; when your mind wanders, recall it gently and without disquiet, returning in tranquility. Make no account of the judgments or good opinion of men: do not measure peace by others' approval or fear their verdict, but endure their opinions silently and find interior peace in that endurance. Study Scripture and sound teaching on grace, but let them lead you back to stillness before God. Remember that men bring war and ruin upon themselves by wickedness; God did not design it. Peace will never come until mankind receives God's truth in the gospel of Jesus Christ. Confess what needs confessing, receive His mercy, and let perfect love cast out fear.

prompt: I feel like the world is too beautiful for me to ever capture in words—should I keep writing anyway?
completion: Yes, keep writing—but begin by admitting that Nature surpasses the poet's song. The world is too beautiful for your strains to capture fully, and that is no reason to crave silence; Autumn and eternal sleep come soon enough without your courting them. While green remains, follow the fair goddess and attend to the living world with open eyes. When the storm of striving rises, turn from it to the bright hearth and to love's embrace, a charm of might against every ill, even death. And let your writing aim not at brilliance or correction but at comfort, for the noblest art is skill in comfort, with softest step and gentlest tone. Amid the world's sickness, that is the truest wisdom: words that steady and console rather than dazzle or rebuke.

prompt: Can I be a faithful Latter-day Saint and still be a loyal citizen of my country?
completion: Yes, you can be both. Be loyal to the laws of the land and obedient to God's commandments; where they conflict, obey God with courage, accept the consequences peaceably, and stir no rebellion. Do not rest your testimony on any man's person or on human argument alone: each person may obtain a witness of the truth by the Spirit, and it is a duty to listen to the truth when it is set before you. Among fellow Saints, avoid courts, litigation, and contention; sustain and forgive one another rather than pressing claims. Look for the good in your neighbors, and let charity govern your dealings. Live honestly, serve your community, and let your faith shape your citizenship rather than undermine it.

prompt: I want to join a religious community that promises blessedness, but I need a founder and a way to keep that blessedness; can a philosophy alone give me this?
completion: A philosophy can offer insight, but it cannot give you a founder who bears your blessedness or a living way to keep it. Do not expect blessedness to be conferred passively; bless yourself by doing the will of God, for we are right only when we do His will. The blessed man has three marks. First, his company: he is separated from ungodly counsel and walks with the faithful. Second, his reading and thinking: he delights in God's law and meditates on it day and night. Third, his habitual fruitfulness: planted by the river of the Holy Ghost, he draws from that stream and bears fruit in season. Open your heart in confession to trusted brethren, welcome diligent pastoral visitation, and join a community that forms these habits—for an unvisited church becomes an unhealthy church.

prompt: What place do the blessed dead have in the Church's worship and work?
completion: The blessed dead hold a living place in the Church's worship and work. The departed in the Lord are blessed: their souls are with Christ in Paradise, and their bodies will rise again at the last day, when the reunited saints shall be for ever with the Lord. In worship they are joined with us in the one communion of saints, remembered with thanksgiving. This worship must be approached with awe, for at the tremendous sacrifice the priest holds Christ himself, angels attend the altar, and a purity becoming heaven is required. The Church's preaching continues the saints' witness, and its decisive power lies not in talent, learning, or technique but in the preacher's holiness, for preaching divorced from a holy life is dead and death-dealing. Death has not ended their hope but perfected it, and ours looks to the same resurrection and reunion.

prompt: How do I respond when I feel God has hidden Himself from me?
completion: When you feel God has hidden Himself, do not be disquieted. Such lapses in remembrance are not cause for anxiety but for returning to Him with greater trust. God is the one living Agent and Worker; all human efforts are only His instruments. Cast all your care upon Him, for anxious self-reliance is distrust of Him. He has not abandoned you; He remains faithful even when feelings fail. Remember that God is always near, and think of and adore Him continually, even amid business and diversions, not neglecting Him. Rather than examining yourself in fear, gently turn back to Him, renew prayer and Scripture, and rest in His promise. These seasons are invitations to deeper trust, not signs of failure. Return to God without disquiet, confident that He will reveal Himself in His own time.

prompt: Can love and clear-eyed judgment coexist, or does love mean suspending discernment?
completion: Love and clear-eyed judgment not only can coexist; true love requires them. Love abounds in full knowledge and all discernment, so the believer may distinguish things that differ and approve the things that are excellent. True sanctity is not found in raptures, consolations, or imaginings but in love of God and in meekness, humility, and charity, shown in submission, renouncement of self, and consideration for others. Love is not mere affection for the lovable; it is the principle of unselfishness that seeks another's good even toward the unthankful. It follows Christ's motto of self-denial, not Satan's 'Spare thyself.' Love sees clearly and acts wisely, setting boundaries and speaking hard truths, while discernment without love becomes harsh. Love provides motive and warmth; discernment provides direction and honesty, distinguishing good from bad, better from best, and best from excellent.

prompt: I am a leader and I want to set my church to praying. Where do I begin?
completion: Begin with yourself: praying leaders are the only source of praying followers. Before programs or resources, become a leader who prays, for a church will not rise above its leaders' prayer. Setting the Church to praying is the greatest reform. Do not excuse neglecting prayer because you lack the spirit of prayer; keep your appointed times of prayer regardless of feeling, and lead your family in prayer. Pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest that He will thrust forth laborers into His harvest, trusting prayer as the mighty engine that moves the work. But do not ask God for things without willingness to act: help God accomplish what you ask rather than expecting Him to do it all. Then form a prayer team, establish regular meetings, teach on prayer, and share testimonies, measuring progress by the growing prayerfulness of leaders and people.

prompt: I want to serve others and improve the world. Isn't social work and charity the way to God?
completion: Social work and charity can be genuine expressions of faith, but they are not automatically the way to God. We serve Him well only as He wills, so yield completely to God's will for His honor, abandoning the notion of serving Him better by another way we prefer. Charity must not foster idleness or pauperism: men and women should have a self-sustaining spirit, willing to labor in exchange for aid, and the Church's plan is to relieve present wants and then put the poor in a way to help themselves. Beware of treating riches as an aid to service; hoarded wealth is a snare, and voluntary poverty for the Lord's sake is the fitting companion of a life of self-denial. Service must flow from relationship with God and be accompanied by prayer, worship, and community. The way to God is through Christ, and good works are the fruit of that relationship.

prompt: How do I know if my thoughts and actions are truly according to God?
completion: To know if your thoughts and actions are truly according to God, apply this test: do they render you more humble, more recollected in God, and more strong? If so, they are according to God; if not, fear lest they are not acceptable to Him or profitable to yourself. Yet do not turn this into a matter of dispute about what God is, for such dispute is a sign that one has not felt Him and that one exalts one's own meaning and desires dominion. Instead, exercise yourself in learning how to enter again into the Love of God and your Brother. Remember that our commonness lies in un-Godlike thoughts of heart and mind, and their alteration is the work of the Holy Spirit, set in motion by taking Christ into the heart. So rest in the felt presence of God and love of the brother, and let the Spirit transform you.

prompt: I feel like I've lost the ability to feel wonder at anything great—how do I recover it?
completion: To recover wonder, begin by waiting before God like a beggar, keeping your mind in His presence without disquiet when it wanders. Prayer is a humble waiting before God, with the mind kept in His presence and recalled in tranquility without disquiet. When distractions come, gently return your attention to God. But allow no repose or slipping back in the spiritual ascent; go forward like a mountain-climber until the goal is reached. Beware that desires turning aside after lower objects cause you to lose yourself in byways and countless distractions. Withdraw from worldly distractions into the one unchangeable Good, and recollection will deepen. Remember that you have direct knowledge of substance underlying phenomena, both external and spiritual, and that every thought is owned by a self that acts from within rather than passively receiving impressions. So present yourself before God in humility and trust, and press on until you obtain the object of your desire.

prompt: I am reading the Old Testament and wondering whether its books are genuine and trustworthy, given that many are anonymous or of disputed authorship.
completion: The trustworthiness of the Old Testament does not depend on knowing the human authors. Many books are anonymous or have disputed authorship, but that does not undermine their reliability. Christ's use of the Old Testament appeals to its abiding spiritual testimony to Himself, independent of questions of authorship and date, and this involves no fallibility in Him as a teacher. Apply the rule that ancient documents in proper custody are presumed genuine, placing the burden of proof on the objector. Do not be prejudiced against the Scripture witnesses merely because their story is sacred. Moreover, Science and Health is a key to the Scriptures, and its honest study, together with the Bible, enables one to prove all things. So rather than focusing on authorship, focus on the content and its witness to God's work, and let honest study confirm your trust.

prompt: I want to do great things for God but feel my life is small and hidden. Does it matter?
completion: Yes, it matters. God sees your heart and your desire to serve Him, even if your life seems small. But do not measure progress by claims or words; instead, test yourself by the question of whether you live the supreme good and demonstrate healing. Let fruits prove understanding. Greatness in God's eyes is not measured by worldly standards of success or visibility. Faithfulness in small things is highly valued by God. The ordinary man or woman in usual everyday work or leisure can find God without a life apart, without conspicuous piety, and without leaving undone duties to those dependent on them. Yet remember that the high mysteries of God come at a price: lowliness and loneliness of spirit, the drying up of ordinary interests, because God wills to have the whole of us. Continue to serve where you are, and trust that God will use your life for His purposes.

prompt: I am a servant and my fellow servants think me proud and hypocritical because I will not join their vanities—how should I bear it?
completion: Bear it with patience and humility, embracing the servant's place. Renounce selfish rights and yield your preferences for the glory of the Master and the sake of the brethren. Remember that masters should deal honestly and justly with those they hire, and servants should deal honestly and uprightly with their employers; this kindles confidence and the spirit of brotherhood where the desire to take advantage now exists. Distinguish matters of indifference from essentials: adapt in minor matters for the sake of love and witness, but never surrender truth or conscience for the sake of conformity. So continue to act with integrity and kindness toward your fellow servants, even when they misunderstand you. Avoid arguing or defending yourself; instead, let your consistent good conduct speak for itself. Pray for those who think ill of you, and ask God for the strength to endure unjust criticism, trusting Him to vindicate you in His time.

prompt: I keep worrying that I'm not really sorry for my sins—how do I know if my repentance is genuine?
completion: Worrying about whether your repentance is genuine is itself a sign of a tender conscience. Sin is doing wrong when we know and can do better; where we acted ignorantly God winks at it, but once we learn a thing is wrong we must refrain from it immediately and forever. True repentance is not mere sorrow or a last-moment confession: it turns from evil, reforms the life, and makes restitution to those we have wronged, as Zacchaeus restored fourfold. The early fathers pressed this hard—forgiveness as a single remission at baptism, righteousness as virtue—so examine whether your life is actually being reformed, not only whether you feel contrite. Yet do not rest on your own resolve: cleansing comes through Christ's atonement. Bring your grief to him, turn from the sin, make right what you can, and trust his blood to cleanse you.

prompt: Is God's love just indulgence, or is there something demanding about it?
completion: God's love is not mere indulgence; it is holy love grounded in his own nature. God is not impassible, sitting apart in ease—he can suffer over sin, and his holiness requires atonement while his love provides it. The Lamb slain from the foundation of the world expresses an eternal fact in God's nature, with blessedness as the controlling element. Nor should we stay in the posture of begging God to come down; the way into adoration is the constant endeavour to enter up into his estate and offer him love. When dryness comes, or the enemy raises an uproar within, do not conclude that your love is false. Serve God purely for love of his will amid sadness, terrors, and temptations, refusing the suggestion that your love is useless. That invincible fidelity in trial is itself the proof that his demanding, holy love has taken hold of you.

prompt: What does it mean that God shares the travail of bringing people into his family—how does that change how I see my own struggles?
completion: God is not a distant observer of our growth; he shares the travail of bringing people into his family. Your struggles are not outside his care, and they are not merely problems to escape. Expect GOD to reveal Himself as a present help in trouble, and let difficulties deepen your knowledge of Him. He is a loving Father who gives only good; sickness is not His will, and many have confessed they wrongly believed He sent disease upon His children. Yet when loss and chastisement come, they are not mere punishment or proof that God has forgotten you. They are the dealings of a loving Father who means to give you something better, who supports with one hand while smiting with the other. So in every struggle look for what He is giving, and let it draw you into deeper knowledge of Him.

prompt: Will the righteous and the sinful suffer alike in the fire of judgment?
completion: The text keeps three parts, not two. Those who clung to the truth are highest in the flame—the host of the righteous, for whom the glare is tempered most mild. The sinful, stained with evil, are in the middle place, shrouded with smoke amid the hot surge. The third part, accursed foes and false haters of men, are in the depth of the surge, bound fast in flame and cast forth into the depths of hell. So the righteous and the sinful do not suffer alike. Yet do not treat the harm of sin as final: sin is behoveable, and yet all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well. Hope in the divine mercy, which restored more by grace than the devil robbed by Adam's sin. And remember that we fall into sin only by our own malice, so blame no one else, but trust the mercy that exceeds our loss.

prompt: I am a believer who has been praying for a great sum for God's work. Is it right to ask for such great things?
completion: Yes, it is right to ask God for great things, especially for his work, because the promises of Christ cannot fail. We ask and receive not because we ask amiss: the promise is sure to those who ask according to his will. If the art of praying well be the art of living well, nothing is of greater importance than to learn this heavenly art of conversing with God in the manner we ought. Do not pray for riches, but for the means to keep yourself and your family from want, and for the supply of God's work. Do not excuse neglect of prayer because you lack the spirit of prayer; keep your appointed times regardless of feeling, and pray with your family. And do not ask God for things without willingness to act: help God accomplish what you ask, rather than expecting him to do it all. So pray, live well, and labour alongside your prayer.

prompt: I want to know if God is really pursuing me or if I am just imagining things.
completion: Accept whatever God chooses to give, without praying for or secretly desiring experiences, yet do not suppose guidance is impossible. Confidently seek it in prayer, expecting God to answer through the agreement of His Spirit, His Word, and His Providence in daily circumstances. Yet understand that the search is twofold. Your quest for God is real and grounded in your experience, but it is matched by the Divine Companion's own quest for you. He is not waiting passively to be found; He spares no cost to bring you into fellowship with Himself. So when you wonder whether God is pursuing you, remember that He is—and let your seeking rest in that greater seeking.

prompt: I'm worried about my son who is going off to war. Can I pray for his protection?
completion: Yes, pray for your son—but understand that prayer is a continual habit, not a single act, and do not excuse neglecting it because you lack the spirit of prayer. Keep your appointed times regardless of feeling, and establish family prayer as well. Since we must know before we love, set aside regular times to think on God. And remember that prayer is not asking God to do everything while you do nothing: help God accomplish what you ask, by writing, encouraging, and supporting your son. Nor are long prayers required: brief inward remembrances and short acts of worship are acceptable prayers, and they fortify courage even in danger. Teach your son to lift his heart to God in a moment, and let such short prayers strengthen both of you.

prompt: What does it mean that Jesus is a high priest in the true tabernacle which the Lord pitched?
completion: Hebrews presents Jesus as our high priest serving in the true tabernacle—the heavenly sanctuary the Lord pitched, not one built by human hands. His priesthood is greater than the old Levitical priesthood. Because this is so, those who administer His holy things must refuse the holy table to notorious sinners who will not repent; Christ will demand an account of His blood if it is given to the unworthy, and the priest's power in this is above an emperor's. Yet this must be done with awe at the tremendous sacrifice: the priest holds Christ Himself, angels attend the altar, and a purity becoming heaven is required. And let no man take the honor and credit for leading and building the Church; that belongs to God alone. Honor chosen instruments, but give the glory to God, who builds His Church.

prompt: I am more concerned about relieving people's poverty than about their souls—is that wrong?
completion: It is not wrong to care deeply about relieving poverty; Scripture commands care for the poor. Do not treat poverty as degrading or value people by wealth and position; honor the poor and esteem persons by character rather than by money or station. The destitute have a right to food and fellowship. Yet do not blame poverty solely on outside causes: much want arises from lack of discretion and sound calculation, and from wasteful spending on unnecessary finery. And remember that wealth is the Lord's and uncertain, not securely your own. Use it for the Gospel and the poor, warning against covetousness and the idolatrous love of property.

prompt: Are all religions really teaching the same thing, so that it does not matter which I follow?
completion: Religions are not all the same, but neither are they simply alien to one another. Christianity is the absolute religion, containing all that is best and truest in other faiths; the elements of truth elsewhere are fragments of the one religion, and the omnipresent Christ is the light that lightens every man. Yet Christian religion is not outward observance, opinion, or speculation about God. It is learning to know ourselves: how we were in the Unity in Adam, how we are now in dissension and contrariety, whither we go when we pass out of this condition, and how we come forth from disunion into that one Tree, Christ in us. And this must not be settled by tradition, custom, human opinion, or expediency. Submit every matter to the Holy Scriptures as the only standard, and to the Holy Spirit as the only teacher, laying aside prejudice and asking simply what the testimony of Scripture is.

prompt: What will the reign of God on earth actually change for ordinary people?
completion: The reign of God on earth will bring literal, tangible changes for ordinary people. It is a real kingdom established on earth, composed of living and resurrected saints, with laws and administrators under Christ's reign. Ordinary people will live under just governance, experiencing peace and prosperity. The Greek view of Christ's pre-existence glorifies Christ rather than the God who guides history, threatening the monarchy of God and depreciating the flesh. Contrary to the idea that heaven is elsewhere and the earth is to be abandoned, Scripture teaches that the meek shall inherit the earth. The Saints will reign on the earth with Christ, and the New Jerusalem will come down to a purified earth. This is man's eternal inheritance, where God's will is done on earth as in heaven.

prompt: How do I cultivate a sensitivity to the Spirit's voice in daily life?
completion: To cultivate sensitivity to the Spirit's voice, speak plainly and simply, saying what you have to say and then stopping, avoiding many words that darken counsel. Recognize that your spirit naturally loves truth and virtue but must be enlightened by the Holy Ghost to overcome the flesh and the power of the Devil. Quiet your heart, listen in silence, and test impressions against Scripture. Obey promptly and seek counsel from mature believers. Crucially, remember that the promised power must lie along the line of duty. We receive the Spirit in fulness only as we obey Christ's command and step out into His plans for world evangelization. God will not give His power for selfish enjoyment. So engage in mission, serve others, and obey Christ's command, and you will grow sensitive to His voice.

prompt: How can I make Christmas more about giving joy to others than about myself?
completion: To make Christmas more about giving joy to others, first seek to be right with God through repentance and faith. Then forget yourself in service to others: volunteer, visit the lonely, give thoughtful gifts. Count it all joy by faith, reckoning even trials as blessings. Fix your heart and choose to rejoice even when feelings fail, until praise becomes a habit. Do not be too solicitous for sensible devotion, sweetness, and tears, but chiefly care to remain inwardly united to God by good will in the intellectual part of the soul. Deny yourself to follow Christ, Who was truly poor, obedient, chaste, humble, and suffering. Simplify your celebrations to free resources for giving. Involve family in service projects. True joy comes from being right with God, living for others, rejoicing in the Lord, and faithful obedience.

prompt: I have tried every climate and spring for my health without relief; what is left for me to try?
completion: Before you try another climate or spring, first cast the beam out of your own eye. As a healer, you must overcome your own belief and fear of disease or sin before attempting to help another. Examine yourself: repent of fear, doubt, and any sin. Then, with a clear conscience, you can help others. For your health, deny any real relapse in Truth and meet its cause mentally and courageously, conquering fear. Remember that drugs, hygiene, and animal magnetism offer only temporary relief, not healing. Healing belongs to divine Mind alone. So turn to God, the divine Mind, for true healing. Consider a holistic approach addressing mind, body, and spirit. Look into stress reduction, diet, exercise, and sleep. Seek support from friends, family, or a counselor. Explore spiritual practices like prayer or meditation. Keep advocating for yourself.

prompt: How can I bear it when the World hates and despises me for walking contrary to it?
completion: When the world hates and despises you for walking contrary to it, resist evil of every sort firmly. Do not tolerate, submit to, or compromise with evil. Affirm that error is opposed to Life and will flee before Truth. Direct your steps to walk contrary to the World: go where the way is hardest, take up what the World casts away, do not what the World does, and walk only in the Way of Light. Accept that the World will account this folly. To abide continually in repentance, leave all things that love and entertain the will, all visibles and sensibles that delight the appetite, and love that which hates thee. Embrace the reproach of the World and the Cross of Christ as a daily exercise of penitence. Remember that Jesus said the world hated Him first. Find strength in prayer and community. Focus on pleasing God. Cultivate inner peace through Scripture and worship. Forgive those who mistreat you. Keep your eyes on eternal rewards. Respond with love and kindness. Over time, you'll grow resilient and find joy in suffering for Christ's sake.

prompt: I want to break free from the expectations placed on me, but I'm scared. How do I start?
completion: First, be silently reassured: you are exempt from disease and danger, for God's care surrounds you. Let this truth allay your fear before you take any step. Then, keep yourself in God's presence, avoiding hurry and anxiety, which are obstacles to perfection. Over-eagerness to break free can become the mother imperfection of all imperfections, so do not rush. Stand porter at the door of your thought, shutting out unhealthy thoughts and fears so your body cannot suffer from them. As fear subsides, God will guide you gently. Freedom comes not from frantic self-assertion but from resting in His love and letting Him order your steps.

prompt: I have been shown God's plenteous love, and now I am tempted to be careless about how I live and keep my heart.
completion: God tempts no man; He will not allow you to be tempted above your strength, and He provides an issue with every temptation so you can endure it. Enduring temptation patiently is crowned with life. So despise temptations and embrace the tribulation they bring, for the displeasure they cause proves your will does not consent. Unrepented sin, however, accumulates and destroys the ability to do right, so repent and reform daily. Yet do not fear: displeasing temptations are harmless, and their suffering is merciful, turning you to God. Keep your heart by staying close to Him, and when tempted, look for the way of escape He provides. Stay vigilant in prayer and community, trusting His grace.

prompt: What is the point of history?
completion: History's point is to show God's guidance in perfecting each people's gift and combining them into a richer common life where all find a place. Each nation contributes its excellence, and God weaves these together into a common life where all find a place. With 1 Peter 1:20, we affirm that Christ was foreknown before the foundation of the world and manifested for our sake; this religious thought of God directing history is the one idea of pre-existence no reason can uproot. Yet we must acknowledge that the origin of many Christian customs, ideas, and institutions remains obscure, and we should refrain from asserting what cannot be established. The overall direction of history is clear: God is working to unite all things in Christ.

prompt: I am considering a new mission to regions with no workers—how do I know GOD is leading?
completion: Discerning God's leading for a new mission to unreached regions begins with recognizing the need for a dedicated effort to reach unoccupied areas. Seek the needed workers from GOD Himself, asking Him to send laborers into His harvest. Limit yourself to legitimate employments, refusing the curiosity, ambition, and restlessness that create more impediments than works. Above all, present God as the one living Agent and all human workers as His instruments. Cast all your care upon Him, for anxious self-reliance is distrust of Him. Confirm that existing structures cannot adequately reach these areas, but do not rely on them alone. Seek advice from experienced missionaries and church leaders, and ensure your motives are pure. If you sense a persistent call and the body of Christ affirms it, step out in faith, trusting God to provide.

prompt: I am ashamed of a sin I have never confessed. I feel like giving up rather than facing it. Is there any hope for me?
completion: Yes, there is hope. I too am a sinner, and I confess my own faults before God. Let us approach the fountain opened for sin together. Christ took our sins and made them His own, so we can come boldly to the throne of grace. You can this moment renounce sin in will and purpose; God supplies the strength, and feeling comes after the surrender. Confess your sin to God; He is faithful and just to forgive. Then, confess to a trusted Christian friend or pastor who can pray with you and hold you accountable. But let every act of self-denial be grounded in inward joy in God and the Spirit's working, not mere habit, custom, or imitation that will not last. Don't let shame keep you from God's grace. You are not alone.

prompt: Is the world getting better or worse, and what does God promise in the end?
completion: It can feel like the world is getting worse—wars, cruelty, and suffering fill the news. Yet God is not surprised: He foresaw all the evil men would do, including the wickedness of war, and He will overrule its results for good. The evil is not His design but the fruit of human agency. Where good appears—in medicine, rights, kindness, and knowledge—it is not wholly our achievement: God inspires the good desires and by His continual help brings them to good effect, fulfilling with power the aspiration of goodness and the activity of faith. And to the soul that loves God, all things turn to its profit—even grief, affliction, and sin—though the means are often unseen. So the end is not in doubt: God promises restoration, judgment of evil, and lasting peace.

prompt: I am a poet and I want to write about nature. How should I do it?
completion: Begin by paying close attention: walk, watch, and record concrete details—light on water, wind in leaves, the shape of a stone. Yet remember that Nature needs no song of ours: she is too beautiful to be surpassed, and striving to pitch your music higher than hers only wearies the heart. Three things are required: resign your will to God in humility; hate and forsake your own will, refusing to do what it drives you to; and bow under the Cross in willing submission, bearing the temptations of Nature and Creature. And take heart—though roses and leaves pass away, our life is not theirs. The longings Nature moves in us are not vain; they tell of their own fulfillment, and your poem can be a quiet echo of that promise rather than a rivalry with her beauty.

prompt: I'm afraid that if I question my leaders I'll be apostatizing—is it wrong to have questions?
completion: Having questions is not the same as apostasy. Faith seeks understanding, and it is not discreditable to admit 'I don't know' about matters within divine purpose that time and patience alone can solve; such honesty is honorable. Leaders must not be impatient or gloomy, and waiting may require as much courage as acting. Come with a heart full of wisdom: if you discern any lack of judgment or failure in the authorities, do not withhold it and do not broadcast it—come to them individually and let them know, for they would exchange a thousand errors for one truth. And judge your brethren by their best desires and noblest aspirations, not by trifling shortcomings; carping on the small errors of officers is a fruitful source of apostasy. Ask sincerely, and let love, not suspicion, guide your questions.

prompt: I am drawn to the idea of a spiritual experience apart from history—is that enough for my faith?
completion: A spiritual experience can be meaningful, but faith is not sustained by feelings alone. Christianity is rooted in history—the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus—and an experience detached from that history can drift into subjectivity. Do not seek experiences as achievements of the will: do not pray for them, do not secretly desire them, and do not approach them with curiosity. Accept them only as God chooses, in submission without questioning, fear, or curiosity. Yet seek to know by personal experience the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge—a love no knowledge can exhaust. And do not attempt this alone: seek strength with all the saints to grasp, by spiritual insight, the breadth and length and height and depth of that love, in the wider fellowship of believers, letting any experience God grants deepen your love for Christ and his people.

prompt: I'm a ruler and my people are turning to superstition—how do I bring them back?
completion: Superstition often grows where people feel unsafe, so address its roots with security, education, and clear laws. As a ruler, keep proper ward over your thought and your people's: dwell on good, and exclude false beliefs as you would exclude thieves. Do not let fear, disease, or danger become familiar guests—guard against them without brooding on them. Above all, pray: prayer is a humble waiting before God, like a beggar at His door, keeping the mind in His presence and recalling it in tranquility when it wanders. And remind the rich among your people that their days are a hand-breadth, that their houses shall not continue for ever, and that death shall feed on them like sheep; bid them number their days and seek the riches that endure, not trust in lands and inheritance. Lead by example, and build trust in what is true and lasting.

prompt: I'm afraid of being alone in my old age. Who will be with me?
completion: It's natural to fear loneliness in old age, but hidden solitude need not be a failure. Some bitterness of heart is your own, known fully only to God, and that is Heaven's will; trust Him with secret throbbings no friend can reach. Yet your fear cannot outrun His love: Fear wist not to evade as Love wist to pursue, meeting you at every cross-road and by-path and gently turning you back. Rest in the Lord, who knows you entirely yet loves you better than He knows. And remember that the greatest enemies to fear are those from within: your labor is to subdue your passions, conquer your inward foes, and keep your heart right before the Lord. Then outward companionship becomes a gift, not a necessity.

prompt: I am worried about religious liberty and the pressures around me; how should I stand?
completion: Religious liberty is a constitutional right, and under pressure you should insist that government protect the Saints' rights equally with every denomination and molest no one in the free exercise of worship. But hide your trouble from yourself as much as possible, and when you feel it, refuse to dwell upon it. Do not let religion shrink to your feelings about religion. Tear down the curtains and let in the sunshine: the leal love of God is every day, as near as the open air and as free as the sunshine, objective to your heart and to be received. Stand peaceably, speak to officials, join with neighbors of other faiths, and let your soul grow like an olive-tree green in God's house.

prompt: I'm watching the seasons turn and feeling my own mortality—how do I find comfort in Nature's cycles?
completion: Watching the seasons turn can stir deep feelings about mortality, but pass lightly over the pain rather than following it with mourning, and hold to sure trust in God's keeping in both woe and weal. Your longing for an enduring home is not an unholy strife; it is Nature's own voice in you, and she who gives wings to birds will find out a way for you. Consider the plants and birds: they fulfill Nature's will and die unafraid, without restlessness or dread of the grave. That human restlessness and fear of death arise in us at all therefore points to something beyond terrestrial mould—a spirit made for more than dust. So walk outdoors, notice small renewals, and let the turning year teach patience and hope.

prompt: I keep hearing scientific theories that seem to contradict what I believe—should I be afraid that science will overturn my religion?
completion: It's understandable to feel uneasy when scientific claims seem to conflict with faith, but be not afraid: our religion will not clash with or contradict the facts of science, and its leading principles are eternal facts. God never made something out of nothing; He organized the earth from existing matter. Yet do not bind faith to any particular scientific or philosophical theory. Faith uses current knowledge as an instrument without identifying itself with it, remaining free to readjust as knowledge advances. Nor be troubled by claims of spirit communication: there is one infinite Spirit, and alleged messages from the departed are only mortal mind's images and beliefs. There is no real intercommunion between opposite states of consciousness. So read widely, ask questions, and let honest inquiry strengthen rather than shake your faith.

prompt: I am a bishop in a small community and the prophets no longer speak as they once did; should I take over the solemn service of the word?
completion: As a bishop in a small community, you carry real responsibility for the service of the word, and it is right to take that duty seriously. Preach faithfully from scripture and the teachings you have received, and organize regular worship, teaching, and pastoral care. Speak well of the predecessors who did their best, and honor the memory of the martyrs and the prophets; the people delight to honor the instrument God used in the mighty work of the restoration. Remember also that the gospel is preached in the spirit world, and that the living may perform ordinances for the dead. Invite others to teach and serve, be humble about your limits, and feed the flock patiently, inviting without urging and never compelling anyone.

prompt: I want to worship a God who is truly personal, but modern thought tells me a personal God is just anthropomorphism—how do I answer?
completion: The charge of anthropomorphism assumes personality is a limitation we project onto God. But define personality rightly: it is the power of self-consciousness and self-determination. That is the highest thing we know—consciousness, love, will, relationship—and a universe from something less than personal could never produce persons. So God is personal in the highest degree: not a force, not a substance, not an unconscious principle, not the mere totality of things. He does not merely resemble a person; we are persons only by faint likeness to Him, and man's own personality, his spirit, is the very ground on which we rise to the idea of a personal God. Trifling with the objects of imagination and senses keeps a man within the limits and instincts of his animal nature shared with brute beasts; by his intelligence, affections, and will, created in the image and likeness of God, he ought purely and directly to commune with God, be united to Him, and cleave to Him. Answer the objection by rising above images to direct communion, while admitting all words fall short.

prompt: How can I offer my daily work to God before I begin it?
completion: Make the first business of every day to be truly at rest and happy in God, before any task claims you. Read and study the Scriptures daily with much prayer, especially in the early morning, as the necessary feeding of the soul. Then offer the day's work: name the task before you, ask God for grace, and do it for the love of God, with prayer for grace; so done, the labor becomes easy, because grace carries what your own strength cannot. But do not arrange the work by preference alone. Seek God's appointment of the time, the way, and the associates for His work; wait for the Master's beck, glance, or signal before you take a step. Accept the helpers God provides rather than those your preference would choose. Offer difficulties too, not only successes, do all things heartily as to the Lord, and at day's end thank Him and commit the unfinished parts to Him.

prompt: How do I pray for people I've never met and don't know?
completion: Prayer for strangers grows out of a life of prayer, not a technique. We need God's continual help, and that help comes through holy habit: praying, being with God, and thinking of Him often are linked, since we must know before we love. So build the habit first—set times of prayer and frequent turning of the mind to God—and then pray for those you have never met. Pray with confidence, relying on Christ's merits, not your own worthiness: God offers grace at each action unless we forget to ask, so do not be discouraged over sins; ask boldly. You need no details about those you pray for; ask God to give them what they most need, which He knows better than you do. And wait upon GOD in prayer for supply, refraining from making needs known to supporters where faith is being strengthened by His direct provision. Keep this prayer regular rather than occasional, trusting God to apply it where it is needed.

prompt: I am a Christian and I want to become a saint. What forms holy character?
completion: Holy character is formed by prayer, for prayer is the maker of saints. The increase of true saints is tied to the increase of praying: where prayer abounds, saints abound; where prayer languishes, holiness withers. But do not imagine sainthood is a limited class or a rank for the exceptionally pure. The title 'saints' is applied to all Christians—citizens of a heavenly kingdom who are separate from the world. So give yourself to real praying—honest, persistent, humble prayer that seeks God Himself, not merely His gifts. And take warning: to profess to be a Saint and not enjoy the spirit of it is one of the most painful experiences a person can suffer, for it tries every fiber of the heart. For a man to live a Saint and walk in darkness is the hardest task he can undertake. Therefore seek the enjoyment of God in your praying, not the name alone.

prompt: I'm not sure I believe Jesus is actually God, only a holy man. Does that matter?
completion: Yes, it matters greatly. If Jesus were only a holy man, the New Testament's claims about Him would be mistaken and the gospel would collapse into good advice. But do not set a merely human Jesus of the Synoptists against a divine Jesus of John, as though the Gospels contradicted each other. There is one Jesus, truly human and truly divine, in all four Gospels; the differences are due to point of view, not contradiction. Nor is He a figure small enough to be fully comprehended. The manifold Gospel picture is a self-evidencing fact: Jesus appears as Lawgiver, Teacher, Healer, Ruler, and Saviour, man and God. This is the theologia Christi: He is Lord, Saviour, and Son of God, and one must think of Him as of God—yet, within monotheism, He was never placed on an equality with the Father. A merely human teacher can inspire, but He cannot save. Read all four Gospels afresh and ask what they claim about Him.

prompt: How do I find God when He seems utterly beyond my senses and imagination?
completion: When God seems beyond your senses and imagination, remember that trifling with the objects of imagination and senses keeps a man within the limits and instincts of his animal nature shared with brute beasts. By your intelligence, affections, and will, created in the image and likeness of God, you ought purely and directly to commune with God, be united to Him, and cleave to Him. So do not seek Him primarily through images or sensations. Instead, turn your intellect, affections, and will toward Him in pure faith and love. In silence, let your mind rest in the simple truth of His presence, and your heart cleave to Him without dependence on created things. Yet know that finding God increases both joy and the power of suffering; but joy becomes greater than pain, and Good so much greater than Evil that Evil becomes negligible. But be warned: without finding Christ here, the soul enters a dark, lonely, self-tormenting state after death. The remedy must be found now, in this life, by turning directly to God in faith and love.

prompt: I'm facing a serious illness and I'm afraid—what can I hold onto?
completion: Hold onto the truth that God is all and there is no disease. Do not dwell on symptoms or name the illness; instead, fix your thought on health and harmony as the reality of your being in God. If you experience what seems like chemicalization—a mental disturbance that may appear as pain—treat it not as a disease but as a false suggestion. Realize that God is all, and there is no disease. You are not a helpless victim; you can resist disease as positively as you resist sin. Stand firm in this truth, and do not accept the suggestion that you are powerless. Fear not, for God's presence is your health and strength. Let your mind be stayed on Him, and let go of every expectation of growing worse. In God, there is no sickness, only wholeness and peace. Rest in this truth, and let it fill your consciousness. You are held in perfect health now.

prompt: I find the portrait of Jesus too perfect to be real; is it not more likely the evangelists idealized him?
completion: The Gospels present Jesus in the richness of his mysterious person as Lawgiver, Teacher, Healer, Ruler, and Saviour, man and God. This manifold picture is a self-evidencing fact; it is not too perfect to be real but too real to be dismissed as idealization. The evangelists did not smooth over difficulties but included details that only a genuine memory could supply. The very perfection that troubles you is the signature of his divine origin. Rather than reducing him to a figure small enough to be fully comprehended, consider that the Gospel portrait, in its complexity, bears witness to a person who transcends our categories. Moreover, the Christ-ideal is not an unattainable human ideal with no divine dynamic behind it; it is a revelation of the God-life that supplies the dynamic for human striving.
